item.title: New York Yankees vs. Los Angeles Angels: Series Preview
item.author: Joshua Diemert
item.content:encoded: After a hard-fought and ultimately successful four-game series with the Red Sox, winning three of four and securing the tiebreaker between the two teams, the Yankees head west to take on the dreadful Angels. Perhaps the most dysfunctional organization in baseball, which is saying something, Arte Moreno already cleaned house earlier this year firing longtime GM Perry Minasian, but the problem may be Moreno himself. On pace to lose 101 games, the Angels have wasted one of the likely last strong years of Mike Trout’s career, as well as a season where a number of pitchers proved themselves valuable.All of this is to say, this isn’t a trap series exactly, but it’s almost a trap series. After the endorphins of a good series against Boston wear off, the Angels are still a major league team, and anyone can beat anyone two out of three times. This is a series the Yankees should win, almost have to win to keep up the pressure on the Rays, but we’ve seen how those kind of circumstances can go awry in the past.vs. Mitch Farris (9:38pm Eastern)With Ryan Weathers on the IL, ERC will get at least two more chances to show off within the MLB rotation, his fourth stint with the team this year. His last outing was the longest of his young big league career, throwing six innings against the hated Astros, allowing a trio of runs and striking out a batter per inning. He looks to be beginning to find a handle on his pitch mix — the stuff has popped since his debut, but he’s shown a struggle with his control that seems to be improving. This is a pretty ideal setup for a young pitcher, as the Angels boast the third-worst offense in baseball.The Angels are a fascinating group because a man named Mitch Farris is expected to get the ball on Monday night. Farris has not started a game for the Angels this year, used in a variety of bullpen roles, and will be called on to give an abbreviated beginning. The left-hander features a slowwwwwww changeup that’s probably his best offering, but his fastball gets clobbered and the Yankees are in a bit of a lefty-slugging mood lately.Tuesday — Gerrit Cole vs. Walbert Ureña (9:38pm Eastern)In a season with so many incredible pitching stories, Gerrit Cole’s may be the second-most impressive after only Cam Schlittler. The veteran has hardly missed a beat in coming off of Tommy John surgery, already eclipsing his innings total from the 2024 season, throwing the ball harder than that year as well. His 3.19 ERA is backstopped well by a 3.37 FIP, and even if he’s slightly overperforming his HR-allowed baseline, what you’ve seen from Cole this year should mostly be believed.Walbert Ureña has looked like a real pitcher in his rookie season, throwing 118 innings of 2.94 ERA that might just net him some downballot Rookie of the Year votes if anyone is paying attention to Orange County. He doesn’t strike many out, and he walks a few too many, but in a ballpark that surrenders a lot of home runs he keeps it in the yard.Wednesday — Cam Schlittler vs. Grayson Rodriguez (9:38pm Eastern)It’s #CamBumpDay and with Cam tied with Dylan Cease at 5.1 fWAR, a big performance against a bad team could give him a slight edge in a dynamite AL Cy Young race. The added benefit for Cam is the game coming on the road, where eagle-eyed viewers have noticed a bit of a home/road split for the young righty:On paper, everything is set up for the youngster to pull just a bit ahead of Cease, but execution is still everything in this game.Rodriguez, the white-hot hope of the rebuilding Baltimore Orioles’ rotation, has flatlined in his first season with LA. Worth just half a win, a 6.04 ERA actually belies a FIP that’s stronger, but Grayson finds himself with poor results with an organization not known for improving performance, whistling past the proverbial baseball graveyard.

item.title: Defence spending is an insatiable beast. John Healey is right to tame it | John McTernan
item.author: John McTernan
item.content:encoded: The MoD grossly overspends then claims poverty. It’s high time it was treated as just one part of a progressive governmentNowhere was the confidence of the prime minister, Andy Burnham, shown as clearly as in his appointment of chancellor. There were weeks of speculation that this appointment was a choice between the energy secretary, Ed Miliband, and the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, with their contrasting political economies.It has been a hallmark of Burnham’s politics that he and his team do not get involved in briefing wars, so it was only when former defence secretary John Healey appeared in Downing Street together with Mahmood that it was clear that the prime minister had cut the Gordian knot, reassuring the markets with a cool, calm political operator with extensive Treasury experience as chancellor. Healey’s two years in defence meant that he would know both sides of the argument when it came to one of the biggest questions of the forthcoming budget: how to meet the bold new Nato defence spending targets without derailing the social ambitions of the Burnham government.Continue reading...

item.title: Without Tadej Pogačar, the Vuelta a España is about to descend into a level of chaos the peloton hasn't been used to for years – Philippa York analysis
item.content:encoded: The early action in the Vuelta a España had been as expected. Though it was a slight surprise that Tadej Pogačar seized the red jersey in Monaco, from then on it was highly likely he intended to keep the race lead all the way to Granada. Not that it was a stated objective to do so from start to finish, but seeing as he would be joining a select group of riders who had achieved that feat, it would have been rude not to seize the historic opportunity. Six days in, three stage wins, and an overall lead of nearly four minutes, the predictions of him reaching Granada with an advantage somewhere in double figures were looking ominously on track.A brief hailstone-induced interlude on stage 5 reminded everyone that nature was one of the uncontrollables and yet even that didn’t dent the certitude of the World Champion riding serenely to his first overall Vuelta victory. A bad day, an untimely mechanical, or a damaging fall were all possible, but given Pogačar had avoided all of those more typical incidents since he first emerged as a star, no-one really imagined them happening. The great Eddy Merckx may have been attributed with the saying 'La course en tête' but Tadej Pogačar and his UAE squad have refined it to such a degree that all challengers have largely been swept away when they dared to question how and when the Slovenian was going to win. Never out of position, never distracted, never in the wrong place at the wrong time. He and his teammates are the new standard upon which everyone is judged.It is shown in the rival team selections as they have paid homage to the seemingly inevitable Pogačar triumph by sending riders and squads with objectives adjusted to the situation. Most are a mix of talents, hopefully covering each possible scenario of the day-to-day racing without triggering a reaction from UAE and their overall mission. Those with sprinters planned to do their thing with the reassurance that UAE would be there in the background if there was a fire to put out. The WorldTour teams with breakaway specialists prayed they would be given a chance once a hierarchy was established in the points and mountains classifications. And the smaller outfits lined up for some television time and local interest. The few experienced GC riders present already suspected when they rolled down the starting ramp covering the steps of the Casino de Monte Carlo that they were racing amongst themselves for the lower places on the overall podium. An entirely realistic ambition and one not to be mocked as in years to come they could at least say they had photographic evidence they had been alongside one of the greatest ever riders, even if it was only briefly. Everything has now changedFor the sprint teams, there’s no relying on UAE to control anything for the two weeks ahead. The daily breakaway fights will go on for far longer. They will be harder to get in, as those same UAE riders who dragged the peloton for hours on end are now in amongst the attackers, just like they were in the Giro d’Italia when Adam Yates and Jay Vine abandoned. The mountains prize, which Pogačar would probably have won by being first on the mountaintop finishes, is wide open and even the green jersey will be looked at again as the racing descends into a level of chaos that the peloton hasn’t been used to for a number of years. That’s the daily expectation to which everyone has to reconfigure, and compared to the teams now involved for the overall honours, it’s a lot more complicated. Only Decathlon CMA CGA have what you might call a purely GC team and they have showed that when they have taken control of the peloton in the hope of giving Felix Gall the chance to distance his rivals. However, it’s not quite worked out as they hoped because the Austrian hasn’t always been up to the task. Tactically he makes mistakes, illustrated on the Aitana climb on stage 9 when he placed a number of accelerations and then didn’t follow Enric Mas when he attacked. His positioning is questionable and at times he’s been closing gaps instead of opening them. Steep climbs are no problem, but everywhere else his consistency is slightly lacking, and does the team have the depth to control the race for more than an hour at a time? It doesn’t look like it, but then we could have said that about Movistar before they were faced with the responsibilities of the race lead. On the roads of the Costa Blanca they stepped up and Enric Mas finished off their first defence of the red jersey brilliantly but again question marks remain on how they’ll cope for the next 12 stages. This is new territory for most of them and it comes with the added pressure of being a Spanish team leading their national Tour with a Spanish rider. The whole outfit is going to be under immense pressure; Directeur Sportifs, PR people, all the staff and of course the riders themselves. Thankfully, they have Enric Mas in super form and with enough experience to read the race well. The danger that's slowly developing is the continued presence of Primož Roglič, who knows this race inside out. The knowledge of winning here on four previous occasions is invaluable and he will be looking at the time trial three days before the end and thinking if he continues to improve then he has more than a chance of winning the overall. He hasn’t been wasting energy and always been well positioned which is just as well because in the final moments of the hard stages he has been without any teammates. Red Bull have been playing two games since the start: the sprints with Jordi Meeus and talking down the chances of Roglič for the overall, but now they have to adjust. Matthew Brennan looks to be the fastest if it’s not a kamikaze sprint scenario, therefore changing slightly to be more Primož-focused might be their best hope of success. In the white jersey classification Oscar Onley is a level above the others. However, Netcompany has a similar dilemma in terms of what are they racing for. Do they commit to the sprints with Ben Turner, put hopeful riders in the breakaways, or focus on the young Scot’s bid for at least a podium place. He’s been consistent but paid the price for trying to follow Pogačar on the crazy gravel climb heading to Castelló and never recovering. That was his worst day, though until Aitana he looked to be susceptible to the Felix Gall accelerations. That he was the only one able to stay with the race leader on the toughest day so far bodes well for what is to come. There are indications that Enric Mas has the edge on his GC rivals at the moment but it looks very likely we are going to have a chaotic and surprise-laden Vuelta from now. The so-called sprint days where Matthew Brennan would have cleaned up aren’t guaranteed to happen, the mountains could go any way as there’s no one contender strong enough to be in the escape each time and even Wout Van Aert in green isn’t a done deal. Lidl-Trek will have noticed Skjelmose is swinging on the back of the GC fight and it might be time to wake up Mads Pedersen. There are going to be a few more Bryan Coquard type moments in the weeks ahead.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to . item.title: The return of the Philly Cycling Classic is just what North American road racing has been longing for - Analysis
item.author: laura@cyclingnews.com (Laura Weislo)
item.content:encoded: It's been a long ten years since the last time the Philadelphia Cycling Classic was held, and the race's return was a smashing success for fans, riders and the city itself.I raced the old Liberty Classic three times back in the days when Ina Teutenberg and Petra Rossner were ripping everyone's legs off in the sprint and covered it for after recovering from my delusions that I could be a pro bike racer, so I've seen what this race meant to the North American peloton. It's difficult to put into words the amount of joy that fills my heart having it back.I felt the vibe from the moment I left the airport, and the train pulled into the city centre: the monuments of the very foundations of the United States tucked in between shining high-rises just feels very grounded in history and vibrant at the same time.That same feeling carried into the race morning as the women's peloton lined up along a stretch of the Benjamin Franklin Parkway lined with flags from around the world.It was an early start for the women at 8:30 a.m. but the crowds were already out and continued to grow throughout their race and the men's until Manayunk Wall and Lemon Hill were heaving with bodies - nearly equal to the height of the race's glory in the early 2000s.The top finishers had nothing but positive things to say about the race."It means everything, honestly," Sheehan told . "I saw this race before — I watched it growing up. The course, the environment here, the production of this event — it's so incredible, and all the people behind it."It's back in the US where I'm from, and it's so cool to have this here. Honestly, it means the world to me. There were so many emotions behind it today, just giving my everything."The steep Manayunk Wall creates an atmosphere that would be at home amid the most prestigious Classics."It was crazy! Honestly, it was phenomenal," Sheehan said. "Deafening loud, and you can't even... It's just such a rush. It's so present in the moment and just crazy chaos. It was like going on the Oude Kwaremont in [Tour of] Flanders! Full gas, so phenomenal."Donaldson agreed, saying the course had everything: "A big climb where the spectacle there was massive. The noise from the side of the roads — it doesn't get louder than that in cycling."The course, while mostly flat, is punctuated by the Manayunk Wall and two smaller climbs, Strawberry Hill and Lemon Hill, on the long 23.2-kilometre laps. A grand finale with two short laps including only Lemon Hill brings the race to a frenzy."It created some really aggressive racing," Donaldson said.Third-placed Jonas Rutsch agreed, saying, "The crowds were amazing, the spectators were amazing, and I think it was a really, really good comeback for this race."Third-placed Ella Sabo (Virginia's Blue Ridge TWENTY28) was ten years old the last time the Philly Classic was held, but was schooled in the race's history by her teammate Sofia Arreola, who raced the 2016 edition."It's a bridge to the past, and so [Arreola] made sure that we all soaked it in - enjoyed the environment. On that wall, there were so many people cheering. It was so insane, and so cool to take in the atmosphere that is the Philly Cycling Classic."Second-placed Alexandra Volstad (EF Education-Oatly) agreed, saying, "I love racing in the U.S. I was in Maryland last year, and I loved it, and I'm super happy to come back and race. The fans are next level. We always get people shouting on the streets, so it's pretty fun."The race was a bridge to the past and one across the oceans, too. There were 22 different nations represented in the women's race and 18 in the men's. The majority were from the United States in both races, but there is no doubt that those 53 women and 37 men all felt the surge of adrenaline of being a part of the biggest one-day bike race on their calendar.The fact that the organisers revived the old course - not the finish at the top of the Manayunk Wall - connected the modern event to the race's deep roots that date back to the mid-1980s.Back in 2004, this race meant the world to my tiny little amateur team from North Carolina. When our guest rider, the late Becky Conzelman, finished fourth the next year, it meant everything to us. She was a brilliant track and road rider and donated half of her winnings that day to our team - which helped fund most of our season.It's those riders who profit the most from a race like Philly. To the WorldTour teams, it's a nice chance for lesser-known riders to get a result, but mostly, it's a lot of travel for a one-day race. For smaller teams like Competitive Edge, Team Skyline or Team Winston Salem-Flow it's a massive opportunity to pitch the team's value to sponsors.There has been a lot of loss in the US road calendar, the demise of Tour of California, the USA Pro Challenge, Tour of Utah, and the Joe Martin Stage Race.Most of the WorldTour teams signed on to race here with the hopes of linking it up with the Maryland Cycling Classic, which never really got off the ground, being hampered by the pandemic and the Key Bridge tragedy.Finally, the return of the Philadelphia Cycling Classic gave us some good news, and the city delivered, going above and beyond expectations.Maybe it's because the people here know their history - they live steeped in 250 years of it - and they remember the good old days of this race. Even O'Brien's water hole on Manayunk Wall, which is a hose connected to a shower that hangs over the course for riders to cool themselves off, made a comeback.Philadelphia's leaders were incredibly generous to support this race in the same year the city also hosted the FIFA World Cup, and the fans came out in droves.Yes, there was a bit of an issue at the end of the men's race where lapped riders got in the way on Lemon Hill, but none of the riders I spoke to faulted the race organisation.The Philadelphia Cycling Classic reboot was a glimmer of hope in what has been a struggling road racing scene in the United States. Let's hope that the momentum continues, and we see more races coming back. Hello, Tour of California?For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to . item.title: The underlying upgrade that boosted McLaren's performance jump
Happy 30th Birthday, Cap!
item.author: Russell Richardson
item.content:encoded: Another Knick turns 30 this week! Days after Mikal Bridges reached the milestone, Captain Jalen Brunson celebrates his birthday today.Born August 31, 1996, in New Brunswick, New Jersey, the Knicks captain hits the 30-year mark about 11 weeks after delivering New York its first NBA championship since 1973 and earning Finals MVP. Brunson capped the series with 45 points in the championship-clinching Game Five against the Spurs, a Knicks Finals record. Not a bad year so far, all things considered.Brunson spent much of his childhood in southern New Jersey, including Cherry Hill, but his father’s basketball career kept the family moving. Rick Brunson played nine NBA seasons before transitioning to coaching, and the family eventually settled in the Chicago area, where Jalen attended Stevenson High School in Lincolnshire, Illinois. His mother, Sandra, played volleyball at Temple, where she and Rick were both student-athletes.At Stevenson, Jalen won a state championship and Illinois Mr. Basketball honors. At Villanova, he won national championships in 2016 and 2018, then became the consensus National Player of the Year as a junior. Dallas selected him with the 33rd pick in the 2018 draft, making him the last of four Villanova teammates called—a fact most definitely not lost on the uber-competitive Jalen. Over his first four seasons, he developed from a reserve into a central figure on the Mavs team that reached the 2022 Western Conference Finals.That summer, Jalen inked a four-year, $104 million contract with the Knickerbockers. The deal drew skepticism at the time, but Brunson quickly became the lead guard New York had spent decades seeking. He has since earned multiple All-Star and All-NBA selections, won the 2025 NBA Cup and its MVP award, and led the Knicks to the 2026 championship. On August 6, 2024, he became the 36th captain in franchise history.Before Jalen arrived, the Knicks had made the playoffs once in the previous nine seasons. Four years later, they were champions. Rick had played for the 1998–99 Knicks, the franchise’s previous Finals team, and Jalen completed the circle by leading the orange-and-blue past the Spurs, the same team that defeated Rick’s Knicks.The connections that brought Brunson to New York ran deep. Knicks president Leon Rose began his career as Rick’s agent and later represented Jalen. Tom Thibodeau had known Brunson since childhood through Rick’s NBA and coaching career, then hired Rick as an assistant in June 2022.And the personal connections continue: the front office not only traded for Jalen’s BFF and Villanova teammate, Josh Hart, but also surrounded him with former teammates Bridges, Donte DiVincenzo, and Ryan Arcidiacono. Sometimes it seemed like Leon’s long game was less about Jalen and more about luring Jay Wright to the NBA.Brunson practices his trade with strength, footwork, and deception. The 6-foot-2 left-hander changes pace, backs down larger defenders, pivots through traffic, and uses his body to create space. He absorbs contact, is a league leader in drawing charges, and is unafraid of smashing his way through much taller trees (especially French ones) or taking the game-winning shot as the clock expires. The steel in his veins and his big-shot helped make Captain Clutch the King of New York.At 30, the mileage from that contact-heavy style will be worth monitoring, and coach Mike Brown may increasingly look for ways to preserve his champion. The injuries start to pile up as the seasons tick by: Jalen has suffered numerous ankle sprains, fractured his left hand during the 2024 playoffs, and played through a left wrist injury during the 2026 championship run before undergoing surgery in July. But his unparalleled craft should age better than a game dependent primarily on vertical explosiveness.His 2024 extension includes a player option for 2028–29, allowing him to negotiate another contract before his 32nd birthday. By signing early rather than waiting for free agency, Jalen gave the Knicks the financial flexibility to build a championship-caliber roster around him. Reports estimated that decision left hay bales of money on the table, but he has trusted the organization to take care of him in time.

item.title: Apollo Funds to Sell Data Center Cooling Firm Kelvion to SLB
item.author: Emma Sanchez

item.title: Pocket's AI made my game ideas real. Now Meta controls the results.
item.author: Kyle Orland
item.content:encoded: Meta's latest AI-based project launch wants to make that kind of vibe coding as instantly accessible as posting on social media. Pocket—which launched in the US last Friday, August 21, after Meta acquired the staff behind the now-defunct vibe-coding app Gizmo in March—is a mobile app that lets users create fully functional interactive "gizmos" just by typing prompts into a text box, without even the option to look at a line of code. Those gizmos can then be shared with the world in a TikTok-style endless scroll complete with likes, comments, reposts, and all the other hallmarks of social media addiction.After playing around with Pocket for the better part of a week, I found myself getting hooked on the simple process of quickly standing up functional, relatively feature-rich game prototypes simply by chatting with an LLM. But the result of all that time and AI effort is a couple of interactive toys that are effectively trapped in Meta's new walled garden, without any real way to turn them into something separate.

item.title: It’s time to get shirty about the short life of the football top
item.author: Tanya Aldred
item.content:encoded: With millions of club shirts going to waste every season, a radical recycling rethink is neededWhen Joanna Czutkowna buried a Manchester United jersey, a cotton T-shirt and a wool-cotton jumper in her Lancashire farm and dug it up a year later, the video went viral. The T-shirt had disappeared, apart from the seams (sewn with polyester thread), the jumper was 80% gone, but the United shirt remained – grubby but indestructible. (Insert joke here)The big reveal was not a surprise, certainly not to Czutkowna, who has worked in textiles and sustainability for 20 years, but it was a reminder: a football jersey is not just for Christmas, or even the next hundred Christmases.Continue reading...

item.title: Trump’s plan to sell off a part of Yosemite is what oligarchy looks like | Rebecca Solnit
item.author: Rebecca Solnit
item.content:encoded: Public lands belong to all of us. No one should plunder those lands for profitDo people still say a car was “sold for parts”? Because the US is being sold for parts or just handed over to the oligarchy. It’s a fire sale, a bankruptcy auction, it’s a planned dismantling of everything from its military to its institutions of higher education to its scientific research to its public lands.And while the threat to sell off part of Yosemite national park is about a quarter-mile parcel on the park’s edge, Yosemite is a crown jewel in the national park system and, arguably, the world’s first national park.Rebecca Solnit is a Guardian US columnist. She is the author of Orwell’s Roses and co-editor with Thelma Young Lutunatabua of the climate anthology Not Too Late: Changing the Climate Story from Despair to PossibilityContinue reading...

item.title: Today on Pinstripe Alley – 8/31/26
item.author: Jake Devin
item.content:encoded: The Yankees are heading West, and they do so after a pretty cathartic weekend. They played four games against their hated rivals with playoff seeding at stake, and after a tense first couple of matchups, New York awakened in the final two contests, unloading on the Red Sox for a combined 25 runs across two games. It was a triumphant showing, and on the heels of the news that Aaron Judge will traveling with the team to Anaheim, things are looking up. There’s a real chance here to keep the momentum going, with the Yankees taking on the Angels for three starting tonight. Josh will have you covered with the series preview this morning. Later, Kevin recaps Sunday in the American League, and also profiles Claudell Washington as part of our Yankee Birthday series. And in the afternoon, John discusses the most recent CBA proposals that have been reported. New York Yankees at Los Angeles AngelsVenue: Angel Stadium, Anaheim, CA1. What was your biggest positive takeaway from this weekend’s series win over Boston?2. Now that Aaron Judge is traveling with the team to California to ramp up on-field activities, do you expect him to be activated for the next homestand?

item.title: What's killed off the F1 driver market
item.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
item.content:encoded: The Formula 1 driver market is dead. But who killed it? And when will it truly return?Max Verstappen and Lando Norris's huge new Red Bull and McLaren deals mean many of F1's prime seats are locked down until the end of the decade.So why aren't star drivers moving very often? Is it good or bad for F1? And is there any hope for aspiring F1 drivers and fans who want a more volatile driver market?Is our perception accurate?The statistics are clear: there’s a very, very strong downward trend in what you might call driver market volatility. Measuring driver changes from one year to another, it’s about half of what it was at the start of the 1990s - with a pretty continuous trend downwards.There are also extreme spikes - such as 2019 and 2025 - featuring a huge amount of change. But they’re the exception.The trend applies very clearly when you limit it to changes among the top four teams at any time. Driver market movement has declined by around half.If you count Toro Rosso as effectively part of Red Bull, Verstappen and Norris could realistically be ‘lifers’ for their F1 teams. Norris is on course for at least 12 seasons at McLaren and to cruise past Mika Hakkinen and David Coulthard’s records of nine after next year. Charles Leclerc is on course to beat Michael Schumacher’s record 11-season run at Ferrari.Bar Hakkinen and Nico Rosberg (who both still started at smaller teams), every F1 champion in the last 40+ years has made at least one significant team move in their career - until most recent champions Norris and Verstappen. They’re at the vanguard of this new trend of extreme career stability.Exact figures for deals such as Verstappen and Norris’s are kept secret, but they’re known to be in the mega-millions. And they’re outside the limits of the cost cap - the early-2020s bid to introduce a driver salary cap within that too having been rejected.Throw in the explosion in team valuations and the commercial popularity of F1, and there’s more money flowing around the top teams but a hard limit on what they can spend on car development, which means spectacular amounts of money are available for top teams to spend on driver salaries. And that gives teams the financial firepower to tie down their ‘franchise’ drivers long-term - and gives drivers plenty of financial security.Being able to promise driver continuity also helps for tying down long-term deals with potential sponsors, so it’s in teams’ interests.Reason 2: F1's very slow 'social mobility'What you might call the ‘social mobility’ of F1 teams - the potential for their competitiveness to rise and fall - has slowed significantly. Drivers have to be more long-term strategic. Remember Norris being linked with a Red Bull move in Red Bull and Verstappen’s heyday, while McLaren was still yet to resume winning? Norris could’ve jumped ship just as McLaren usurped Red Bull at the top.Even pre-cost cap there were very few potential or proven championship-winning teams. Now the baked-in facilities advantages of the teams that could spend heavily before the cost cap and the way the cap limits the potential for big development leaps from season to season make it much harder - and slower - for ‘upwardly mobile’ teams to actually progress.It’s therefore a much bigger leap of faith for a driver to pick an ambitious midfielder such as an Audi, Alpine or even Aston Martin, than it would’ve been just a few years ago. If you’ve got a seat in an established top team secured, you want to keep hold of it. Drivers are no longer chasing the elusive great team to leap into next.Reason 3: The adaptation period has got longerIt takes longer to adapt to a new team than ever before, and that means any big team move guarantees an adaptation period that might effectively waste a first season. Lewis Hamilton’s 2025 struggle and much better 2026 at Ferrari are a prime example, and Carlos Sainz - a prolific 'mover' who's raced for five different teams - recently told The Race that he feels he gains at least a tenth of a second per lap just from team familiarity in his second season at a team.These are now very, very complicated cars, with a lot of subtleties. Teams are bigger than ever, with more personnel and processes to adapt to. It takes a long time to get the last fractions of a second out of a new car and team. Drivers can no longer be confident of jumping into a new team and very quickly getting the best out of its car.Does it matter and should anything be done?We love a driver rumour mill, but it’s not purely a media-confected thing. Fans want to see different drivers in different teams taking on different challenges - it’s a fundamental part of F1.But it can’t be forced. MotoGP, for instance, is eyeing up a rider transfer window for different reasons, and has a convention of two-year rider contract cycles anyway. Something like a contract-length limit would be contrived and restrictive for no real benefit.If F1 can create more opportunity for teams’ form to fluctuate, drivers will have more incentive to move around. With four teams in the mix to a degree at the front right now, this feels like a less urgent priority than in eras of clear single-team domination, but keeping hold of the recent influx of new and returning manufacturers will be easier if they see tangible routes to the top. F1 also needs to think more about what it’s doing to bring more young drivers through.Where are there signs of hope?One significant move could still trigger a domino effect, and the most obvious contender is Hamilton. He’ll be at Ferrari next season but will be approaching 43 years old by the end of it. Will he retire at the end of 2027? That create a lot of changes… but equally Ferrari could simply slot Ollie Bearman in and it would remain something of a closed system.Remember that even in deals such as Verstappen at Red Bull there will be performance clauses. He’s not going to completely handcuff himself to Red Bull. If a once-top team is suddenly ninth in the championship, a leading driver won’t get stuck there.And will Oscar Piastri decide he wants a move out of McLaren? He's still got a few years on his deal, but it's possible. Does George Russell see life alongside Kimi Antonelli at Mercedes as what he wants for the long term?Based on where we know some of these contracts are now, it could be 2031 - which is currently scheduled to be when the rules change, likely pivoting to V8 engines - when we next see major movement.But you never know. And that's the tantalising thing with the driver market. It may feel flat and locked, but you never know when that bombshell happens that will change everything and the market scrambles again. As the data shows, the general picture is much calmer now than it used to be, but when there’s a spike in movement, it tends to be a very big one.

item.title: 'Happy to have shown that I am stronger than Mathieu van der Poel on a mountain bike' – Tom Pidcock celebrates off-road world title but concedes multi-discipline rival's supremacy on it
item.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
item.content:encoded: Tom Pidcock almost made the monumental effort to work his way up the field at the UCI Mountain Bike World Championships in Val di Sole look easy. Though, just in case anyone needed a reminder that it was anything but, even the powerful form of on road rival Mathieu van der Poel couldn't follow in his footsteps. The pair had both swapped over from the Tour de France, and had just one World Cup round under their belt this season to earn points and get their eye in. They also started alongside each other on the fifth row, but the similarities ended once the race got underway."Getting back towards the front was complicated: I crashed in training on Friday and I had some back pain," said Pidcock in a media statement put out by race organisers. "I could not make extreme changes of pace, so I tried to ride at my own tempo and keep the energy I needed to make the difference at the end."It turned out to be a hand played to perfection for the British rider, who worked his way to the front group and then attacked on the penultimate lap. That move took Pidcock to the top step of the podium, delivering another world title to the 2023 victor, who also has claimed gold in the discipline at the last two Olympic Games.“Along with the Tour de France, these UCI World Championships were my target for the season," said Pidcock, who before the World Championships had walked away from the French Grand Tour with two trips to the stage podium in third and ninth place overall. The path, from there, has had its challenges."It has been a difficult period, marked by the death of Finlay Tarling. This win is for his brother Joshua,” said Pidcock of his compatriot and former Ineos Grenadiers teammate.Van der Poel, who has a swathe of world titles across cyclo-cross, gravel and also on the road, walked away from the Tour de France with two stage victories and a clear demonstration of strong form plus an impressive Les Gets effort to instill confidence. Still, as he continued his pursuit of the missing mountain bike world title, he failed to gain any moving-up momentum in Val di Sole, so the Dutch rider watched Pidcock ride away and had to settle for 30th place.Now the question is what will happen next, with another rainbow battle set to unfold in Montréal at the UCI Road World Championships at the end of September."I am happy to have shown that I am stronger than Mathieu van der Poel on a mountain bike," said Pidcock. "I think he is stronger than me on the road, but one day I want to win the UCI world title there as well."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to . You'll get comprehensive race coverage of La Vuelta a España, subscriber-exclusive analysis from our expert columnists, in-depth features and industry-leading tech insight. Plus, the Cyclingnews app lets you follow the action wherever you go!

item.title: OnlyFans and AI training: why gen Z doesn’t care where our money comes from | Alice Lassman
item.author: Alice Lassman
item.content:encoded: With traditional goals such as stability and home ownership feeling out of reach, young people are focused on the presentBy now, we all know the shape of financial nihilism: the throw-your-money-at-anything reaction to the dissolution of the slow, linear path to wealth; the prediction markets, meme stocks, cryptocurrencies and microluxuries growing in its place. We’re left in an economic no man’s land. But financial nihilism only describes where we put our money. What about how we earn it in the first place?The modern economy has long relied on our need for stable employment – to pay the mortgage, to keep our kids fed, or, for some, to chase prestige and power – to generate the work ethic that keeps the wheel of production turning. None of this is going well for young people. Our jobs are insecure, we can’t afford houses, we’re deferring having kids (if we have them at all), and only 6% of us say a leadership position is our primary career goal. Hope is one of the economy’s most productive inputs, powering our willingness to endure long hours. When the production function of income – the mechanism that turns hard work into a stable salary, then a mortgage, then a pension – breaks down, so does our relationship with the input. I call this production nihilism: my generation’s growing indifference to the kinds of work we’re willing to participate in, and where we’re willing to earn.Continue reading...

item.title: Yankees news: Aaron Judge to travel with Yankees on West Coast trip
item.author: Jake Devin
item.content:encoded: MLB.com | Bryan Hoch: The Yankees are off to the West Coast, and Aaron Judge is coming with them. The plan is for Judge to really start ramping up this week, including taking on-field batting practice. “Hopefully out there, he’ll start to get on velocity and things like that,” Aaron Boone said. “He’ll be part of the pregame stuff and just get more entrenched into getting ready to come back.” Though it’d be a major surprise to see Judge play during this trip, it seems possible that the team’s next homestand could see him return.ESPN | Jorge Castillo: Rookie George Lombard Jr. left Saturday night’s game after tweaking his knee, and though he’s avoided any structural damage, he’s could still hit the injured list. “It feels fine,” Lombard said. “It’s definitely better than yesterday. It felt a little stiff, and there’s still a little soreness, a little inflammation in there, but not terrible.” Jose Caballero, who was the starting shortstop for the first several weeks of the season, started at short on Sunday. Anthony Volpe is also biding his time at Triple-A, with the erstwhile starter at short having moved around the infield in the last month, taking several starts at second, and even starting at third over the weekend.New York Post | Mark W. Sanchez: The Yankees called up Luis Gil yesterday, the 2024 AL Rookie of the Year giving the club a fresh arm and taking Yerry De los Santos’ spot on the roster. Things are set up for the Yankees to have something of a bullpen audition in September, as there’s plenty of room in Aaron Boone’s Circle of Trust. Gil could toss his name into the mix, as could Clarke Schmidt, who made a rehab appearance over the weekend. Most everything is up for grabs beyond David Bednar, Brent Headrick and Paul Blackburn, so anyone that performs well over the season’s final month could become a factor come October.

item.title: Why Quartararo is now refusing to help Yamaha
item.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
item.content:encoded: The Aragon MotoGP weekend has exposed fresh tension between Yamaha and its Honda-bound star Fabio Quartararo.It came amid an uncharacteristically subpar outing for the 2021 MotoGP champion, who struggled to competitively assert himself against the other Yamaha riders - and finished the grand prix last, nearly 52 seconds back from the winner, after going off multiple times.Quartararo and Yamaha seemed to have settled into a 'truce' of sorts after the Frenchman resolved his future. Disappointed with Yamaha's development efforts for nearly half a decade, Quartararo never entertained penning a 2027 deal with his current employer - admitting recently that he never initiated any renewal talks before committing to Honda instead in the off-season.But this ultimately seemed to settle things. With Yamaha firmly in a 'rebuilding' year as it focused on exploring its first attempt at a V4 engine, Quartararo has produced the occasional heroics and fairly reliably led the line within its four-rider regular roster.He has also publicly accepted that Yamaha would deprioritise improving the current 1000cc bike ahead of the 2027 switch to 850cc and Pirelli tyres, acknowledging that this made sense for the project.Yet doing development work that could benefit that 850cc project appears to be where Quartararo draws the line.He was uncomfortable with the bike during the Aragon weekend but also unsettled by Yamaha's requests to re-test a new chassis that he had already found lacking."It's worse," he insisted on Saturday. "Yesterday I said it was worse, they wanted me to compare again this morning, it was worse [again]. I was more of a test rider this weekend, testing three times the chassis, it was not working. We had a new linkage also, it was not improved."He took a firmer line on Sunday, saying that he will "stop trying 100 things in a weekend".More revealing, though, were his reported comments to French media in attendance - in which he said he would not be aiding Yamaha's development due to "personal reasons".This comes off as particularly unseemly given Quartararo has been very well-compensated in this contract cycle for limited on-track results (though they have clearly been limited by machinery rather than his own underperformance), and perhaps Quartararo himself is aware of this - because, according to French reporters, he subsequently revealed that these "personal reasons" were what he claims is a Yamaha refusal to allow him to try the Pirelli tyres in the Red Bull Ring test after the Austrian Grand Prix.Yamaha will never put him on the 850cc bike, which it is developing with testers Augusto Fernandez and Andrea Dovizioso - but one idea that has been floating is at least giving riders in contractual situations like Quartararo's a shot at running Pirellis on the current 1000cc machines.Whatever the precise details of that test, there's now again an added needle over the final eight rounds of the Quartararo-Yamaha partnership - which was once one of the best stories in MotoGP.

item.title: 'The first day I felt back to normal' - Oscar Onley defeated in stage 9 sprint at Vuelta a España but remains in GC battle as illness fades
item.content:encoded: Afflicted by illness earlier in the race, Onley's fast-improving condition saw the Scottish racer follow Mas closely to the line when the Vuelta leader launched his key move, some two kilometres from the summit of the mammoth 22-kilometre climb.Mas then made a driving long acceleration on the finishing straight to emerge the clear victor ahead of Onley and strengthen his overall advantage into the bargain. At the same time, though, Onley's second place and the time gap of 12 seconds to the next finisher Primož Roglič (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) helped him consolidate his fourth place on GC, and confirmed that his illness is behind him. After Saturday he had already felt much better, though this was a further step up. "Today was the first day I felt fully back to normal," Onley told "It took longer than I was expecting, I actually felt good on Andorra, but then it hit me and now I'm back to normal."The finale of the hardest day of climbing so far in the Vuelta, with more than 5,000 metres of elevation gain, was conditioned by Decathlon CMA CGM's determined and lengthy drive to pull back the break. However, things turned slightly awry for the French team when their leader Felix Gall was unable to either anticipate or follow the key move made by Mas (Movistar) and Onley."I think it was a bit different to the other days, Decathlon burned through their guys [quicker] than they'd have liked maybe, or that I was expecting, so by the time we turned right onto the last part of the climb we were all isolated," Onley explained to ."There were a lot of attacks, we were all looking at each other, and to be honest, a final like that, it's hard to create bigger time gaps, so it was a lot of stop-start, which kind of worked in my favour.Onley admitted he made a mistake in the sprint, reflecting that in a drawn out sprint at a summit rather than a conventional mass dash for the line, it's normally the rider that opens up the moves that gets to finish first. But as he also pointed out, Mas had been superior to him all the way up the last part of the ascent so the result reflected the reality of the racing."to him, he was obviously stronger, he was pulling in the last couple of ks and I just had to sit on his wheel. So of course I'd like to have won, but I think the stronger man won," he concluded.The Briton reached the rest day in fourth overall, all the same, 2:20 down on Mas and with his GC options very much intact and the best young rider jersey on his shoulders. Given his position, climbing form and the four major summit finishes still to come in the two weeks remaining, after Sunday's performance, there's every reason for him to feel optimistic.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Weather tracker: Warm Yellow Sea strengthens storms in South Korea
item.author: Morgan Thomas for MetDesk
item.content:encoded: More than 200mm of rain forecast in parts of South Korea, while parts of southern Europe to be 10C above averageSouth Korea’s prime minister, Han Seong-sook, met officials to prepare for heavy rain expected this week, with rainfall totals across central and northern parts of the country forecast to exceed 200mm in some areas.South Korea was battered by heavy rainfall earlier this month and some areas were particularly hard hit. Over the weekend further thunderstorms pushed into the region and these are expected to cause disruption through Monday. This heavy rain is caused by a series of severe thunderstorms that developed over the Yellow Sea, on the western side of South Korea, and will slowly push eastwards on Monday before easing on Tuesday. These storms have been strengthened by the very warm Yellow Sea, which now has a surface temperature of 29C, 4C above the climatological average.Continue reading...

item.content:encoded: Newcastle players look revitalised, Liverpool’s curious transfer strategy and a worrying start for PalaceAmid the concerns at Manchester United, one player unquestioned is Senne Lammens. The goalkeeper produced some important first-half saves against Ipswich to keep his side in the game in difficult circumstances. A relaxed character, the Belgian is a calming influence in an emotional environment, especially with a panicked defence. When Julio Enciso was through on goal, Lammens had to decide when to come and how far, getting his distance and angles perfect to ensure the Paraguay attacker was repelled. item.title: ‘Breakthrough’ as Turkmenistan starts fixing ‘mindboggling’ methane mega-leaks
item.author: Damian Carrington Environment editor
item.content:encoded: Secretive state begins repairs on ageing facilities after being revealed as worst country for leaks of potent greenhouse gasTurkmenistan has started plugging the mega-leaks of methane that spew from its ageing oil and gas facilities, the latest UN data shows, in a move hailed as a breakthrough.Methane, also called natural or fossil gas, is a potent greenhouse gas. It traps 80 times more heat than carbon dioxide and causes 25% of global heating today. Stopping leaks can be quick and cheap and, because methane breaks down in the atmosphere far quicker than CO2, this has a rapid impact, with some experts calling it the climate “emergency brake”.Continue reading...

item.title: 'I just wasn't good enough' –Mathieu van der Poel rues another year where promising mountain bike form fades for World Championships
item.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
item.content:encoded: Jumping away from the road and chasing that elusive UCI Mountain Bike World Championships with just one race for the season under the belt was never going to be an easy mission, but Mathieu van der Poel had delivered every reason to hope when he rocketed straight to the World Cup Cross-Country Olympic podium in Les Gets.Just the week before the rainbow race the Dutch Alpecin-Premier Tech had moved seamlessly through the field and taken part in a two-way battle for the victory. It wasn't just the form that had taken him to first in the Tour de France on the Champs-Élysées that was clearly evident, but also a degree of comfort on the challenging terrain that boded well for the all important appointment at Val di Sole just a week away.He was, however, even further back on the start grid for the World Championships race though he wasn't the only road regular facing that awkward starting position, with Tom Pidcock facing a similar challenge. The difference was that the rider from Great Britain quickly chipped away, steadily moving up, but Van der Poel seemed to hit a wall.There was progress as he moved into the top 20 through the opening stages of the seven-lap race but then Van der Poel headed in the other direction, dropping out of the top 20 to cross the final finish line in 30th place, 4:40 back from a victorious Pidcock."I just wasn’t good enough. I don’t really know the reason. It was more or less the same as last year: a good feeling in Les Gets, but bad at the Worlds," said Van der Poel in a media release from the event.Last year it was sixth at Les Gets and then 29th at World Championships. The rider has a hefty collection of rainbow jersey's from other disciplines – cyclo-cross, gravel and road – the pursuit of this one is proving difficult, particularly with the time to race the mountain bike hard to come by."Those bad results are indeed piling up a bit now," Van der Poel told reporters after the event according to a report on . "But last year I could feel it coming that I wasn't 100 percent at the World Championships. I had expected a lot more from it this time. But I can't change anything about it now. Unfortunately, days like this happen too."Now, though, he'll be hoping they don't come again for the rainbow jersey battles ahead, either as he continues the pursuit of a mountain bike title in the years to come or the one he will be facing far sooner, at the end of September in Montreal on the road.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to .
