item.title: Every 2025-26 Formula E driver ranked from worst to best
item.author: Sam Smith
item.content:encoded: Eight drivers went into the Formula E season finale weekend with a chance of the 2025-26 world championship after a typically wild campaign.But who actually did the best (and worst) job?Sam Smith ranks all the drivers’ performances from worst to best.Points: 20Championship position: 19thBest result: 5thNato’s season was barely an improvement over his last. In fact, in terms of points, it was actually just worse with one fewer than he achieved in 2025.Forty-one points across 33 races tells only some of the story of Nato’s two-season return to Nissan after what was a decent initial campaign in 2023 before a one-off season with Andretti in ‘24. His net return was clearly never going to be good enough to stay as Oliver Rowland’s team-mate, yet his actual performances, particularly in the first half of the season, were reasonably strong. Jarama in particular looked promising with a fine fourth on the grid. But things went south quickly in the race with a mistake at Turn 1 and then a cycle back through the field thereafter. That became a familiar story in his season, as strategic missteps and a lack of race execution cost he and the team dearly.Victor Martins was seriously considered as a replacement for Nato after the Jarama weekend but Nissan stuck by him at least to the end of the season. There was genuine poor luck too for Nato, such as being shunted off by an errant Pascal Wehrlein in Sanya when he was in line for strong points. He then got serious salt sprinkled into the wounds at Shanghai, with a penalty for new components as a result of Wehrlein’s mistake.Nato showed some grit in taking a strong sixth in Tokyo but by then he knew his time at Nissan was over.A fine racing driver and a positive influence on any team, Nato has had a lucrative Formula E career, but now his six-season stint there is done. Points: 3Championship position: 20thBest result: 10th x3If there is a contest for the most ludicrously unlucky driver in 2026 then Maloney takes the top step of that podium, and by a huge margin.It seemed at stages that whatever the F2 race winner did, it ended with proverbial egg all over his face to match his garish yellow overalls. The Lola driver could not catch a break throughout the season as whatever ill luck was floating around he inadvertently caught.In Jeddah he got swiped out by a wayward Pepe Marti, then qualified an excellent 10th next day and then got a bizarre penalty for an energy overspike on the way to the grid, at Shanghai his driveshaft broke; in London he had another breakage…and on it went. Most of the incidents Maloney could do little about. He must have felt like howling at the moon.His pace and understanding of Formula E was much improved from his rookie season in 2025. It was telling that it all led to an opportunity at Nissan for Gen4, in which the Bajan is expected to be able to reveal his potential in Formula E much more. After an exasperating season of underachievement, due largely to circumstances way beyond his control, many feel as though he deserves it.Points: 32Championship position: 17thBest result: 1stDi Grassi’s final significant act in Formula E was typical box office from the rumbustious Brazilian polymath. A sensational call by him and his engineer Markus Michelberger paid off beyond their own imaginations for an unforgettable win at Shanghai. It was like Formula E’s own little weird fairytale.As a send-off for a driver who has been an integral part of Formula E’s growing up over the last 14 years or so it was perfect.Di Grassi will likely always be a central part of the Formula E paddock but his final season was ultimately 90% frustration and 10% Shanghai sensation.Again, poor reliability and a lack of out-and-out efficiency meant that aside from freak chances like Shanghai both he and team-mate Maloney were anchored to lowly positions.Di Grassi didn’t make it out of the qualifying group stages at all. That was telling because although he was in his final season, he was still able to turn it on when allowed to but it just didn’t happen for him in qualifying. His racecraft was typically robust but this year there were markedly fewer contacts - tactical or otherwise - with his rivals. Ultimately, despite his best efforts the deficits to other cars just couldn’t be overcome and the two season deficit that Lola Yamaha Abt had to others told pretty starkly across its two seasons of Gen3. But di Grassi should be afforded huge kudos for the manner in which he led development and the team as a whole, which with a recalibration and new hires for Gen4 could become a surprise package.Di Grassi meanwhile will celebrate the birth of another child in the coming months and spend some much needed time with his family. But it won’t be too long until the competitive urge strikes and he’s at Interlagos in a Stock Car or two. Points: 23Championship position: 18thBest result: 6th x2Although not Guenther’s worst season in Formula E (that came in 2022 in his single campaign with a transitional Nissan team), this was punctuated by scrappy team strategies, misguided race plans and an inherently mediocre DS Penske technical package. It’s therefore really hard to gauge Guenther’s season properly because it was essentially ruined by these factors and not by anything he could tangibly control.For DS Penske to finish the season 91 points off stablemate Citroen kind of told its own story. Decisions on race tactics fell way short. Guenther was fast in qualifying and races but was rarely in the position to use that speed to gain material benefits. With Penske not able to tell him what car he’d be racing in Gen4, Guenther took the decision to accept an offer from Envision, where he will line up alongside Zak O’Sullivan. He will immediately try to banish the memory of recent struggles to the back of his mind and rebuild the strong momentum of fine seasons with Maserati MSG and DS Penske prior to 2026.Points: 68Championship position: 12thBest result: 2ndVergne’s switch from DS Penske to Citroen felt like a seamless one until it became clear around the mid-season mark that he was never going to get close to the potential of new team-mate Nick Cassidy in being able to fight for wins and podiums. By downscaling his racing programme and taking a season off from Peugeot sportscar competition, it was assumed Vergne would be fully attuned to FE and at least getting one final Gen3 win to add to his Hyderabad E-Prix success back in February 2023.But it really never looked like happening, other than a surprise chance at Shanghai when he gambled on dry settings and just lost out to old rival di Grassi.Vergne loathed the Gen3 car concept completely. He was never truly comfortable with it but he can still race, as he proved at Shanghai and Tokyo in particular. Yet, there were also too many races where he barely featured. Yes, he had far from the best car out there but for a second consecutive season Vergne was generally beaten on pace by his team-mate, which would not have been countenanced in the late Gen1 and early Gen2 eras.There were a lot of misfortunes but it all ultimately felt like Vergne was just counting down the days to when he could kick his Gen3 experience into touch.He will now attempt to rekindle the potent force he was in Gen2, and that mission starts now as he pounds around desolate European test tracks developing the Stellantis Gen4 car. Points: 55Championship position: 16thBest result: 3rdVery few fancied Eriksson’s chances at Envision and although he won’t retain his seat there for Gen4, the amiable Swede can feel quite hard done by after a promising season. Eriksson’s CV is one of racing’s hidden gems. A reasonably close runner-up to Lando Norris in European F3 back in 2017 and a DTM race winner, he has a seriously strong pedigree.He also had some real believers at Jaguar where he was a very highly rated reserve and sim driver. It was a recommendation from Jaguar’s Gary Ekerold that helped Eriksson seal the Envision drive and he pretty much made the most of the chance by making strong impressions on tracks he had no experience of.One of Envision’s leading engineers, Connor Summerville, pulled this writer aside in Sao Paulo in December and essentially said that The Race’s pre-season questioning of the decision to hire Eriksson would be proved wide of the mark. He was right. Eriksson scored points in half of the races, claimed a mega podium at Shanghai and kept ultra-experienced team-mate Sebastien Buemi honest throughout.Buemi’s 22 point haul at the London finale pulled him away and out of sight of Eriksson but generally the two were evenly matched. Eriksson’s median gap to the fastest driver in qualifying was the same as Buemi’s and the overall fight in qualifying went Eriksson’s way at 9-8.So, while Eriksson strives for drives at Penske and Lola now, he can at least look back on a very credible return to one of motorsport’s toughest pound-for-pound grids.Points: 66Championship position: 13thBest result: 2ndA little like Eriksson, no one really fancied Marti’s chances in Formula E, as he embarked on a huge career change just after he’d turned 20. A late deal meant just a few days of testing and his signing was really a big risk for Cupra Kiro team. Those thoughts soon faded into the distance in what ultimately became one of Formula E’s strongest rookie seasons ever.Two podiums and nine points scores from 17 races was a super strong haul from the Spaniard. Yet it all looked to be heading for disaster initially, after he barrel-rolled his Porsche to destruction when a full course yellow mistake played out in Sao Paulo.This is where not only Marti, but also Kiro, need a special mention because other teams and drivers may have panicked a bit at this point. They didn’t and the resulting calm brought results.Marti was a chunk off team-mate Dan Ticktum on out-and-out pace but that was no disgrace at all in a first season, especially in the last of a rules set, and against a talent like Ticktum. Marti’s racecraft was naturally impressive, especially from round three in Miami onwards, and his layered races were tactically excellent. He has an exciting Formula E career ahead of him.Points: 65Championship position: 14thBest result: 2ndIt’s simultaneously true to say both that Drugovich under-delivered on what was expected of him in 2026 and also that he ultimately delivered enough to make him stand out as a definite future E-Prix winner.He had a horrible start to the season with mistakes in several of the opening races, most notably when he threw a podium away in Miami after he misjudged his braking and clouted the back of Antonio Felix da Costa’s Jaguar.It was after that incident that Drugovich changed his approach a little and started to look at the longer game. That philosophy played out nicely in Monaco with a stealthy runner-up place, which in turn triggered a series of good results, including fifth in Sanya (should have been a podium but for a penalty) and fourth at Shanghai.Finally, Andretti had a team-mate capable of scoring big points when Jake Dennis didn’t. It made for a much more cohesive camp at the US team and Drugovich, despite a sloppy end to the season in Tokyo and London, felt like a driver really on the cusp of doing something quite special in Gen4.Points: 97Championship position: 10thBest result: 2ndBuemi bowing out of Formula E came quickly and perhaps the appreciation he really deserved wasn’t quite as fulsome as it should have been because of the timing of the news. He will, like di Grassi, still be involved but in a much different capacity in the future, yet his legacy will live on as one of the true original greats. His final season was a consistent one with six top six positions, the highlights of which were his incredible pole position at Mexico City and a strong second in Jeddah to da Costa. Each of those races he could possibly have won in different circumstances but in Mexico he made an embarrassing error by out-braking himself at the first corner.There were mistakes and lost opportunities but in a team that had been slightly cut adrift from partner Jaguar in the mid-phase of Gen3, Buemi’s experience held things together and he was, unlike di Grassi, always a threat in the top six during his final season.For that Buemi deserves extra credit because at the age of 37, like Edoardo Mortara, he showed that he still had a turn of pace and finally a strong understanding of pack racing. He left the championship very much on a high.Points: 68Championship position: 11thBest result: 1stBarnard’s win in the London finale, while brilliant and thoroughly deserved, couldn’t hide the disappointment of a season which tested his resolve greatly. Changing from a Nissan to a Stellantis Gen3 car was never going to be easy but Barnard prepared and honed himself excellently, fitting into the Phil Charles led Penske environment with aplomb.But wrong steps on race strategies, poor team calls and mediocre efficiency from the powertrain all combined to leave Barnard scratching around the lower points reaches for the vast majority of the season.He was the fifth-best in the average starting position ranking (8.18), with Cassidy the only other Stellantis runner in that top 10.In group qualifying his median gap to the front was a tiny 0.139s, so he definitely had the pace.But when moored to the lower echelons in races frustration creeped in and he had a few erratic days, notably at Jarama and Monaco. He managed to wipe out Vergne on both occasions, much to the double champion’s chagrin.Barnard calmed it down quickly and had a very strong end to the season, dealing with not only a slowly dying DS relationship but also a lack of knowledge of what he would be driving in Gen4.He now knows and is relishing the Gen4 period when like Marti, O’Sullivan and Theo Pourchaire he will be aiming to make Formula E’s youth movement surge to the top.Points: 115Championship position: 7thBest result: 1st x2A position in the top 10 looked a bit fanciful for de Vries after a succession of mistakes in the first quarter of the season left him cut adrift of his Mahindra team-mate Mortara by a huge 79 points as he rocked up in his town of Monaco in May.It was there that he quenched Mahindra’s almost five-year thirst for a win after an assured and patient display. It kick-started his season nicely and the errors stopped. Yet, those blunders, such as clouting team-mate Mortara and Ticktum off the start line in Sao Paulo (unbelievably not punished!) and his reckless assault on Pascal Wehrlein at Jarama threw away points that otherwise might have meant he actually usurped Mortara in the final standings.De Vries’ propensity to sometimes drive like a thrashing electric eel was still there but it dissipated as the season went on. His win in Tokyo was sublime, as was his pole position in the final race in London, which should have been the platform for a third win but for tactical sloppiness.On the whole, this was a strong season for de Vries but he himself knows that he and Mahindra were actually capable of a lot more. Expect a stronger and more consistent de Vries in Gen4Points: 102Championship position: 9thBest result: 1stMueller had plenty of doubters after a tricky first half-season when he was seconded to Porsche customer Andretti in 2025. But a recovery in the second half of that campaign gave Porsche the confidence it needed to ensure he replaced da Costa in the factory team and would be a long-term solution. It was a shrewd move because Mueller was strong from the start, already bringing big points by the time he arrived in Miami in January. It was there that Mueller went from solid team player to potential race winner when he scored an exceptional pole position in tricky conditions.He followed that up with a fine second place before his day of days came in Berlin, when he brought home the bacon with his ‘Rosa Schwein’ Porsche, taking a conclusive win.But weirdly that then seemed to trigger some rare erratic driving in Mueller too. There was a clash with da Costa in the second Berlin race, for which he was fortunate not to get penalised, and then his ramming of team-mate Wehrlein at La Rascasse was embarrassing in Monaco.Those aberrations apart, Mueller had a strong season, one in which yes he was occasionally a bit of a patsy for Wehrlein, but there were enough strong races and 102 points. While not quite enough for the teams’ title this time, that score was a big part of Porsche’s manufacturers’ crown, as well as being by far Mueller’s best ever points total during his five seasons in Formula E. Points: 62Championship position: 15thBest result: 1stImagine a giant malfunctioning neon sign that occasionally flashes ‘genius’ then sparks out, and on other occasions flashes up ‘irritant’. Ticktum operates like a human glitch flashing up those two traits spontaneously around the racetracks of the world.Quite how an individual can weave pure magic like he did in Monaco to deliver two of Formula E’s best ever qualifying laps, but then flounce out of the paddock in a sulky huff soon afterwards, is really hard to explain or comprehend. But this is Dan Ticktum. Plenty love him as much as they are utterly baffled by him. And vice versa. On the positive side, Ticktum proved again that occasionally, when the circumstances are right, he can deliver exceptional things at the wheel of a racing car.He was, from the first qualifying session in Sao Paulo, ‘on it’. The problem was that difficulties with aspects of how Cupra Kiro treated and prepared the older version of the Porsche 99X Electric frustrated Ticktum and he didn’t seem to be capable enough to address them properly himself.Monaco was a prime example. When trying to get a solution for the overheating tyres just didn’t materialise, he went into a perpetual loop of frustration that ended in a meltdown. That is always going to have repercussions and so it proved.There was then an ill-advised blast at stewards at Shanghai and a highly scratchy finale in London when he refused orders to allow team-mate Marti through, clearly and concisely telling his own team principal Russell O’Hagan to f*** off.’Ticktum has chances at Lola and Penske for next season, as well as a remote possibility of staying at Kiro. Gen4 should be right up his street and the notion that he won’t be part of the grid at all, which is a real prospect, seems ludicrous for a driver capable of truly great things albeit with a side garnish of volatile madness.Points: 114Championship position: 8thBest result: 1stOn one level Cassidy deserves to be much higher in this list simply because of the way he adapted to a new manufacturer so quickly, after his move from Jaguar to Citroen.To win in only his second race for Citroen, in what was arguably the best victory of the season and perhaps in the Kiwi’s whole Formula E career, was a remarkable accomplishment. At that stage it felt genuinely like he could fight for the title.Yet, as Cassidy said privately at the time and something that was corroborated by his late team boss Cyril Blais, such a notion as a title tilt was always going to be way too far-fetched in 2026.Jeddah was the real realisation of that realisation. That was when strategic conflict cul de sacsplayed out and caused irritation between driver and team. It wasn’t the only time it happened and occasionally Cassidy got a bit scrappy, especially in the second race at Berlin and then again in Monaco when he shunted Dennis off.Some high points came Cassidy’s way again, especially with a double podium in Tokyo. In light of Blais’ death just a week before, his races there were hands down the grittiest and bravest performances of the season.The bigger picture though for Cassidy is Gen4. This is the real reason he jumped ship from Jaguar at the end of 2025.The overt pack racing of Gen3 was Cassidy’s own private plaything and he was the best at it. A growing theory that he won’t be as good in Gen4 should be deemed well wide of the mark. The last time he was in a big powerful single-seater was in Super Formula, a series which he won handsomely in 2019.Points: 137Championship position: 5thBest result: 2nd x2 It seems absurd to think that di Grassi won a race this season and Mortara did not. Such was Mortara and Mahindra’s pace and performances across most of the campaign that it feels a complete injustice he didn’t stand atop the podium.He had his best season since 2021-22 with a suite of performances that were as dynamic as they were consistent. After the first race in Berlin, Mortara led the title fight. But after that he was simply hanging on as a contender and never really felt like he could challenge the Wehrlein, Evans, Dennis axis.Mortara’s superpower is being super aggressive with the Hankook tyres and getting them into a pliable state so that he can retain the heat for his qualifying laps. His average starting position was the third best after Wehrlein and da Costa, but it was his ability to pivot his Mahindra so incredibly in Jeddah, Berlin and Tokyo that really took the breath away.There was real misfortune for Mortara too this season. He should have won at Mexico City but for a slight technical issue, and then in Sanya when he was right in contention for what would likely have been at least a second place a stray piece of debris hit his car's external emergency shut-off loop, instantly killing its power. That was also essentially the kill switch for Mortara’s title chances.At 39, Mortara is enjoying a great Indian summer at Mahindra. It will continue into Gen4 and don’t bet against him really featuring in that era too.Points: 137Championship position: 4thBest result: 1stThe points were good, so were a lot of the performances, yet there also seemed to be something missing from Rowland’s title defence season. After the dream first three-quarters of the season in 2025, the final part was tetchy and a feeling of unease permeated his 2026. It all came to a head in July when Rowland looked at one stage to potentially be flying the Nissan nest. It settled down but some questions still remain about their working relationship as Gen4 looms.The 2025-26 campaign began reasonably strongly for Rowland but Miami and Madrid disasters ultimately lost him a foothold in the title battle, one which he never at any point headed.A brilliant win in Monaco was his only top step of the year appearance but equally excellent podiums at Berlin and Sao Paulo were definite highs too.But the lows were like depth charges. He was furious after Jarama when the team all but fell apart tactically and then amid a damp end to the season he acquiesced the title with nothing but a whimper. That's not the Rowland way or style and it should trigger a significant retaliation and rejuvenation in Gen4.Points: 128Championship position: 6thBest result: 1st x2A combative season from a driver who for the first half of it was still learning the ‘Big Cat’ ways at Jaguar after a torrid couple of seasons at Porsche. The hangover from that though was not too painful, as da Costa quickly adapted to getting quick wins at Jeddah and Jarama. They were both well-deserved after races that were constructed elegantly with his new engineer, Kazuto Shiomitsu. Monaco was a crossroads in the sense of a title quest for da Costa. After the dust had settled on his controversial coming together with Ticktum, da Costa himself admitted he might have been a bit more patient.It all cost him at least 18 points, which combined with being swiped out of a similar position in Miami by an errant Drugovich, was ultimately the difference between finishing sixth in the final standings and still having a proper title challenge in London.With better luck and a little more patience, da Costa will be a factor for the title next season. His grasp of the Gen4 car is already said to be highly impressive and his hunger to add to his 2019-20 title, which he couldn’t celebrate properly because of the pandemic, is now off the scale.But some caution is needed as well. What he can’t afford to do is get sucked into another chapter of his bitter feud with Wehrlein next season. Because the only winners out of such antics as the two displayed at London are the opposition and rabid headline hunters.Points: 164Championship position: 2ndBest result: 1st x2Walking back to the nearby hotel from the Sao Paulo paddock last December, Dennis swung his trophy with one hand and fought to send a text message with the other. Simultaneously, as drivers seem to be able to do, he also held a conversation with this writer about the final Gen3 season, which he had just started in the best way possible.His overview was essentially that outright consistency would be the key and that if he and Andretti did what they did in 2023, when he fought back from a mid-season slump to take the crown with a stellar end to the season, then they had a chance to top and tail the Gen3 era with titles. He was nearly proved right because his 2026 had some eerie similarities with that 2023 campaign.The mid-season trough came with a barren period between Miami in late January and Monaco (where he rarely gets any joy) in mid-May. Again, he picked up zero points in the Principality, and as he headed to his home near the track, any thought of a 2023 repeat was surely over, such was the gap (62 points) to Wehrlein the leader.But then, as the series embarked on its Asian leg, Dennis’ hopes were reborn with a win in Sanya, a podium at Shanghai and then two poles and a pair of podiums in Tokyo.It was Tokyo where the title was really lost, however. In the first race he had one hand on the winner’s trophy until a slight energy overspend allowed Ticktum through on the final lap. Then in the second race a compromise on his attack mode, via a full course yellow, shattered his plan to hunt down de Vries for what would have been a relatively simple victory.The messy circumstances of his rude exit via Wehrlein from the London finale were quickly digested, with Dennis telling the Race that having one title already it was easier to take such bad fortune.He will surely be a champion again, though. But if it transpires against him and he doesn’t reprise 2023, he’s got a decent claim to being some kind of moral winner in 2026 after a brilliantly built season and a great degree of class in how he reacted to a bad-tempered final race.Points: 169Championship position: 1stBest result: 1st x3Only Formula E’s second double champion, and the first to be able to use the double world champion moniker, Wehrlein thrust himself into all-electric greatness in 2026.His campaign was not perfect. But as a driver who had the ‘favourite’ tag ahead of the season he dealt with the pressure well, despite the vast majority of his competitors actively not wanting him to win.Wehrlein is a monster of a competitor. Fast, agile, often uncompromising and most of all a cleverly effective racer, who utilises relationships in his team to a devastating degree of efficiency. A prime example of that was the pace and immediate understanding he had with his new engineer for this season, Robert Sattler. They gelled incredibly well together and had each other’s backs throughout the season. An ‘us against the world’ mentality, reminiscent of football managers like Jose Mourinho and Sir Alex Ferguson, soaked through their side of the garage and it was used to decent effect.A brilliant pole and win in Jeddah, a pocket picking third at Jarama and a clinical win at London in the penultimate race were all important milestones in his successful title season.But it was the way he came back from his mid-season slump in Monaco (hit by Mueller) and Sanya (mistake overtaking Nato) that really pointed to Wehrlein as a clear champion elect.At Shanghai he smashed in some of the best qualifying laps of the season, before then taking a commanding win in the race. It took him from a 27 point deficit after Sanya to a nine point lead after Shanghai. Psychologically that was a very firm strike of the hammer from Wehrlein and Porsche.While Wehrlein was a deserving champion, he was far from a popular one. A bit of a lone wolf in the paddock at times combined with that ‘us against the world’ mentality, while positive in getting the job done, is not popular outside of Porsche’s four walls. Others feel it unnecessary and insular.Wehrlein will not care about all of that, and perhaps neither should he, because he has the silverware and the added kudos of now being a double champion.At the same time some of his remarks after he took the title in London were on the wrong side of crassness. Maybe with the benefit of the doubt being the high-adrenalin, high-stress nature of that finale weekend he might look back and re-evaluate the veracity of some of the words he expressed that afternoon.Points: 160Championship position: 3rdBest result: 1st x2Fairytales rarely play out in motorsport. For Mitch Evans they don’t even try to.Knowing pretty much since the start of the season that this would be his final campaign with Jaguar, the sentimental script was surely already written. After coming so close, so many times, one of Formula E’s greatest competitors would surely do it this time at the final time of asking.Inevitably it went from despair to triumph and back again to despair over the nine month duration of the season. When Evans and Jaguar are involved nothing is ever straightforward or linear.From a messy start in Sao Paulo in which he ended up in the barriers, to another scrappy non-score at Mexico City, it was hardly the foundation for that fairytale to happen. But then came a reflex win in the damp and cold of Miami and a string of results to the end of the Berlin weekend where he was all of a sudden just three points behind leader Wehrlein. That win in Berlin was epic in the sense he gambled hugely on saving a set of tyres and came through from 17th on the grid. It was one of his best ever performances but actually his run from 16th to second at Jarama really set Evans apart.This was an exquisite drive on a track much more difficult to overtake on than Berlin. Creating new racing lines and overtaking positions, Evans would have won it had it not been for a recalcitrant Mueller protecting Wehrlein (sound familiar?). That scenario came back to haunt Evans a bit in London, but before that came Shanghai where a spec part failure made him a non-starter. This was the stake in the heart for his fairytale, and despite fighting performances in Tokyo and London, where again he was dealt a poor hand with the FCY, he just fell tantalisingly short.But context is everything for Evans this season. And because of that final season scenario, the poor start, the incredible Jarama and the other many stand-out performances, Evans should be considered across the season as the absolute outstanding performer.

item.title: Everything Ferrari's changing to try to win at Monza
item.author: Rosario Giuliana
item.content:encoded: Ferrari's Zandvoort weekend marked not only its return to action after Formula 1’s summer break, but also the start of a new phase in the development of the SF-26.A new floor and diffuser specification made its debut in the Netherlands, although the package represented only part of the upgrade Ferrari had originally planned for this stage of the season.The initial plan was to introduce a more extensive update at Zandvoort. Ferrari ultimately decided to split the development programme, bringing forward the solutions that had already reached sufficient maturity while allowing more development time for the lateral section of the floor edge.The floor used at Zandvoort was therefore mainly revised around the front floor boards and the diffuser.The Race understands that the revised lateral floor edge will arrive later in the season, within a window currently stretching from Baku in late September to Austin a month later, with its exact introduction date still to be decided.Overall, the Zandvoort package is estimated to have a potential worth around 0.15 seconds per lap.So this is not a transformation of the SF-26, but another refinement of its aerodynamic platform, building on the floor evolution Ferrari had already introduced at Barcelona in mid-June - after which it won two of the next three grands prix.Results have been harder to come by since the Silverstone win in July. Now it comes to Monza still with a degree of title hope for Lewis Hamilton in particular, and somewhat in need of home success. This is what it's doing to maximise its chances.Monza package is more than a wing trimThe Italian Grand Prix is inevitably one of the races Ferrari places particular emphasis on, but this year the technical significance of its home event goes beyond Monza's traditional importance to Maranello.On paper, the circuit's characteristics could play more to the strengths of the Mercedes- and Red Bull-powered cars.Monza’s long full-throttle sections put a premium on outright power and energy management, while aerodynamic efficiency remains crucial. It is not simply a question of how much power is available, but how much downforce a car can retain for a given level of drag.That makes finding the right configuration for the SF-26 particularly important.And this is where Ferrari's work on the floor takes on a second purpose.With active aerodynamics and the extensive use of straight-line mode, the compromise required for Monza could be less extreme than it has historically been.The Italian circuit has traditionally been associated with the lowest-downforce wing configurations of the season, but The Race understands Ferrari has taken a somewhat less conventional approach in its search for low drag in 2026.The rear wing will naturally form part of the circuit-specific adaptation, but it is not where all of Ferrari's work has been focused.A high-downforce specification was introduced in Hungary, some elements of which – including the hanger flaps – were retained for the Dutch GP.Those additional devices will be removed for Monza. But there will not be a completely bespoke 'Monza-spec' rear wing.Instead, Ferrari will remove or revise elements across the bodywork and wings. The front wing is not expected to undergo any significant changes, while the rear wing will be cleaned up through the removal of the hanger flaps.A significant part of Ferrari's low-drag work has instead focused, once again, on the floor.Ferrari has developed a Monza-specific adaptation of the floor aimed at reducing drag, following a similar direction to one it had already explored in Austria and Britain two months ago.At those two races, the single vertical element in the floor-board area reappeared on the SF-26. That configuration is set to return at Monza.It had previously been used through to Miami at the start of May before Ferrari switched to the subsequent three-element arrangement, which was revised again as part of the Zandvoort update.This makes the timing of the Dutch GP upgrade particularly interesting.The new floor represents the latest development baseline for the SF-26, but individual components can still be adapted – or removed altogether – according to the requirements of a particular circuit.For Monza, Ferrari's approach is therefore not simply to take downforce off through the wings. It is also looking at how the floor itself can contribute to reducing the car's overall drag.Why the exhaust wing staysThe ‘FTM’ or flick tail mode system – the small winglet positioned ahead of the exhaust outlet – has also been part of Ferrari's low-drag evaluation for Monza.One of the options considered was removing it altogether, something Ferrari had already experimented with at the Red Bull Ring with both Spa and Monza in mind.At Spa, however, the grip compromise and uncertain weather conditions led Ferrari to retain the winglet rather than sacrifice the downforce associated with it.Its removal was considered again for Monza as Ferrari looked at ways of cleaning up that area and minimising drag.However, The Race understands Ferrari has ultimately opted to keep the FTM, preferring to find drag reduction elsewhere on the SF-26.The other element that could make Monza particularly significant for Ferrari is the power unit.Maranello has a new internal combustion engine specification ready, developed using the second of its two available ADUO opportunities, after the first update was introduced in Austria alongside a new Shell fuel specification.The ADUO 2 engine represents only a partial step compared with the broader development work Ferrari is carrying out on its internal combustion engine for 2027.But some of that work can be transferred to the 2026 unit, and the new specification is already ready to race.The question is when Ferrari chooses to introduce it – and Monza is a realistic possibility.Ferrari is looking to align the introduction of its ADUO 2 engine with the addition of the fourth internal combustion engine and fourth turbocharger of the season to each driver's pool.Both Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton have so far used three ICEs and three turbochargers.Synchronising those two steps would allow Ferrari to introduce its latest engine specification at the same time as it brings a fresh unit into service anyway, then maximise the use of the upgraded version over the final part of the season.There is no obligation for Ferrari to introduce it at Monza and a final decision has yet to be made.The engine is ready, though, and the combination of Monza's characteristics and Ferrari's power-unit pool management makes the Italian Grand Prix a particularly logical opportunity to introduce it.

item.title: Monday briefing: Nepal and Tibet’s floods are a warning for the future
item.author: Hettie O'Brien
item.content:encoded: In today’s newsletter: As rescuers search for survivors after catastrophic floods, the disaster offers a stark warning about the climate risks facing the region, and the worldGood morning. Over the weekend, rescue workers in Nepal and Tibet raced to find people who are still trapped in villages affected by catastrophic flash floods. As of this morning, the death toll stands at 903, and more than4,000 people are missing.For those of you reading this in a place where life continues as usual, the scale of devastation is hard to fathom. In a matter of minutes, a torrent of mud and debris engulfed entire villages, snapped bridges and swept away people’s homes and families. Some survivors are marooned on top of buildings that rescue workers can’t reach. Others are trapped in tunnels beneath the ground. Many have no idea if their loved ones are still alive. | PC Andrew Harper’s killers will remain in prison after Andy Burnham announced changes to the early release scheme that will see anyone convicted of unlawful killing, including all forms of manslaughter, excluded from the scheme. | Far-right British media provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos has been deported from the US back to the UK by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in connection with what the agency said was expired authorisation to be in the country. | Iran has launched retaliatory strikes on airbases in Jordan after the United States attacked Iranian rocket launchers on an island in the strait of Hormuz, the first such strikes in a month. | In a blow to Brussels, Iceland has held a referendum that has narrowly ⁠rejected ⁠the government’s proposal ​to hold ⁠accession talks with ⁠the ​EU.| A headteacher in Nepal evacuated 900 children from a school moments before a deadly wall of water struck their town amid the devastating flash floods that have killed almost 800 people and left thousands missing.| Justice secretary Alex Norris is due to present the government’s revised plans for the prisoner early release scheme, which includes a headroom review aimed at freeing up more space in the system. | In the first UK visit by an EU leader of Andy Burnham’s tenure, the prime minister is will host talks with French president Emmanuel Macron. | Officials from Jamaica will visit the UK to lodge a petition with King Charles to seek legal guidance from the privy council on the country’s request for reparations over Britain’s involvement in the slave trade, on the anniversary of the 1781 Zong slave ship departure from West Africa.Continue reading...

item.title: Ogier apologises to FIA and Paraguay presidents for "out of line interaction"
Mads Würtz Schmidt goes solo to defend men's European gravel title as Femke Markus sweeps up women's jersey in Houffalize sprint
item.author: simone.giuliani@futurenet.com (Simone Giuliani)
item.content:encoded: Mads Würtz Schmidt (Denmark) continued to make himself at home on the top step of the podium, going solo to defend the men's elite UEC Gravel European Championships title on Sunday, while Femke Markus (Netherlands) was victorious in the three-way sprint that decided the elite women's race in Houffalize.The 138km elite title races with 2,190m of elevation gain played out over three laps of a 70% off-road loop, starting and finishing in Houffalize, taking in forest roads and with the the climbing concentrated in the first half of each lap.Würtz Schmidt came into his elite men's title defence with the confidence of a string of big name victories this season, including The Traka 360 and Unbound 200, and also having won the UCI Gravel World Series round in the same location last year."It's a really hard course but it suits me very well," said Würtz Schmidt in an interview shared on race social media. "I had a plan and I stuck to it and luckily for me I could take the win."The two-time European champion made his move in the second half, breaking away to claim victory after 4:09:57, with more than a minute gap to Wout Alleman (Belgium), who has worn the Marathon Mountain Bike European jersey. Belgian gravel champion Niels Vandeputte was third, more than two minutes back from Würtz Schmidt but in a close battle for the final podium spot with Eddy Le Huitouze (France).In the elite women's race the top four were all within 30 seconds and the podium was decided by a sprint.Markus, fellow Dutch rider Shirin van Anrooij – who on the road is swapping from Lidl-Trek to Canyon-SRAM in 2027 – and Axelle Dubau-Prévot (France) all charged toward the line together. The Dutch gravel champion and her compatriot Van Anrooij gapped Dubau-Prévot on the uphill run to the line. SD Worx-Protime rider Markus proved the strongest in the sprint, with the WorldTour racer crossing the line with a two second winning margin as she threw her arms up in celebration. Larissa Hartog added to the Dutch strength at the top of the results table, crossing the line 23 seconds back to take fourth."OMG I can call myself the European Champion Gravel," said Markus in a social media post, adding that she would wear the jersey with pride.Last year's winner, Erica Magnaldi (Italy) crossed the line in seventh. item.title: Philadelphia Cycling Classic men: Tim Torn Teutenberg sprints to first pro victory from late breakaway
item.author: laura@cyclingnews.com (Laura Weislo)
item.content:encoded: Tim Torn Teutenberg outsprinted his two late breakaway companions to win the revived Philadelphia Cycling Classic. The German rider launched his sprint early to claim the victory ahead of Ronald Donaldson (Jayco Alula) and Jonas Rutsch (Lotto-Intermarché).Advantaged by Lidl-Trek’s numbers in the race, the 24-year-old had two teammates in a group of 10 inside of the final five kilometres with Seb Grindley and US champion Quinn Simmons who had just chased back on.Along with Rutsch and Donaldson, the lead group also included Luke Lamperti (EF Education-EasyPost), Riley Sheehan (NSN), Simone Gualdi (Lotto-Intermarché), Ben Oliver (Modern Adventure), and Eder Frayre (L39ION of Los Angeles).Rutsch attacked the group with 3.5 kilometres to go with Donaldson and Rutsch quickly jumping on his wheel as they tackled Lemon Hill for the final time with Teutenberg coming across around one kilometre later.With 800 metres to go, the three had a 10-second lead on the chasers, as they sped towards the finish line, making their way around lapped riders.“I think it was quite a tactical race. You never knew which attack would go and would continue, and then wait to see how we do it and try to be there with numbers. And we knew Quinn was super strong, so that he would somehow find his way and make to the front, and that's what he did. And then I tried slowly a bit down in the group, and then when he arrived in the group, he immediately attacked. It was super good. I think the guys had to invest a lot, and then we played the numbers.”Having beaten Donaldson in a sprint in the past, and taken the win at Paris-Roubaix Espoirs in 2024, Teutenberg was confident in his sprint, and then he used the lapped riders on the course to his advantage.“So I knew normally I should be faster, but you never know. And then I don't like normally to go from the front, but then with some people that we left in front of me, so I tried to get a bit of shelter behind them, and then it was a bit of cat and mouse waiting, and then I don't know with 220 [metres] to go or something, I just went with all I had.”After a flurry of attacks came to nought on the first lap, Philadelphia native Robin Carpenter (Modern Adventure Cycling), Colby Lange (Project Echelon), Killian O'Brien (Team Skyline), Joshua Lebo and Thomas Sullivan (Meridian Racing), Luke Walter (Competitive Edge) and David Lozano (Team Novo Nordisk) formed the day's first breakaway, although Walter was replaced by Derek Gee-West (Lidl-Trek) on lap two. Jonas Rutsch (Lotto Intermarché) tried to bridge across the gap of around one minute, but eventually went back to the peloton after the effort proved too much.The breakaway's advantage stabilised at 1:40 even after Lebo lost contact on the fourth lap. However, with 97km to go on lap five of eight 23.2km circuits, an attack split the peloton until a crash of two riders, one each from Modern Adventure and Lotto Intermarché, caused a slowdown and the peloton reformed.Lozano led the breakaway across the top of Manayunk Wall for the fifth time to extend his lead in the mountains classification but the escapees' advantage was falling quickly. Once the team cars were pulled out from in between the groups, it signalled an imminent end for the breakaway. A group of 11 riders split from the peloton on the climb and were in hot pursuit, and, after Lozano dropped back as the chasers drew closer, the two lead groups came together with a larger group making contact, too.Not long after the start of lap six, Filippo Magli (Bardiani-CSF 7 Saber) made a solo move that was quickly brought back by a peloton with only about 25 riders.On the Manayunk Wall for the sixth time, NSN drove the pace into the climb, with Riley Sheehan forging a very promising four-rider breakaway with Bob Donaldson (Jayco Alula), Luke Lamperti (EF Education-EasyPost) and Tim Torn Teutenberg (Lidl-Trek). The peloton shattered to bits because of the injection of pace, and four riders formed the first chase: Lidl-Trek's Sebastian Grindley, Rutsch, Ben Oliver (Modern Adventure) and Eder Frayre (L39ION of Los Angeles).The first two groups came together before the start of lap seven of eight, with Gee and teammate Tao Geoghegan Hart, Cedric Beullens (Lotto Intermarché), Lange and Martin Marcelussi (Bardiani) chasing at 1:15. They were joined by Magli and five others, including US champion Quinn Simmons (Lidl-Trek), with the rest of the peloton seemingly out of the race.After the wall, it was only Simmons and Simone Gualdi (Lotto Intermarché) left in pursuit at 35 seconds. Another group was 40 seconds further back, with two Bardiani riders, Magli and Marcellusi, Colby Simmons (EF Education-EasyPost) - Quinn Simmons' younger brother - Luka Mezgec (Jayco Alula), Gee, and Filippo Rodolfo (Novo Nordisk)was behind at 1:05.Quinn Simmons and Gualdi had closed to 30 seconds before the Manayunk Wall when Grindley punctured out of the lead group and, after a wheel change, was able to get up to his teammate and help chase.Donaldson, Sheehan, Lamperti, Teutenberg and Rutsch led over the top on the last ascent of Manayunk Wall, having lost Oliver and Frayre on the climb, but the pair were able to rejoin after the descent.As the race headed into the two short laps, the chasing trio still had 25 seconds to make up on the leading seven, who were cooperating nicely, with the US Champion doing most of the work.The two groups came together on the first of two frantic short circuits, with Rutsch, Donaldson and Teutenberg powering away on Lemon Hill. item.title: Marcus Rashford’s Manchester United return feels like a marriage of convenience | Will Unwin
item.author: Will Unwin at Old Trafford
item.content:encoded: A lack of offers and problems in finding a replacement may be behind the move, but that does not mean it cannot workThe first chant of the match was for Marcus Rashford, Manchester United’s returning rogue son, the one banished for 18 months, first to the Midlands and then Catalonia. Every football fan loves an academy product who has risen up the ranks, from scrawny child to getting 76,000 off their seats. Rashford is one of these, living out the dream of everyone inside Old Trafford and they are willing to forgive but want something in return.Not since 7 December 2024 has Rashford been seen in red at Old Trafford. Then it was as a substitute forlornly trying to turn things around in an eventual 3-2 defeat by Nottingham Forest. His relationship with Ruben Amorim was already deteriorating, the second head coach to have become irritated with Rashford. After loans with Aston Villa and Barcelona, everyone is surprised to see him back; it feels like a marriage of convenience because of a lack of offers and securing a replacement was deemed complex.Continue reading...

item.title: Aragon Grand Prix 2026 MotoGP rider rankings
item.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
item.content:encoded: Marc Marquez picked up the 37 points he had targeted at the Aragon Grand Prix - but was he the true star of the MotoGP weekend?... OK, yes, he was, but there was another rider who shone every bit as bright, and it was very close between the two of them for number one honours in our rider rankings this weekend. 6th 4th 2ndThis isn't a perfect Acosta weekend - crashed in FP1 (as he does), crashed in Q2 (as he does), damaged his bike while dragging it back into its sprint grid slot after overshooting the mark.But I feel zero hesitation placing Acosta as the number one here, despite the exceptional job Marc Marquez did, and below is the stat that swung it for me.Acosta's fastest Aragon GP lap: 1m47.093sAcosta's 20th-fastest Aragon GP lap: 1m47.457sKTM's fastest non-Acosta Aragon GP lap: 1m47.734s 2nd 1st 1stTitle rival Marco Bezzecchi correctly identified on Friday that Marquez was "for sure hiding a little bit". Despite Bezzecchi and Acosta's best efforts, he never really looked beatable when points were on the table this weekend.A couple of rough edges here and there - a Turn 14 mistake chasing pole in Q2, a ride height device error while divebombing Bezzecchi at the start on Sunday - never looked like anything his sheer pace wouldn't overcome.I suspect he could've won both races by a fair bit more if that were the target. 1st 3rd 3rdThe left knee gash he suffered at Assen two months ago is still troubling Bezzecchi, and was a particular hindrance at Aragon - but as far as the battle within Aprilia goes, he was in total control all weekend, leading the line in every session but FP1.It's fair to ask whether he did enough to protect his lead at Turn 1 in the sprint - Bezzecchi himself seemed to wonder exactly that - but the grand prix result seemed as good as it was ever going to get. 9th 9th 15thAwesome to have him back - and better still that he looks like he's never left.Zarco said his only physical limitation was a bit of Friday cramping that he correlated with "six coffees on Thursday" - and the timesheets looked like a rider at full fitness, though also one who still needs to get back into the groove of wheel-to-wheel racing.In the end it was incident-free and with the two long lap penalties for the crash in which he got hurt back in May finally served (and the Sunday pace was very solid, even if the long laps ruined the result).Impossible to be unhappy with this. 10th 7th 9thMoreira has ranked higher than this a couple of times this season, but I suspect this was actually his best weekend yet in MotoGP, or at least his most purely competitive.He under-delivered a bit on Friday and nearly denied himself Q2 by crashing late on in Q1, but his sheer pace carried him through - and for once he seemed comfortable enough doing his laps by himself, without a reference rider, which bodes incredibly well for his future.Both races were strong, though Sunday in particular required him to hang on a bit - and he felt he could've kept Enea Bastianini behind for eighth with a cleaner final lap. 3rd 2nd 4thThe younger Marquez ran his brother impressively close over one lap (faster on Friday, only a bit slower in Q2) and in the sprint - but had no answer in the longer distance.His grand prix was partially determined by a messy run through the opening corners, including a missed gear through Turns 2-3, but Bezzecchi and Acosta were probably out of reach anyway - and Marc definitively so.Nonetheless, he continues to impress. 11th 6th 6thAnother injury returnee albeit from a shorter absence, Aldeguer was firmly in Ducati's B-tier this weekend - far off the Marquez brothers but probably stronger than the others - and seemed happy enough with that.He found the low-grip Aragon wasn't punishing him physically, and seemed to have good pace - though he underwhelmed in Q2, so had to work hard for a pair of sixth places (which seemed about right for his performance). 13th 10th 11thCrashing on Friday afternoon while trying to stick with Marc Marquez for a laptime was the only bit of tangible underperformance from Miller all weekend, as he really impressed otherwise.Equipped with an "old-new concept" swingarm, Miller led the Yamahas in qualifying and was pace-y in both races, though on Sunday ultimately had no answer to the straightline speed of the KTMs late on. 5th 5th 5thMartin's track record at Motorland Aragon in grand prix racing is unremarkable, and he didn't much improve it here - but also kept the weekend from being a disaster.He plainly wasn't competitive relative to team-mate Bezzecchi but picked up a decent chunk of points, despite a very robust battle with Aprilia stablemate Raul Fernandez in the sprint.Martin admitted this was "a really bad weekend, I think the worst almost of the season in terms of speed" - yet in that context was happy with the yield, and believed his struggles were more track- and low-grip-specific rather than a recurrence of his mid-year woes with the RS-GP's front end. 19th 12th 13thThe second-best Yamaha rider this weekend, Rins quietly put together maybe his best weekend of the season - never the lead M1 rider but never particularly far from it.He was competitive enough to be actively disappointed with a feisty enough P13 in the end, feeling he had the pace - but not the engine power - to at least beat former team-mate Joan Mir. 15th 16th 12thMir found his usual strength - braking - "a nightmare" this weekend, so settled into a fairly anonymous, unremarkable rhythm.He was out of contention in the sprint right away via Turn 3 contact with Bastianini that relegated him to last, in which Bastianini may have been slightly more at fault but Mir anyway seemed a touch too ambitious.In any case, the grand prix itself showed there was just not much on offer. 18th DNF 14thMarini hopes and believes his side of the Honda garage has found something extra in qualifying trim - but wasn't quite able to exploit it this weekend. He was again solid on Friday but just on the wrong end of the Q2 cut-off, then again disappointing in Q1.A crash early in the sprint raised eyebrows as being un-Marini-like and was quickly determined to be a consequence of contact with Bastianini for which Marini bore very little responsibility. He did a reasonable job bouncing back on Sunday, though the extra two points are fairly immaterial. 7th DNF 7thA weekend that feels like it's snuffed out any realistic chance of Di Giannantonio being a major player in this title race from here on out - given Ducati matched up well with Aprilia at Aragon and yet he just couldn't capitalise.A crash from eighth in the sprint was a symptom rather than the biggest issue. He hinted that he believed this was down to a bad rear tyre, but much of the weekend beyond that just felt a little off - and Di Giannantonio indicated there have been various 'need-to-know basis' disruptions that cost him both at Aragon and Silverstone.Di Giannantonio wants to believe that even weekends like this one can still keep his title bid on track as long as he picks up some points - but I am not particularly optimistic. 16th 14th 8thBastianini looked very slow on Friday - and complained of the rear pushing the front again - and was then involved in a couple of early incidents in the sprint (with the Honda factory duo) that he might have had a decent bit of culpability for, though were not enough to penalise.He was struggling badly for front tyre longevity but seemed to find an improvement on Sunday, allowing for that classic Bastianini charge - but still in a different part of the race to where KTM stablemate Acosta was operating. 20th 17th 16thEspargaro found the second part of his return to the current 1000cc bikes a little easier at Aragon - but maybe not as much easier as you'd have expected.He was again fairly anonymous relative to his late-2025 heroics, not terribly far from KTM stablemates Brad Binder or Bastianini but with Acosta completely out of range.The picture was slightly better over one lap than race distances. In the sprint, he was spooked by the Marini crash and Fabio Quartararo engine blow-up, while on Sunday he found he "doesn't know how to act" with this bike right now on used tyres. 4th 8th DNFFernandez was in the top eight in every session until the grand prix, where he had an unspecified (seemingly gearbox-related) mechanical failure while running sixth.That moment was also the best he'd felt through the weekend, after some Sunday warm-up set-up tweaks, before which Fernandez wasn't really in the groove with his Aprilia despite some decent single-lap efforts.There was potential in the grand prix to significantly bump up his ranking, but as it turned out his Aragon GP was mostly notable for roughing up Martin in the early going into the sprint before running out of speed. 21st 13th DNFIn the more familiar confines of Aragon (relative to the Sachsenring and Silverstone) this was a much better outing for Razgatlioglu, a 13-time podium finisher at the track in World Superbikes... though only a one-time winner.Podiums and wins weren't on the table here but Razgatlioglu was acceptably competitive among the Yamahas - though found it difficult to overtake or avoid mistakes.One such mistake snuffed out a shot at points on Sunday, when - already struggling badly to maintain consistent pace due to the front tyre drop - he crashed with Zarco in pursuit. 14th 15th 10thBinder's farewell tour in MotoGP is playing out with few highlights. Aragon was never going to be one - what Acosta was doing the other KTM riders clearly could not do - but Binder also admitted execution let him down.Qualifying was reasonable for the pace (better than a disappointing Friday 'Q0' effort) but he had several offs in the sprint, then was barged down to 20th on Sunday in a cascade of overtakes that began with a Turn 11 error.Tenth from 20th is not bad. Tenth when your team-mate is second, 25 seconds up the road, is rough. 22nd 19th 17thLike Espargaro, Savadori has found the adjustment from his regular 850cc/Pirelli test work to this stand-in gig very complicated - and unsurprisingly he was last in every session, until the grand prix in which Quartararo dropped behind him and never repassed.Ultimately, it's nice that Trackhouse and Aprilia didn't leave Ai Ogura's bike vacant this weekend, but it didn't make a huge competitive difference. 17th DNF 18thQuartararo and Yamaha's 'post-divorce' run in 2026 hasn't been so bad - but this was one weekend where both may have been better off had he stayed at home.Unhappy to do multiple runs with a new chassis that he insisted was no upgrade and describing himself as "more of a test rider this weekend", Quartararo didn't qualify particularly well and didn't race particularly well at all.He is not culpable for the poor sprint, which was plagued by an engine issue even before the V4 finally gave out in smoke, but was a calamity in the GP - going off the track multiple times to eventually finish 52s off the winner. 8th 11th DNFA second profoundly bad weekend in a row, with Bagnaia pointing to a common culprit in having "completely zero" rear grip.Saturday morning's race pace session FP2 was his only truly good session (Q1 and Q2 were alright), but he was badly outmatched in both races and was already struggling for tyre life when he lost the rear and crashed out of the grand prix.He's still having work done on the arm that required surgery during the break but says, to his credit, that this is "not affecting the speed", of which there is very, very little right now. 12th 18th DNFA very poor weekend that never looked like much of anything, save for a glimpse of promise on Friday when Morbidelli did get into Q2 - again favouring a fast-lap reference from VR46 team-mate Di Giannantonio on track.He had a Q2 lap deleted for yellow flags that would've put him a row higher - but anyway just wasn't terribly competitive on race pace.He went off at Turn 12 early in the sprint and didn't have the pace to make any progress back up, then went down early on Sunday while in the pack - having gone "too aggressive on throttle", with the rear coming around.

item.title: Canada erects giant ‘Lake Ontario’ sign as spat with Trump over name escalates

item.content:encoded: Meanwhile, Trump posts video of himself kicking over a Lake Ontario sign and replacing it with Lake America signDonald Trump and Canada continued a verbal duel on Saturday over the US government’s administrative renaming of Lake Ontario, with the Ontario premier erecting a giant sign saying “Lake Ontario. Now and Always” – and the American president posting a video of him tearing down an avatar of that sign, erecting a replacement saying Lake America, and dancing to YMCA.Rhetoric over the naming of Lake Ontario is the public face of an escalating trade dispute between the US and its northern neighbor involving a 50% US tariff on Canadian steel and retaliatory tariffs from Ottawa.Continue reading...

item.title: 'A question of patience' - assured climbing display gives Vuelta a España leader Enric Mas a long-sought stage win
item.content:encoded: 'Enric Mas has been buried so often he should have a discount at the funeral parlour' Spanish newspaper wrote recently about the Vuelta a España leader. But the veteran Movistar leader's latest racing renaissance, stunning the opposition with an assured climbing display and outduelling of Oscar Onley (Netcompany-Ineos) at the summit of the Aitana is surely his finest revival yet.After taking over as Vuelta leader on Saturday following Tadej Pogačar's crashout and abandon, Mas had followed unwritten race etiquette to the letter by refusing to wear the red jersey on the winner's podium, as a sign of respect for the Slovenian.On stage 9, though, with Mas now clad in and his team expected to control the toughest climbing day of the 2026 Vuelta to date, it was equally an unspoken given that his rivals would test the new race leader through the mountains of southern Valencia to the absolute limit.Sure enough, Decathlon CMA CGM tried their utmost to sink the veteran Spaniard on the interminable ascent to Aitana, and Mas was isolated by the time the tiny peloton of favourites moved onto the crunch final six kilometres of the climb. However, Decathlon's leader Felix Gall was also on his own at that point, as were all the other contenders, and if Mas' capacity to defend the lead was truly under the microscope from then on, so too were the major rivals' ability to challenge him.Rather than crack, Mas more than rose to the occasion, responding time and again to the opposition's attacks and then finally making a searing move of his own with 3.9 kilometres to go. Even if Primoz Roglič (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe), second overall, did come close, only Oscar Onley was able actually to follow him directly.But by that point, in the closing kilometres of the Aitana ascent, the Spaniard was simply unstoppable. After dragging Onley to the line and then opening up his sprint from distance, the roar of delight as he crossed the line to clinch his first Grand Tour win since a stage of the Vuelta back in 2018 and confirm his status as race leader made it clear how important this victory was."Oscar is a very, very fast rider, but I had the chance, and from the team car they really handled me well psychologically on the climb, so I could finally do it," Mas said."The team deserve a 10 out of 10 for their work with me, and many thanks to the directors, telling me how they saw the others on the climb so I knew what to do."I'm a cautious kind of guy, and I've had lots of setbacks, but I think this is the best form I've had in my career. "It's also one of my most beautiful moments of my career, one of the best since I won that stage and finished second overall in the Vuelta as a young rider back in 2018.”Since then, Mas has seemingly always been condemned to a role as the 'nearly-man' in the Vuelta, taking four podium finishes overall, but never quite finding a pathway into red. On top of that, the Aitana marks the end of a massively complicated 15 months for Mas, forced to end his 2025 racing season prematurely due to being diagnosed with thrombophlebitis in his left leg, subsequently missing out on the Tour de France this July for the first time since 2018 and fighting to get back on terms ever since. By winning such a prestigious stage just a day after taking his first-ever Grand Tour lead, for Mas, then it's no exaggeration to say that it's as if Christmas has arrived early. For the 31-year-old's team, too, having their first lead in their home race since Nairo Quintana held the top spot for a day in 2019 and then backing that up with a stage triumph could not be more timely, either."It's been a question of patience," Mas explained. "Since a year last July, I've had lots of difficult moments, but I went home, saw the family and they helped me get back on it."Then after a very difficult start to the season, this summer I had a training camp at altitude, went to San Sebastian and then the Vuelta a Burgos and I've started having lots of good moments. And this is definitely one of them.”Before the Vuelta, Mas had refused to state if he had any specific objectives in the race, other than delivering the best performance possible. But already at Andorra, he managed to stay with the main GC favourites, and then on stage 6 there was a colossal moment of surprise when he succeeded in tracking down Pogačar close to the summit of the Puerto de El Bartolo, late in the stage.Since then, Mas has gone from strength to strength, and by lying second overall when Pogačar was forced out of the race, the Movistar veteran was waiting in the wings, and now the lead is his to defend.Asked if he needed the stage win to confirm that he was a rightful leader of the Vuelta, Mas replied, "I'm not sure, but now I'm proud of wearing it.”"This morning, I talked it through with the team a lot, because obviously what happened [Pogačar abandoning] was a very great disappointment for the race. Tadej is the best rider in the world and to get the jersey like this, you know…but the team was great, and now I've seen what I can do, too."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: 'I was motivated to do this for Tadej, for the team and for myself' - Pavel Sivakov narrowly misses Vuelta a España stage win for injured Pogačar
item.content:encoded: The French allrounder was off the front for nearly all of the toughest mountain day of the race to date, but after 175 kilometres ahead of the field, Decathlon CMA CGM determined acceleration on the Aitana proved fatal to his chances.Sivakov, Italian sprinter Alessandro Romele (XRG Astana) and Spanish national champion Marcel Camprubi had a gap of 1:20 at the foot of the final mammoth 22-kilometre climb on a large break. More importantly, they also enjoyed a 5:02 lead on the peloton.However, Decathlon's furious counter-charge relentlessly reeled in one attacker after another, and for all Sivakov had dropped Camprubi with 10 kilometres to do, his courageous bid to pay tribute to Pogačar just failed to pay off.Asked by Eurosport if he and his team had found it hard to change their attitude to the race following Pogačar's abandon and switch to chasing stage wins, Sivakov answered rhetorically, "I mean - do we have the choice really?"It's normal, we are here now to try and win some stages, and today I was really motivated to give it a go, for Tadej, for the team and also for myself.""You work really hard all year, so when you have an opportunity like this you have to try and take it."With his last win the overall of the Vuelta a Andalucia in 2025 and just seven wins to his name to date, the 29-year-old explained that he had done his utmost to claim what would have been a hugely emotive and symbolic victory. But he ran out of legs on a brutally challenging ascent, finishing 20th at the top behind stage winner Enric Mas (Movistar)."I went really deep, but unfortunately the climb was just endless. I couldn't see the end. When we turned right at the end onto the smaller roads, I could see the top, but it was just unfinishing," he explained."The legs were pretty good. I was fighting for the victory, and actually that's not a situation I was in so often. So I was nervous about how to manage it, but in the end I put myself in a good position. I just didn't have the legs to finish it off."Awarded the 'Most Combative Rider' prize by the organisation for his efforts, Sivakov promised that he and his teammates would do their utmost to get a win for themselves - and for Pogačar."Of course, there are many other opportunities," he told Eurosport. "It's only the first week now, and there are many other days to give it a go. We'll keep trying with all of the team."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Why it matters that President Trump just dialed in to a NASA news conference
item.author: Eric Berger
item.content:encoded: As is standard procedure for major NASA missions, the US space agency held a post-launch news conference on Sunday morning at Kennedy Space Center in Florida to provide information about how the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope was faring during its initial maneuvers.What was not standard, however, is what happened in the middle of the news conference. A little less than half an hour in, NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman looked down at his mobile phone, and then stood up and walked away from the dais where he had been seated behind a table along with other NASA officials. He briefly left the room.Isaacman returned about a minute later, phone in hand, apologizing for interrupting NASA's chief of science, Nicky Fox, as she was speaking about the mission. "The President of the United States of America would like to address and congratulate everyone on this mission," Isaacman said, returning to his seat.

item.title: 'Some guys were too fast'- Primož Roglič back in contention after difficult start to Vuelta a España
item.content:encoded: More than words, Primož Roglič's huge smile as he slowed to a halt at the summit of the Aitana spoke volumes about how he felt after the toughest mountainous stage of the Vuelta a España so far.The Slovenian veteran lost a little time to race leader Enric Mas (Movistar) and Oscar Onley (Netcompany-Ineos) but remains very much in contention for the overall, shedding 12 seconds at the line to finish third.With the time bonus and a six-second advantage on fourth-placed Felix Gall (Decathlon CGA CMN) at the finish, Roglič remains comfortably in second overall. But more than the result itself, his ability to stay fighting with the best after such a difficult build-up to the Vuelta was the real benefit.The four-times Vuelta a España winner's major crash when training had meant he began the race suffering badly. But after a reasonable opening time trial, and staying with the other top contenders when Tadej Pogacar (UAE Team Emirates-XRG) attacked at Andorra, the closing kilometres of stage 9 was the first time he really showed signs of a fuller recovery.Whilst not attacking, he was the only rider able to close the gap on Onley and Mas when they moved away towards the top. Mas then was sharp enough to attack again just as soon as Roglič closed in, but the Slovenian's limitations of the gaps bode very well for the two weeks to come."Like I said, we can always hope, but good, I'm super happy mate," Roglič said afterwards in a brief interview with the media at the summit of the Aitana."I didn't do much [but] it's beautiful to ride a bike now, outside in nice weather."They were hard climbs and some guys were too fast, but I'm happy.""For sure it's open definitely, but you know, I don't wish anything bad to anyone, so I wish him a fast recovery," Roglič, who has had more than his own fair share of crashes, concluded.It remains to be seen whether Roglič can now close the gap even further on his rivals and perhaps even start to gain time on Mas in the mountainous stages to come, with the time trial at the start of week 3 another big opportunity. Historically, too, Roglič has always tended to improve steadily throughout a race, and if there are repeats of the cat-and-mouse game that developed on the upper slopes of the Aitana, that'll also be the kind of scenario in which he thrives.But regardless of what happens, there can be no doubt that the Slovenian veteran is on the comeback trail, and determined to make an impact on GC in the Vuelta. Ten days ago in Monaco, that he could hit the heights again was anything but certain, but Aitana has shown that he is moving in the right direction again.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: UCI Mountain Bike World Championships: Sina Frei takes solo win to claim elite women's Olympic cross-country world title
item.content:encoded: The Swiss rider powered away on the third out of seven laps, quickly gaining time on her rivals before enjoying a victory parade on the last two laps, then punching the air in delight as she crossed the finish line with a 1:07 lead.Behind her, a heated duel raged between Martina Berta (Italy) and Nicole Koller (Switzerland) with Berta taking the sprint for second place ahead of Koller.Frei had already been showing good form, taking the double win at Les Gets last weekend, and two third places in the World Cup season so far.“I think it was more a dream,” Frei answered when asked if the XCO World Championships was a goal this year.“After two years where I really struggled, for me, it maybe in the middle of the season it became maybe a dream or a goal. But in the beginning of the season, it was for sure only a dream somewhere.”“I just wanted to focus only on myself. I can only influence myself, and because of that, I just tried to ride my own race and then I could also just go fast where it was for me. Kind of a little bit easier to go fast and recover in the parts where it was better for me, and somehow I managed to win.”Alessandra Keller (Switzerland) had to grapple with an early mechanical, pulling over in the start loop as defending champion Jenny Rissveds (Sweden) rode at the front. By the end of the first lap, the rider from Sweden had settled into a leading group of three with Frei and Berta, though the gap to a group including Puck Pieterse (Netherlands, Haley Batten (United States), Koller and Savilla Blunk (USA) was just eight seconds.Rissveds fell prey to a mechanical, and by the end of the third lap Frei was out front alone with an eleven-second gap to Berta. That gap just kept growing for Frei, but Berta was joined by Koller with the pair not so much in pursuit of Frei, who had a commanding 1:10 gap to the pair by the time the bell was rung for the final lap, but dicing for the silver.Sina Frei (Swi) SwitzerlandMartina Berta (Ita) ItalyNicole Koller (Swi) SwitzerlandPuck Pieterse (Ned) NetherlandsSamara Maxwell (NZl) New ZealandEvie Richards (GBr) Great BritainJenny Rissveds (Swe) SwedenLaura Stigger (Aut) AustriaSavilia Blunk (USA) United StatesHaley Batten (USA) United StatesGwendalyn Gibson (USA) United StatesIsabella Holmgren (Can) CanadaAlessandra Keller (Swi) SwitzerlandJolanda Neff (Swi) SwitzerlandGinia Caluori (Swi) SwitzerlandJanika Lõiv (Est) EstoniaMadigan Munro (USA) United StatesRonja Blöchlinger (Swi) SwitzerlandSofie Pedersen (Den) DenmarkVita Movrin (Slo) SloveniaLuisa Daubermann (Ger) GermanySina van Thiel (Ger) GermanyEmilly Johnston (Can) CanadaCandice Lill (RSA) South AfricaMona Mitterwallner (Aut) AustriaEmeline Detilleux (Bel) BelgiumAna Santos (Por) PortugalRebecca Henderson (Aus) AustraliaTatiana Saitarova (Rus) RussiaCaroline Bohé (Den) DenmarkGiuliana Salvini Morgen (Bra) BrazilCatalina Vidaurre Kossmann (Chi) ChileAdéla Holubová (Cze) CzechiaGabriela Wojtyla (Pol) PolandRamona Forchini (Swi) SwitzerlandYana Belomoina (Ukr) UkraineKristina Ilina (Rus) RussiaRaiza Goulao Henrique (Bra) BrazilTereza Tvarůžková (Cze) CzechiaKaren Fernandes Olimpio (Bra) BrazilEstibaliz Sagardoy Zunzarren (Spa) SpainMaria Carolina Flores Garcia (Mex) MexicoEkaterina Kovalchuk (Cyp) CyprusMaria Sherstiuk (Ukr) UkraineFatima Anahi Hijar Marin (Mex) MexicoAmélie Mackay (NZl) New ZealandTereza Kurnická (Svk) Slovakia
