item.title: Pet owners at risk of being ripped off by private equity firms as vet ownership rules change
item.author: Helena Horton
item.content:encoded: Critics say changes by CMA will allow multinationals to obscure their ownership of vet practicesPet owners have been warned that they could be unknowingly ripped off by private equity firms who have bought local vet clinics, after the Competition and Markets Authority (CMA) removed requirements for multinational companies to disclose which practices they own.The CMA recently ran an investigation into the monopolisation of vet practices, and found that the lack of competition and transparency of ownership had led to high prices and a lack of information for customers. Pet owners were often unaware their local vet practice could be owned by an international private equity company.Continue reading...

item.title: 'Stayin Alive' – Tadej Pogačar posts update from Barcelona hospital bed as question marks linger over cause of crash and rest of season after Vuelta a España abandon
item.content:encoded: Tadej Pogačar has been transferred by ambulance to a hospital in Barcelona following his abandon of the Vuelta a España, with surgery on his injuries from his crash late on stage 8 delayed until he has recovered sufficiently from a concussion.TV footage from late on Friday evening showed the former Vuelta leader leaving the hospital in Gandia – the nearest facility to where he crashed in southern Valencia and where Pogačar was initially treated – on a stretcher before being placed in an ambulance.The 350km journey by road from the southern Valencia region to the capital of Catalunya, where Pogačar is expected to undergo surgery for a broken collarbone, typically takes around four hours.The operation itself will need to be delayed, according to multiple media sources, because Pogačar suffered a concussion in the crash. He also sustained a fractured C7 vertebra, the lowest bone in the neck. Thankfully, the vertebra fracture is stable, Pogačar's UAE team have reported, meaning there's no risk of vertebra movement affecting the spinal cord.There were unconfirmed reports on Spanish TV that Pogačar could have his operation later today or tomorrow [Monday] in the Barcelona hospital, but for now the only definitive information is the need for a delay.The postponement of the operation raises even more questions about whether Pogačar will be able to return to racing before the end of the season, or if his year is now over.Before crashing out of the Vuelta, the Slovenian was next due to race at the Road World Championships in Montreal, Canada. After that, he was set to head for the European Championships in Slovenia before pulling down the curtain on his year, as usual, at Il Lombardia – a race he has won for five consecutive years.However, after such a serious crash and extensive injuries, it remains very unclear whether he will race again before the season ends.Another large question mark hangs over the exact cause of Pogačar's crash, which took place in the middle of a large peloton. Judging from the available television footage, it did not appear to have been caused by a collision with another rider.The team themselves did not blame anyone for the accident, describing it simply as a "race situation". Although there is speculation it may have been caused by the Vuelta leader riding over a small rock at the roadside and losing his balance, there is no definitive evidence. Until Pogačar himself provides an explanation, the exact cause remains uncertain.Pogačar posted a selfie to his Instagram story on Sunday morning. Soundtracked by Bee Gees' 'Stayin Alive'. The photo shows him lying in his hospital bed wearing a soft neck brace with plasters on his face and hand wounds.Meanwhile, the Vuelta itself continues with a new leader in Enric Mas (Movistar), who refused to wear the red jersey on the podium after stage 8 as a sign of respect for Pogačar. He leads with a minute's advantage over four-time Vuelta winner Primož Roglič (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe).Today's mammoth mountain stage 9, featuring more than 5,000 metres of climbing and a summit finish at the Alto de Aitana, should provide the first major sort-out of the remodelled GC.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. You'll get comprehensive race coverage of La Vuelta a España, subscriber-exclusive analysis from our expert columnists, in-depth features and industry-leading tech insight. Plus, the Cyclingnews app lets you follow the action wherever you go!

item.title: Nobody wins from trying to divide F1's fanbase
item.author: Glenn Freeman
item.content:encoded: "There are diehard motorsport fans who talk about clipping during a Formula 1 weekend, but there will also be many who think of a clip as something you put in your hair."Domenicali has had to fight back against a lot of criticism this year and, as you'd expect from someone in charge of a global institution that is flying high but also under huge pressure to succeed, he'll defend F1 with all he's got. As he should.But I think it's a risk to regularly paint the "diehard fans" as a minority group who are too negative, prompting Domenicali's recent quotes given to media that featured the suggestion that "negativity gets us nowhere".I'd agree that after a while, endlessly moaning about F1's engine rules gets a bit old and we all have to live with it. Although, let's not forget, the controversial not-quite-50/50 power split between electrical power and the internal combustion engine is changing for next year to help solve the issues fans and drivers are unhappy with.However, when things are going well - and in F1's case, they are on several levels at the moment - don't forget the people who got you to the dance. Don't forget that those "diehard fans" are people who stuck by F1 through thick and thin, and were the backbone of a fanbase that was big enough to make Liberty Media think F1 was worth buying in the first place in 2016.If the F1 bubble pops one day, or even just deflates a bit, it will need those diehards to stick around. If you alienate them while all the charts are pointing 'up and to the right', you run the risk of not having them as a safety net in future.Glenn spoke about this topic passionately on the latest episode of - you can listen here, or search for it on your podcast platform of choiceNone of this is meant to denigrate the vast wave of newer fans F1 has attracted in recent years. I think it would be unfair to suggest that anyone who has discovered F1 in the Liberty/Drive to Survive era is automatically a lightweight fan who isn't interested in anything beyond the surface level. No matter what George Lucas says.F1's growth should be great for everyone involved, both on the inside and the outside. As someone who remembers being one of only two F1 fans in my entire secondary school at the turn of the century, it's amazing to be on the school run with my own kids today and see how many F1 caps and backpacks there are around. This sport we live and breathe is truly mainstream now and appealing to the next generation, and I love that.That's why I'm uncomfortable with the notion that new fans and old fans, or new fans and "diehard fans", are two groups that can be divided into ones who are interested in technical details and bring negativity about the current cars, and ones who just want to see action on track.As someone once told me, 'people don't remain new fans forever'. Eventually many of the ones who stick around want to immerse themselves in what's going on and understand more about it. That doesn't mean they'll all want to know about super clipping one day - I've been an F1 fan since the late-1980s and I'd quite happily never hear about it again!I wince whenever I see older fans trying to 'gatekeep' F1, but I also don't think it's helpful to declare that people who want to know all the finer details of what's really going on with these highly complex cars are "a niche", as Domenicali recently suggested.Also, if "the vast majority of people" just want to see action on track, why not do more to make that happen? F1 is expected to have more sprint races in 2027, and as our social media team cheekily noted at Zandvoort, that weekend's sprint was so dull it 'could have been an email'.If the main focus is for the on-track action to get people out of their seats cheering lots of overtakes, why is F1 so cautious with its sprint format? Why is it just a stint of a grand prix that runs a day early?I'm all for protecting the sanctity of the grand prix itself. But let's mix the sprints up. Use one shot qualifying to differentiate from the main event and increase the chances of cars qualifying out of position. Or, dare I say it, reverse the grids, even if it's just the top 10.Arguing over super clips, super chips and hair clips is playground stuff. Let's find something proper to argue about, and see if we can create even more of that all-important action on track while we're at it.

item.title: People fleeing Sudan civil war face ‘dire and deteriorating’ conditions in refuge city
item.author: Rachel Savage in Johannesburg
item.content:encoded: More traumatised civilians are arriving every day at ‘shockingly overcrowded’ El Obeid and camps on its outskirtsHumanitarian conditions in the Sudanese city of El Obeid and two camps on its outskirts are dire and deteriorating, according to people on the ground, as civilians displaced by fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia continue to pour in from the surrounding countryside.The UN says more than 15,000 families have arrived since mid-July, joining more than 200,000 people who arrived in the first half of the year, according to government figures cited by Save the Children.Continue reading...

item.title: ‘You’re at war when you get attacked’: Mark Carney shows combative nature in face-off with Trump
item.author: Leyland Cecco in Toronto, Heather Stewart and Kalyeena Makortoff in London
item.content:encoded: The Canadian PM is one of the few world leaders to stand up to the US president. Former colleagues say they are not surprisedMark Carney stood before a walnut-veneered lectern, his face drawn tight, as he announced that talks with Canada’s biggest trading partner had collapsed. “Last spring, I warned that America is trying to break us so that they can own us,” he said. “And I promised: that will never, ever happen. We are keeping that promise.”For years, the former central bank governor had worked hard to calm markets. Now, he was asking Canadians to accept uncertainty and confrontation.Continue reading...

item.title: Westchester dates Knicks fans should circle
item.author: Russell Richardson
item.content:encoded: Bummed out by the ticket prices at Madison Square Garden? Head over to the Westchester County Center in White Plains, where the jerseys look familiar and the seats are much more budget-friendly!The Westchester Knicks released their complete 2026–27 schedule Friday. They open with two road games against the Maine Celtics on November 6 and November 8 before returning to their home gym to face the reigning G League champion Greensboro Swarm on November 14.The G League season begins with a 14-game Tip-Off Tournament, with regional pods of teams playing one another. That leads into the Winter Showcase, held December 19–22 in Orlando, followed by a 36-game regular season in which every team’s record resets. Regular-season play begins around December 27.You might be wondering whether G League games are as exciting as the big-league tilts. To which I counter: You would have had fun watching Tyler Kolek do this last season.Here are a few games we’ll be zeroed in on during the 2026–27 campaign.November 6 and 8 at Maine: Westchester immediately gets two games against Boston’s affiliate. The opening weekend should offer our first meaningful look at the Knicks’ developmental pecking order.November 14 vs. Greensboro: The home opener gives us our first chance to see this roster in the flesh locally, while the Swarm arrive fresh off the first championship in franchise history.Four early games against Long Island: Westchester faces Brooklyn’s affiliate twice during the Tip-Off Tournament and twice immediately after the regular-season reset. Four early games against the same opponent should provide a useful measuring stick, no?January 18 and 20 vs. Cleveland: The Cavaliers’ affiliate comes to town for consecutive games, providing another useful glimpse at how Westchester compares with one of the Eastern Conference’s stronger developmental pipelines.Three 11 a.m. School Day games: The annual chorus of several thousand children returns Wednesday, January 27; Tuesday, February 9; and Thursday, March 11. Bring earplugs.The eventual assignments of Tyler Nickel, selected 47th in this summer’s NBA Draft, and New York’s other prospects will determine how closely we follow each date. Either way, I hope to see you at a few games this season.

item.title: Prediction Markets and States Clashed, Setting Off a Furious Political Battle

item.title: Tadej Pogačar's brutally unexpected exit from the Vueltaa España is a massive reminder of cycling's intrinsic unpredictability - Analysis
item.content:encoded: Four days ago, after Tadej Pogačar's latest knock-out victory at Andorra, when UAE Team Emirates-XRG head of racing Joxean Fernández Matxin warned that nothing could ever be taken for granted in cycling, to be honest, it was hard not to think that this was simply stating a formality.Just look at Vingegaard, Matxin had pointed out, just when he was getting stronger in the Tour de France this July, "there was a roundabout, a crash and that was it." One of the Tour's most established figures, a five-times podium finisher and double winner had suddenly fallen by the wayside for 2026. Or, Matxin added, referring to the hailstorms that battered the Vuelta on stage 3, "who could have imagined that happening two kilometres before it did? Nobody."Certainly, and with all due respect to Jonas Vingegaard, when it came to Pogačar, such has been the scale of his success for the last three years, it was far harder to imagine that the Slovenian could suffer such a brutal reversal of fortune as he did on the roads of Valencia on Saturday afternoon.Since 2024, in fact, the number of races that Pogačar wanted to win and didn't can literally be counted on the fingers of one hand. And as for the ones he did conquer, from the Tour de France and the Tour of Flanders to the Tre Valli Varesine, the list has been almost endless. At the same time, since his heavy fall in Liège-Bastogne-Liège of 2023, breaking his wrist, and the loss of the Tour de France that followed, the setbacks have been minimal, and essentially have served as reminders of his crushing superiority in every race he started. Yes, he took six starts to win Milan-Sanremo this year, and his goal of winning Paris-Roubaix remains - after two attempts - still on the agenda. But there was that crash in Sanremo this year, too, and he still got back up and won. Equally, as soon as he announced he was taking part in the Vuelta a España, the only question, realistically, was who would be finishing second and how quickly he would put the GC out of reach. Pogačar's aura of invulnerability has increased exponentially with each triumph, even if the real reason for his success is due to a huge number of factors, with his own dedication to the sport and the sheer hard graft of training, as well as the constantly rising level of performance across the board of his entire team, not least amongst them. The answer regarding the speed of Pogačar's rise to the top in the Vuelta seemed to have been reached at Andorra, which he ended with an advantage of over three minutes and a leader's jersey that, for all the media speculation about possibly 'loaning' it to another team to ease the pressure on his squad for a while, seemed increasingly unrealistic. Even the unexpected arrival of rival Movistar’s Enric Mas on the summit of Puerto de El Bartolo on stage 6 alongside Pogačar seemed anecdotal, given how easily the Slovenian shrugged off the opposition, almost without trying, 24 hours later on the ascent to Aramón Valdelinares. With that in mind, if we look at it in sporting terms, the sudden exit of the world's number 1 from the Vuelta carries far more impact than any 'normal' abandon by the other top names. Following his crash out, UAE are rightly prioritising the rider's health and wellbeing above any other considerations. But for the race, the Pogačar-shaped power vacuum that so abruptly appeared when he finally had to admit he could not continue and clamber into the ambulance is one with massive consequences for the Vuelta too.Historically, too, for a rider to be dominating a Grand Tour on the level Pogačar was doing at the Vuelta and then to crash out is, fortunately, a real rarity. There was the case of Chris Froome in the 2014 Tour, where the Briton was defending champion and standout favourite, but when Froome abandoned after falling on the Roubaix cobbled stage, he wasn't in yellow and certainly hadn't shown the degree of domination Pogačar has displayed since day 1 of the Vuelta. Possibly the closest in a Grand Tour would be much further back, in 1971, when race leader Luis Ocaña had an advantage of over five minutes on Eddy Merckx and looked set to end the Belgian's stranglehold on Grand Tours. But a sudden fall on the rain-soaked Col de Menté, just when Merckx was on the point of admitting defeat (and had reportedly already done so to Ocaña), upended the race completely, as Ocaña abandoned.Comparisons between cycling's eras don't really work out, but on one level at least, we are now in the Vuelta a España, but not with a non-conformist, erratically brilliant racer like Ocaña, but with the Eddy Merckx of modern-day bike racing himself. As Larry Warbasse sagely put it after the finish of stage 8, the Vuelta GC has suddenly been flung wide open following the absence of the number 1 favourite to win it, but at the same time, as he said, absolutely nobody wanted to see Pogačar leave like this.Either way, Sunday morning's start of the Vuelta will see the race move into a very different kind of terrain to 24 hours earlier. And whoever stands the tallest on the winner's podium in Granada on the evening of September 13, the reminder that nobody, not even Pogačar, can avoid cycling's unpredictable edge will endure regardless, for a long time to come.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Disappointment at SD Worx-Protime as Mischa Bredewold misses fourth consecutive victory at Classic Lorient Agglomération
item.content:encoded: “If we’re honest, the race did not go the way we had hoped. We lost Lisa van Belle, Femke Gerritse and Nienke Vinke earlier than expected, and then Mikayla Harvey crashed out of the race. On the other hand, Elena Cecchini and Mischa Bredewold rode very strongly. At one point, Mischa became isolated, which meant she had to do too much work on her own,” said SD Worx-Protime sport director Christian Kos.Bredewold was seen closing down an attack by Anastasiya Kolesava (Canyon-SRAM) with 25km to go and was also among the riders reacting to a move by Cédrine Kerbaol (EF Education-Oatly) with 13.3km to go.When Célia Gery (FDJ United-Suez) and Eleonora Gasparrini (UAE Team L’Imad) attacked on the Côte de Ty Marrec, less than 6km from the finish, Bredewold was the one who tried to close the gap as soon as possible, recognising the danger of giving these two riders even a small advantage. However, it was only when Lidl-Trek took over the chase in numbers that the two late attackers were brought back, and Bredewold then focused on her sprint, launching with almost 500 metres to go.“She did her sprint the way she wanted to, although she may have started just a little too early. Only Elisa Balsamo was able to pass her thanks to a particularly powerful sprint. Naturally, disappointment is the main feeling at the moment and we are frustrated. But Mischa came very close to a fourth consecutive victory and delivered an excellent performance,” Kos finished.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: 'A lot of people thought they were superheroes today' – Matthew Brennan laments risk-taking in Vuelta a España peloton on a day marked by numerous crashes
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: After a crash-marred day at the Vuelta a España, double stage winner Matthew Brennan has called out the level of risk-taking he saw in the peloton, saying, "A lot of people thought they were superheroes today."Saturday's stage 8 was marked by crashes from start to finish, with one in the neutral zone taking out two riders, Primož Roglič getting caught in one early in the day, a crash involving several riders at 10km to go, a mass pile-up in the final 300 metres, and, most notably, race leader Tadej Pogačar's fall and abandon 32km from the finish.Speaking after the finish, Brennan, who sprinted to 10th place in Xeraco, was less than pleased with what he witnessed during the stage."There were a lot of crashes today, and I think that kind of set the tone for the day. A lot of people thought they were superheroes today. I'm willing to risk it a little bit, but when some people are happy to fall off for the risk of the win, I'm not super comfortable with that," Brennan told ."The team tried their best, and I tried to follow Christophe [Laporte], but in the end, these people were too aggressive for my liking. I lost a wheel, and then I couldn't really go from any good place. I tried to get back, but then you're not really in the position to sprint. So it is a shame because they did work really hard, but it is what it is."You see it all day. Considering I did about 160 watts for three hours, I don't know what people are doing. If you're willing to risk it at 160 watts, then I think you're a bit crazy, but it is what it is."Meanwhile, Brennan's teammate Wout van Aert was on hand to give a first-hand account of the day's defining crash, that of Tadej Pogačar.The Slovenian left the race with heavy wounds to his left shoulder and the left side of his face after suddenly swerving right and colliding with a Visma-Lease a Bike rider before hitting the deck hard. Van Aert said it looked like Pogačar lost control after hitting bumps in the road."I think he was moving up on the left-hand side. From where I was riding, it looked to me as though he lost control of his handlebars due to bumps in the road, which caused him to lose his balance, crash into the peloton and basically do a somersault," Van Aert told ."So I could see straight away that it was a really serious crash. Two of my teammates were down right in front of me, so yeah... it was one of those moments where you briefly forget you're even in a race."'I know what it's like to be injured, and I think the rest of the season is the least of his worries right now'Van Aert wished Pogačar well in his recovery. The world champion left the race in an ambulance, headed straight to hospital for checks.He climbed on board with his left arm in a sling and padding on wounds on his left shoulder, though it's not yet clear what injuries he sustained in the fall."It's certainly not up to me to draw any conclusions about his injury right now. First and foremost, I just hope it's not too serious, that he can recover well and be back soon without any pain," Van Aert said, noting that Pogačar's withdrawal is a "big loss" for the race."I know what it's like to be injured, and I think the rest of the season is the least of his worries right now. If it's not too serious, hopefully he'll be back soon, but I think we'll all just have to wait and see.Pogačar's withdrawal means Van Aert now has total control of the points jersey, leading with 124 points to Brennan's 67.The Belgian nipped out from the peloton to grab 20 points at the intermediate sprint, incidentally just before Pogačar's crash, though their lead-out 35km later didn't go so smoothly. He and Laporte led the peloton into the final kilometres, but Brennan was caught around a dozen riders back and so couldn't compete for the win."I'd been aiming [for the intermediate sprint] right from the start of the day. I think we rode another really good race as a team. Everyone gave everything. We didn't get any help, which we didn't expect either, but we had the race under control," Van Aert said of the stage."The moment Christophe, Matthew, and I were supposed to finish it off, we lost each other. I found Christophe again on the home stretch and thought Matthew was on my wheel, so I actually made the mistake of launching my sprint when I probably should have waited a bit longer. So yes, it's a shame."With 5,000 metres of climbing on the menu for Sunday's stage to the Alto de Aitana – not a day for Brennan or Van Aert – the two sprint stars can take a day away from the stress that permeated stage 8. As Brennan concluded, there will be more chances in the coming fortnight."The thing is, we can go on to the next one. Tomorrow won't be a day for me, but I've already won two stages, so it's not like I'm chasing anything in particular," he said."But yes, we can always try again. That's the beauty of a Grand Tour."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: 'It's a sad way to end it' - exit of Tadej Pogačar sparks wave of sympathy and regret in the Vuelta a España peloton
item.content:encoded: The first show of solidarity that the peloton showed was the way they slowed down completely after news trickled through that Pogačar had crashed, virtually suspending the racing of their own volition in order to give the Vuelta leader a chance to regain contact. Even 30 kilometres further on, though, once they had crossed the finish line, many riders were still trying to get a grip on what had happened. In the case of Pogačar's seven remaining teammates, understandably, they simply headed straight on for the team bus."It's difficult to describe, I'm very happy because it's my first Grand Tour win and I've been waiting for that for 13 years, but I'm very disappointed for Pogi' too," Coquard said. "I will remember this day for my victory, but at the same time, I'm very sad for him, all my support to him and I hope he recovers.""I know that tomorrow, though, all the news headlines will be about him."According to Coquard, even though the road was straight and wide open when Pogačar fell, the speed and the tension because the peloton was approaching the crucial climb of the day made it the kind of situation where accidents were waiting to happen."Every time in cycling, now, we want to get in a good position, because it's a big road, but it was very fast," he recounted. "I was looking at the left when the crash happened, but as I'm small, I don't see so much that's going on in the peloton.""But suddenly I saw a bike flying and after a few minutes we heard Pogačar had stopped.""We were going not too fast afterwards, but then we heard he'd stopped the Vuelta and things started again.""In the town there was a bunch of what do you call them, some bollards in the middle, and then the peloton going left right, everyone's fighting for the bottom of the climb," Larry Warbasse (Tudor) told reporters."Then there was boom, a big crash on the left. I couldn't see, but I heard the crash, we heard that Pogacar went down.""Everyone slowed down in the bunch, everyone was waiting to hear, and then you hear - he's not moving and then a minute or two later - ok, he's out of the race."To call this a game changer for the Vuelta is the biggest of understatements, but as Warbasse said, "to be honest, everybody is a bit sad. There was a kind of heavy feeling in the bunch.""That's kind of funny, because obviously the race is open now, but everybody felt bad because not how you want him to be out of the race.""It's going to totally change the dynamic of the race, so it's a bit too bad, I think everybody felt a bit sad for him, it's a sad way to end it. Hopefully he can recover for the Worlds, but I have no idea."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: ‘Right now we have to be with Tadej the person' - UAE Team Emirates-XRG management prioritize Pogačar's recovery after Vuelta a España leader crashes out of race
item.content:encoded: Shocked, concerned and still trying to absorb what happened in the finale of stage 8 of the Vuelta a España, UAE Team Emirates-XRG management have said that their only priority after Tadej Pogačar crashed out is to support the rider as much as possible.Some 34 kilometres from the finish, what should have been a totally normal transition stage suddenly warped into disaster for the Slovenian champion as he fell heavily on the left-hand side of the road.Visibly shocked and with his shoulder bloodied, after briefly attempting to continue, Pogačar had no choice but to end his Vuelta there and then. It was his first abandon in a race since crashing out of Liège-Bastogne-Liège in 2023, and his first ever in a Grand Tour.After more than a week when everything seemed to be going Pogačar's way in the Vuelta, suddenly the race had morphed into disaster for the world champion. And at the UAE team bus in a side road of the small finish town of Xeraco, team manager Joxean Fernández Matxin explained to a huddle of media that the team's only concern at the moment was Pogačar's personal wellbeing. "I thought in the first moment he would continue, but after [there was] shoulder pain, I understood the shoulder was not in a perfect situation for this," Matxin, who had been with Pogačar when he abandoned, said."He couldn't continue on his bike, he [had to] go to the ambulance. Now he's with the doctors, and we stay with Tadej.""Tadej gives a lot of victories to his teammates, to his team, we will try to continue with high moral, to take stages to give to Tadej."Pogačar initially wanted to go on, Matxin said, but then it quickly became clear that it was not possible. "The reality was the situation was complicated, and his shoulder was in a lot of pain. He couldn't continue."As for what had caused the accident, it remains unclear, although has claimed to identify a small rock on the side of the road as being responsible for the crash. But whatever the reason, the fall was a bizarre one, particularly as even though the pace was high, the road was both broad and completely straight. Matxin himself said that from hereon, in any case, rather than putting the blame on the race or anybody else, the main priority of the team was Pogačar the person."Now we stay with Tadej the person, his personal situation is bad so we need to stay with him. And we'll continue in the race," he ended, before confirming Pogačar was in hospital."At the time, I couldn't talk to him, obviously, about what actually happened, " Matxin then told , "But these are situations that sometimes happen in cycling,""Now in any case, we have to be with Tadej the person, not with Tadej Pogačar the cyclist, or Tadej Pogačar the champion or Tadej Pogačar the leader of the Vuelta.""We need to be with him more in the bad moments than we do in the good ones."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: 'I think it's something to show respect to him' – New Vuelta a España leader Enric Mas refuses to wear red jersey on stage 8 podium after Tadej Pogačar's abandon
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: He took to the podium in Xeraco to conclude a fraught, crash-heavy 171km sprint stage, but didn't wear the red jersey. Instead, the Movistar leader held it out in front of him ahead of his first day in red, tomorrow's climbing stage to the Alto de Aitana.Speaking to after the stage, Mas said that his refusal to wear the red jersey on the podium was a show of respect for now-former leader Pogačar."To be honest, I know this is sport and cycling, but today he crashed. I didn't win the red jersey that way, so I think it's something to show respect to him," Mas said.Speaking to as he warmed down after the stage, Mas wished Pogačar well in his recovery from what looked like some nasty wounds to his left shoulder and the left side of his face.The world champion headed straight to hospital for checks and treatment, and the full extent of his injuries is yet to be revealed."It's a huge shame that first of all there are crashes, then of that kind, and finally that it's Tadej. He was actually wearing the red jersey, and it's a real shame. And well, obviously that he recovers quickly, as we still have quite a few races left, and I hope he can arrive in good shape for them," Mas said."Honestly, I don't know what he has; I heard something about his elbow, but anyway, I'm sure he'll be in the best hands, with the best doctors, and hope he recovers as quickly as possible."With no Pogačar in the race, Mas will be wearing red on Sunday with a one-minute lead over four-time Vuelta winner Primož Roglič (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe), while Felix Gall (Decathlon CMA CGM) lies 11 seconds further back.The 31-year-old may have finished second at the Vuelta – in 2018, 2021, and 2024 behind Simon Yates, Remco Evenepoel, and Roglič – but this will be the first time he has ever worn red. Mas said he and Movistar will take responsibility and defend his new jersey."Another race starts now, and I hope we are ready for it," he told ."Tomorrow is one of the hardest stages, alongside Stage 20. We have to try to enjoy the stage and the place where it is. I know the team will do a super good job."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Winners and losers from MotoGP's Aragon sprint
item.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
item.content:encoded: Marc Marquez has lived up to his status as pre-weekend favourite at Aragon in the sprint, clawing back some much-needed points in the MotoGP title race.With no prizes for guessing which category we're placing him in, here are our winners and losers from MotoGP's Saturday action.Winners: The Marquez brothers (1st and 2nd)A callback to 2025 not just in it being a Marc-Alex 1-2 - but in the fact it looked fairly uncomplicated.Once Marc ushered the soft-shod polesitter Marco Bezzecchi to the outside of Turn 1, he was all but assured a straightforward race. His title bid needs 37 points here - and it looks like he will get them. He has already all but promised to repeat the same Turn 1 move on Sunday.On Alex's side, another morsel of evidence that he is a genuine Aragon master - but also a continuation of an increasingly strong season that's not really reflected by the standings.Loser: Raul Fernandez (8th)Fernandez doesn't owe anything to Jorge Martin's title bid, but it's probably less than ideal that his race was only notable for roughing up Martin on lap one - before settling into a relatively anonymous ride to eighth.Once a dominant Moto2 winner at Aragon, Fernandez says he hasn't felt comfortable at the track since its resurfacing, and here unlike his fellow Aprilias he didn't fancy the lifespan of the soft rear.Eighth is no disaster but being beaten by a KTM and a Honda is underwhelming.Winner: LCR Honda (7th and 9th)Team-mate battles are usually zero-sum games but both Diogo Moreira and Johann Zarco are clearly boosting their value this weekend - and both LCR and Honda, which has both riders under contract beyond 2026, have every reason to be delighted.Zarco really doesn’t look like he’s been out for three months (or even two months, or one month). He led the line for Honda in qualifying and was mixing it in the usual places in the sprint (though he felt a tiny bit of regret in not attacking Fernandez earlier to make his race even better).And Moreira is clearly exceptionally comfortable this weekend, as evidenced not just by his sprint performance but by the fact he decided not to follow other riders in Q1 and advanced by flying solo.Loser: Pecco Bagnaia (11th)This was in some ways what we used to expect from Bagnaia in a sprint - in that he only built into the race once it was already all but over. Except it was transposed much further down the grid than we used to see him.The end result, thus, is a finish comfortably outside of the points - and the evaluation is much the same as on Friday - a lack of rear grip.After a mid-season flourish he is firmly in the doldrums again.Winner: Jack Miller (10th)The best Yamaha in three of the five comparable sessions so far this weekend, Miller has probably profited at least a little bit from Fabio Quartararo's engine issue (which he'd felt all weekend before it finally gave up the ghost on Saturday).But even accounting for that, Miller’s probably the faster Yamaha rider right now - suddenly soaring in what we now know for sure to be his last half-season in MotoGP.Picking off Zarco at the end would've been the cherry on top here, but even without a point a top-10 looks very nice on paper.Loser: Factory Honda (16th and DNF)LCR’s rookie and returnee have relegated Honda's actual factory team duo firmly to the status of afterthought so far this weekend.For what’s supposed to be Honda’s main team, this sprint was effectively over midway through lap one, when Luca Marini slid out of the race - as unlucky collateral in a Miller-Morbidelli-Bastianini incident right ahead of him - three corners after Joan Mir had to pick up his bike and go to last place due to contact through Turn 3 with, again, Enea Bastianini.But even before that it was unlikely to be a particularly productive race for either Mir or Marini, who aren't dreadfully outmatched but aren't on the level of the LCR duo.Winner: Pedro Acosta (4th)Acosta managed to fit in a whole slapstick routine in the moments before lights out, though it was hard to see on the broadcast. Seemingly distracted by Alex Marquez right in front of him, he blew past his grid slot, had to hop off his KTM and reverse, then kicked off a seat winglet as he rushed to hop back on.The result was a less-than-compliant bike through the fast right-handers and thus a disappointed Acosta, but you really wouldn't know something was amiss if you compared him to his fellow KTM riders, who he ran rings around again.It seems far-fetched to suggest he could've got much more out of this one.Loser: Fabio Di Giannantonio (DNF)Di Giannantonio isn't really winning races this season so his title bid demands extremely dependable points-scoring, with no room for errors - which, however, are increasingly creeping in.This crash from eighth is much less of a problem than the DNF from the grand prix in Germany, as the points blow today is negligible, and within the Ducati camp he clearly does not have an answer to the Marquez brothers at Aragon.But the potential confidence blow isn't well-timed.Winner: Fermin Aldeguer (6th)Aldeguer needed to qualify better and probably needed a better first lap - but his pace looks pretty electric this weekend, and he had impressively little trouble working his way through the likes of Bagnaia, Zarco, Fernandez and Moreira.Given his recent injury and given his status as a GP25 rider, this race is another positive signal.

Vuelta a España Stage 8: Coquard Wins First Grand Tour Stage, Pogačar Crashes Out
item.author: sstokes
item.content:encoded: Race leader Tadej Pogačar’s dream of a Tour-Vuelta double ends with bizarre fall, while Bryan Coquard takes breakthrough result.

item.title: Vuelta a España: Bryan Coquard edges out Mads Pedersen to win crash-marred stage 8 as Tadej Pogačar abandons
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: A chaotic day full of crashes at the Vuelta a España ended with the expected bunch sprint in Xeraco, with Bryan Coquard (Cofidis) sprinting to a first-ever Grand Tour stage victory.The Frenchman beat Mads Pedersen (Lidl-Trek) to the line at the end of the 171km stage as Jordi Meeus (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) rounded out the podium in third place.Visma-Lease a Bike had set up the sprint once again for double stage winner Matthew Brennan, but the Briton was out of position and well out of it after launching his sprint from outside the top 10.Further back, a mass crash inside the final 300 metres saw most of the peloton held up, leaving the sprinters to battle it out. Pedersen hit the front first, but it was Coquard, riding the wheel of Meeus, who had the better finish, edging out the Dane in a photo finish."I've finished second a lot of times in Grand Tours, and I'm 34 years old, and I'm very proud and very happy," Coquard, who raced his first Grand Tour at the 2014 Tour de France, said after the finish."My team did a perfect job. We don't have a lot of top lead-out men, but I had Alexis today. All of the climbers tried to take me to 5 km to the finish line in a good position with Alexis, and after that, I just followed Alexis. At 500 metres, I saw Jordi Meeus, and I knew he was very fast in this type of finish. So I waited and waited."I knew it was a little headwind-crosswind, but in the city, it was more of a headwind. I made my effort at the right moment, using the draft, and I'm so proud and very happy. I've waited a long time for this victory, and I've worked a lot as well. It's an amazing, amazing day."I was not unconfident, but yes, I had some pressure because when you don't do a good sprint, it's one opportunity less. You don't have a lot of opportunities for sprinters in this Vuelta. I wasn't in a good position in the first two sprints, but I knew I had good legs yesterday in the breakaway. Maybe I climb a little better now, but I'm fast again."While the sprint finish marked a historic day for 34-year-old Coquard, the big news of the day was the abandon of race leader Tadej Pogačar (UAE Team Emirates-XRG). The Slovenian, who had led the race since winning the opening stage, crashed hard on the run-in to the only climb of the stage 32km from the line.Pogačar suffered heavy wounds on his left shoulder and left side of his face in the fall, and received treatment by the roadside before he climbed into the ambulance, his race finished after eight daysThree-time Vuelta runner-up Enric Mas (Movistar) will now take over the red jersey with a one-minute advantage over Primož Roglič (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe), while Felix Gall (Decathlon CMA CGM) lies in third, a further 11 second back.After the summit finish of Aramón Valdelinares on Friday, the Vuelta a España returned to the flatlands for stage 8 on Saturday with a run past the city of Valencia to a finish on the Costa de Valencia.The 171km stage, running between Puçol and Xeraco, featured few difficulties along the way, save for the late third-category Puerto de Barx (4.7km at 5.6%), which lay 21km from the finish line.The stage began down three riders after Luca Van Boven's (Lotto-Intermarché) withdrawal following a heavy crash on stage 7. Floris Van Tricht (NSN) and Diego Uriarte (Kern Pharma) both left the race after going down in the neutral zone to start the stage.With a sprint finish likely and not much reason along the way to get out in the breakaway, there wasn't much of a battle for the break.After the summit finish of Aramón Valdelinares on Friday, the Vuelta a España returned to the flatlands for stage 8 on Saturday with a run past the city of Valencia to a finish on the Costa de Valencia.The 171km stage, running between Puçol and Xeraco, featured few difficulties along the way, save for the late third-category Puerto de Barx (4.7km at 5.6%), which lay 21km from the finish line.The stage began down three riders after Luca Van Boven's (Lotto-Intermarché) withdrawal following a heavy crash on stage 7. Floris Van Tricht (NSN) and Diego Uriarte (Kern Pharma) both left the race after going down in the neutral zone to start the stage.With a sprint finish likely and not much reason along the way to get out in the breakaway, there wasn't much of a battle for the break.Burgos-Burpellet-BH duo Sinuhé Fernández and José Luis Faura went clear after 12km of racing, though Faura soon dropped away from the move soon afterwards. No threat to the sprint squads, Fernández was allowed to head up the road, racing clear to a 5:30 lead.Mattia Gaffuri (Picnic-PostNL) became the next rider to leave the race after a mid-stage crash. GC contender Primož Roglič (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) also hit the deck but was able to continue without issue.Up front, Fernández raced into the final 100km with a reduced 3:40 advantage as Steve Kruijswijk (Visma-Lease a Bike) and Alpecin-Premier Tech worked on the front to control the situation.That time gap fell as the kilometres ticked by, and Fernández hit the final 50km with a slender one-minute lead. His solo adventure drew to a close 12km later, in time for the intermediate sprint at Simat de Val.Green jersey leader Wout van Aert nipped out of the peloton to grab the 20 points on offer ahead of Jordan Labrosse (Decathlon CMA CGM).There was barely time to digest the Belgian extending his points lead when disaster struck for race leader Tadej Pogačar. The Slovenian, racing near the front of the peloton on the run towards the Puerto de Barx, suddenly swerved in the bunch, colliding with another rider and hitting the ground hard.It soon became clear that Pogačar's race, and his bid for the red jersey, was over. After several minutes of treatment at the side of the road, he climbed into the ambulance and out of the race, his arm in a sling and padding on a wounded shoulder.Up the road, the peloton hit the climb slowly, unsure of Pogačar's status and out of respect for the red jersey. There were no big attacks on the way up, and Van Aert led the way across the summit for Visma-Lease a Bike.Xabier Azparren (Pinarello Q36.5) launched the first move of the finale, jumping clear with 25km to run and racing away to a 20-second lead. The Basque racer's move was a brave one, and he held on all the way down the descent and for much of the road into Xeraco.Behind, Visma-Lease a Bike and Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe led the chase, while the nerves in the peloton remained on the run-in to the line. Another crash struck at 10km to go, with Luke Tuckwell (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe), Carlos Canal (Movistar), Jan Hirt (NSN), Carlos Rodríguez (Netcompany Ineos), and Roland Thalmann (Tudor) all going down.That didn't stop the peloton from racing towards the line, full speed ahead, though, with Netcompany Ineos and Lidl-Trek also joining in the pacemaking. It was the British squad who finally brought back Azparren 2km from the line, setting up the sprint finale.Brennan's lead-out train of Van Aert and Christophe Laporte assumed their positions at the head of the peloton on the final run to the line, though their sprinter was well back, stuck behind almost a dozen other riders. Instead, it was Coquard, Pedersen, and Ben Turner (Netcompany Ineos) who were best-placed, just behind Laporte.A mass crash unfolded just behind the lead-out at the front, taking out a host of riders and holding up much of the peloton. Laporte peeled off with 150 metres to go, leaving Pedersen to launch the sprint as Brennan tried to move up on the outside to no avail.It looked like the finale would be Pedersen vs Meeus, but Coquard manoeuvred well, switching wheels and only hitting the wind inside the final 50 metres. At the line, the Frenchman edged ahead and could celebrate a long-awaited Grand Tour triumph.Bryan Coquard (Fra) CofidisMads Pedersen (Den) Lidl-TrekJordi Meeus (Bel) Red Bull-Bora-HansgroheBen Turner item.title: Tadej Pogačar suffers neck fracture and concussion in crash that ends his Vuelta a España
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: Vuelta a España race leader Tadej Pogačar has crashed and abandoned the race during stage 8, going down hard with 32km to go on the run-in to the day's only climb, the Puerto de Barx.The Slovenian, who had been in the red jersey since winning the opening time trial in Monaco, crashed in the middle of the peloton and was quickly tended to by medical staff. Pogačar suffered deep wounds and cuts to his left shoulder and left side of his face in the fall.After spending several minutes sitting on the road surrounded by race doctors and UAE Team Emirates-XRG staff, Pogačar got up and took his helmet off, his bid to add the Vuelta to his list of Grand Tour victories suddenly over.Pogačar climbed into an ambulance with his arm in a sling and heavy padding on his left shoulder. He will head straight to hospital for treatment and checks. The full extent of his injuries is not yet clear.The cause of Pogačar's fall wasn't immediately apparent on the television broadcast. He was riding towards the front of the peloton on the left-hand side shortly after the intermediate sprint in Simat de Valldigna.In an overhead video shot by the television helicopter, Pogačar suddenly swerved to the right, colliding with either a Visma-Lease a Bike or Uno-X Mobility rider before hitting the ground hard.The crash and abandon is the first ever for Pogačar in a Grand Tour and his first DNF in any race since Liège-Bastogne-Liège in 2023.Team confirms concussion and multiple fractures for PogačarIn addition to the wounds clearly seen during the Vuelta broadcast, the Slovenian has suffered fractures to his left collarbone and to the lowest bone in his neck as well as a concussion."Unfortunately, Tadej suffered a heavy crash during today's stage and was unable to continue the race," said UAE Team Emirates-XRG medical director, Dr Adrian Rotunno."He is stable, and following a thorough medical assessment at hospital, Tadej has been diagnosed with a concussion, a displaced left clavicle fracture, a stable C7 cervical fracture, and multiple abrasions. Fortunately, no other major injuries and no neurological fallout."Thankfully fo Pogačar, the vertebra fracture being stable, means there's no risk of vertebra movement affecting his spinal cord.Pogačar will undergo surgery on his collarbone fracture, Rotunno stated."He will require clavicle surgery, which will be delayed due to concussion precautions. Tadej remains under the care of our medical team, and we’ll provide further updates following the surgery.”For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Classic Lorient Agglomération: Elisa Balsamo overtakes three-time winner Mischa Bredewold to triumph in Plouay
item.content:encoded: Elisa Balsamo (Lidl-Trek) won the Classic Lorient Agglomération - Ceratizit in the sprint of a reduced peloton, passing Mischa Bredewold (SD Worx-Protime) on the final metres to take the victory. Franziska Koch (FDJ United-Suez) completed the podium with third place.After an early breakaway was reeled in on the finishing circuit around Plouay, there were numerous attacks on the last two laps. Maëva Squiban (UAE Team L'Imad) got away with 12.5km to go and began the Côte de Ty Marrec 15 seconds ahead of the peloton but was passed on the climb when Célia Gery (FDJ United-Suez) and Eleonora Gasparrini (UAE Team L'Imad) attacked.Gery and Gasparrini were only a few seconds ahead, though, and when they were caught with 3.6km to go, the race was bound for a sprint finish. Bredewold tried to anticipate by using the downhill into the finishing straight to get up to speed and launch a long sprint, but Balsamo went into Bredewold's slipstream, pulled alongside on the last 100 metres, and just pipped Bredewold to the line.“I need to say a big, big thank you to my team. They did an amazing job. When I saw that I could survive the last climb, we went all in for the sprint. I’m super happy,” Balsamo thanked her teammates for setting up her victory.“On the last climb I was just watching the wheel in front of me because it was so hard. But I was still in the first group, and I fully trusted my teammates. I knew they could close everything,” she looked back on the final time up the Côte de Ty Marrec.Bredewold, winner of the previous three editions, tried to go long in the sprint, but Balsamo just managed to pass her.“She started a really long sprint on the left and I was on the right, but I know this is a super hard finish, so I kept believing until the end because I know it’s super hard, especially the last 50 metres,” said Balsamo.Starting and finishing in Plouay, the 172.6km race consisted of a long 104km loop to the south and east before returning to Plouay in order to climb the Bosse du Lézot out of the town and do another 25km loop including the Côte de Marta Kerhoat. The race entered the finishing circuit with 41.6km to go and would do 2.5 laps, with a total of three ascents of the Côte de Ty Marrec and another two climbs of Lézot.In the first hour of racing Sara Martín (Movistar) initiated a breakaway that also included Cristina Tonetti (Laboral Kutxa-Fundación Euskadi), Alison Jackson (St Michel-Preference Home-Auber93), and Natalie Quinn (Mayenne-Monbana-MyPie), though Jackson soon dropped back after a mechanical.Instead, Anna Henderson (Lidl-Trek), Anouska Koster (Uno-X Mobility), Sophie von Berswordt-Wallrabe (VolkerWessels), and Clémence Latimier (Ma Petite Entreprise) bridged to the front to make it a break of seven, and they increased their advantage to seven minutes.When the live broadcast began with 65km to go, the gap was down to 3:30, and Von Berswordt-Wallrabe had lost contact with the other escapees on the Bosse du Lézot. Latimier crashed on a downhill 180-degree turn with 58km to go. She could rejoin the break, but a few minutes later, there was a big crash in the peloton in the same turn that took down pre-race favourite Kim Le Court-Pienaar (AG Insurance-Soudal), Marte Berg Edseth (Uno-X Mobility), and Mikayla Harvey (SD Worx-Protime), all of whom eventually had to abandon the race.Tonetti was dropped from the break on the Côte de Marta Kerhoat, and in the peloton there were attacks from Antonia Niedermaier (Canyon-SRAM), Nina Berton (EF Education-Oatly), Fleur Moors (Lidl-Trek), and Gery, though none of them could get away.Entering the finishing circuit at Pont Neuf with 41.6km to go, the peloton was two minutes behind. Passing the finish line with 32.2km to go to enter the penultimate lap, this had been reduced to 50 seconds, mainly by EF Education-Oatly.In the breakaway, Martín attacked in the lead-up to the Bosse du Lézot and was followed by Henderson, while Quinn then left Koster and Latimier behind on the climb in an attempt to bridge to the front duo, but all five escapees came back together after the climb.In the peloton, Niedermaier attacked over the top of the climb but was quickly caught again. Daniek Hengeveld (Visma-Lease a Bike) then got away on the plateau and went off to chase down the breakaway, finally bridging the 40-second gap with 22.5km to go, at the foot of the Côte de Ty Marrec, and immediately going to the front of the group.Koster could not follow the pace on the climb and dropped back to the peloton where Cédrine Kerbaol (EF Education-Oatly) had attacked, followed by Niamh Fisher-Black (Lidl-Trek), Gery, Gasparrini, and Sarah Van Dam (Visma-Lease a Bike). They reached the front group on the small roads after the climb but were caught again just after the 20km mark, prompting a counterattack from Koch, who was reeled in with 18km to go at the bottom of the short climb through Kerdalvé.Despite attacks from Loes Adegeest (Lidl-Trek), and world champion Magdeleine Vallières (EF Education-Oatly) on this climb, a peloton of more than 50 riders entered the final lap together. Mavi García (UAE Team L’Imad) attacked with 15km to go, before the Bosse du Lézot, but Vallières went after her, closed the gap, and then led the race up the climb to set up an attack by Kerbaol over the top.Koch reeled in Kerbaol, and after an unsuccessful attack by García, Squiban got away with 12.5km to go, quickly opening a gap. Sara Casasola (Fenix-Premier Tech), Rosita Reijnhout (Visma-Lease a Bike), Célia Le Mouël (Ma Petite Entreprise), Gery, Vallières, Letizia Borghesi (AG Insurance-Soudal), and Ingvild Gåskjenn (Uno-X Mobility) briefly formed a chase group but were soon back in the peloton.Francesca Barale (Movistar), Lucie Fityus (Picnic PostNL), and Katharina Sadnik (Visma-Lease a Bike) all tried to get away, but it was Nadia Gontova (Liv AlUla Jayco) who succeeded just before the turn onto the wide road up the Côte de Ty Marrec.Going into the climb, Squiban was 19 seconds ahead of the peloton, with Gontova having a three-second gap on the bunch. Vallières set the pace on the first half of the climb, catching Gontova, but then Gery attacked. The French champion quickly reached Squiban, who helped Gasparrini jump across before swinging off.Gery and Gasparrini were seven seconds ahead at the 5km mark atop the climb, but Lidl-Trek quickly organised the chase and caught them with 3.6km to go. Vallières launched a final attack into the Kerdalvé climb but was neutralised by Justine Ghekiere (AG Insurance-Soudal) and Niedermaier, and 34 riders entered the final kilometre together.Bredewold launched her sprint just after the 500m mark, accelerating along the barriers on the left-hand side while Balsamo was being led out on the right side. Bredewold was several bike lengths ahead at the 200m mark, but Balsamo had now found her wheel, pulled alongside on the last 100 metres and could beat Bredewold to the line while Koch beat Gasparrini As the current flagship model, the Torch uses Retül biomechanical fit data to deliver the exact power transfer and stiffness that drove its predecessors to victory across the WorldTour Pro Peloton.As expected from the S-Works mark, the Torch packs high-end materials into an ultralight 225g package (per shoe). It boasts a full carbon sole with an internal I-Beam for maximum power transfer, dual alloy Boa S3 dials for precise adjustment, and an adaptive upper that flexes around your foot's unique shape to prevent hotspots.Our expert tester, Aaron Borrill, awarded the S-Works Torch a glowing 4.5-star review, noting that only its steep RRP held it back from a perfect score. item.title: ‘It was fair that I got it' - Alessandro Romele accepts yellow card for crash incident that led to Luca Van Boven Vuelta a España abandon
item.content:encoded: Some 20 kilometres from the finish on stage 7, Romele lost balance and closed off Van Boven on the right-hand side of the road, with the Belgian racer spinning over a pavement and falling heavily. Van Boven remounted his bike and completed the mountainous stage, ending with a summit finish at Aramón Valdelinares, but was later diagnosed with much more serious injuries than were initially thought, including two broken ribs and a collapsed lung. Van Boven spent the night in hospital, and was confirmed by Lotto-Intermarché as a non-starter for stage 8. While Romele accepted responsibility for what had happened, the Lotto-Intermarché team management, talking to Sporza, said they did not blame Romele for the incident, saying "he does not have eyes in the back of his head.""It also wasn’t an ideal moment for him to pass, given that we were coming up to a right-hand turn, but I take the responsibility. I accept the card, it was fair I got it," Romele told a small group of reporters, including at the start. "Like they say in F1, it was a racing incident, a moment in which the peloton was quite relaxed, and we were going quite slowly. I lost control of my bike a bit on a speed bump, and that caused me to veer to the right, just as Luca was coming up after taking on bottles for his teammates.""I wrote a message to Luca straight after the stage just to clarify what happened. To tell the truth, I wanted to do it in person today at the bus, because I don’t really like sending messages, I'd have preferred to speak face to face. But that’s ok.""I heard that Luca was going to hospital, so I got his number and I spoke to him, and he understood the situation and that it was an accident. He understood that he was in the wrong place at the wrong time. "We spoke and cleared the air, and I’m very happy about that because the most important thing is to clear things up between you as riders. In terms of how the yellow card affects him for today's sprint, Romele said it was something that didn't help, but "yesterday was an episode that doesn't represent who I am. I'm at peace with myself.""We'll definitely have to pay more attention because of the card, but we'll try to get through as best we can in the remainder of the race."Lotto-Intermarché were more than prepared to put the incident behind them, saying Romele had expressed regret and concern immediately after the crash, even coming to the Lotto team car during the stage to check on Van Boven's condition."The Astana rider doesn't have eyes in the back of his head, he swerved just when the speed bump was there in the road. It was just a very unfortunate racing incident," Lotto sports director Mario Aerts told .As for the crash itself, Aerts said "At first, he couldn't stand up properly. That doctor checked to see if anything was broken in his back."Luca did feel pain in his ribs, and then of course you know that it isn't good. According to the doctor, the choice was then up to Luca. He wanted to try it one more time and got on the bike anyway, even though it wasn't going easily."For Lotto, the loss of a second rider in less than a week after Roel van Sintmaartensdijk abandoned on stage 5 - also, Lotto said, due to a manoeuvre that led to him crashing out, in the Dutch rider's case with an important knee injury.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: MotoGP Aragon GP: Marquez dominates for sprint win
Marquez regains MotoGP title ground with Aragon sprint win
item.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
item.content:encoded: Defending MotoGP champion Marc Marquez dominated the Aragon sprint after overtaking title rival Marco Bezzecchi.Bezzecchi looked to have got a decent enough launch from pole, but Marquez had enough room on the inside to force Bezzecchi to the outside on corner exit - taking the lead and allowing brother Alex Marquez to sneak through, too.They controlled the race from there, aided by the longer-lasting medium rear tyre, with Bezzecchi never really threatening on the soft rear and ultimately settling into third place.His team-mate, championship leader Jorge Martin, also ran the soft rear but was frustrated in the early going by fellow Aprilia rider Raul Fernandez - which began as Fernandez retook fourth place on the outside of Turn 2 after losing the spot to Martin at the start.Their robust wheel-to-wheel racing later into the lap dropped both behind KTM's Pedro Acosta, before Martin cleared Fernandez and went back past Acosta.But the medium rear-shod Acosta bided his time behind the points leader and when Martin made a mistake at the penultimate corner, Acosta went past and consolidated fourth.Martin's fifth-place finish means he is now 29 points ahead of Bezzecchi and 33 ahead of race winner Marquez. The injury-absent Ai Ogura is 42 back and Fabio Di Giannantonio remains 46 adrift, after crashing out from eighth place early on.Fermin Aldeguer was 10th after the start but scythed his way through into sixth place by the end of the race, overtaking Diogo Moreira on the final lap - with Moreira settling for top Honda honours in seventh.Fernandez and Johann Zarco, Aldeguer's fellow injury returnee and Moreira's LCR team-mate, completed the points-scoring top nine, with Jack Miller just a tenth away from picking up a point from Yamaha.The only other rider to crash besides Di Giannantonio was Luca Marini, who exited the race on the opening lap.Fabio Quartararo also didn't finish, his Yamaha suffering what looked like an engine blow-up just before halfway.1 Marc Marquez (Ducati)2 Alex Marquez (Gresini Ducati) +1.140s3 Marco Bezzecchi (Aprilia) +2.089s4 Pedro Acosta (KTM) +2.648s5 Jorge Martin (Aprilia) +6.237s6 Fermin Aldeguer (Gresini Ducati) +10.475s7 Diogo Moreira (LCR Honda) +11.071s8 Raul Fernandez (Trackhouse Aprilia) +11.213s9 Johann Zarco (LCR Honda) +12.021s10 Jack Miller (Pramac Yamaha) +12.166s11 Pecco Bagnaia (Ducati) +14.575s12 Alex Rins (Yamaha) +14.648s13 Toprak Razgatlioglu (Pramac Yamaha) +15.776s14 Enea Bastianini (Tech3 KTM) +16.051s15 Brad Binder (KTM) +16.761s16 Joan Mir (Honda) +19.845s17 Pol Espargaro (Tech3 KTM) +23.160s18 Franco Morbidelli (VR46 Ducati) +25.074s19 Lorenzo Savadori (Trackhouse Aprilia) +27.798sDNF Fabio Quartararo (Yamaha)DNF Fabio Di Giannantonio (VR46 Ducati)DNF Luca Marini (Honda)

item.title: 'I would like it to be a rest day' – Tadej Pogačar's teammate battling on with a cracked rib at the Vuelta a España
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: American rider Kevin Vermaerke inadvertently revealed that he's racing with cracked ribs during Friday's seventh stage of the Vuelta a España, talking about his injury with the UAE Team Emirates-XRG team car as a television moto lingered close by.The 25-year-old is part of Tadej Pogačar's support squad in Spain as the Slovenian fights to add the red jersey to his palmarès, but he's fighting a personal battle during this final Grand Tour of the season.Vermaerke could be heard saying "It's OK. I have a crack in my rib, so it hurts" while taking a bidon from the UAE car on Friday. He later finished the mountain stage to Aramón Valdelinares alongside teammate Jay Vine, 16 minutes down on winner Andreas Leknessund.He told at the start of stage 8 that he suffered the injury in a crash before the Vuelta."I didn't know there was a TV motorbike right there, but it's just... I crashed a few weeks ago, and I have a small crack in the back of my ribs," Vermaerke said."But it's not anything that affects me on the bike, so it was just a joke I had with the car, and they happened to have a microphone there. But it's all good, so just a viral clip, I think, that went around last night."He's racing the Vuelta for the second time in his career, having finished 20th overall last year. He'll battle on, he said, starting with Saturday's stage 9, a 171km ride to Xeraco featuring the late climb of the Puerto de Barx.Sunday's stage 10 poses an even greater challenge, with 5,000 metres of elevation on the road to another summit finish, the 22km-long Alto de Aitana. Vermaerke said he's looking forward to Monday's rest day."I would like it to be a rest day, but at the end of the day, we still have to ride 175km, and it's never an easy day here," he said."So, with the wind, the roundabouts, and the climb in the final, it's not going to be an easy day. But I think the whole peloton feels the last two days in the legs, and especially with the massive day we have tomorrow, a bit of an easier day would be nice."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews.
