item.title: Jose Alvarado believed, and now he’s an NBA champion
item.author: Russell Richardson
item.content:encoded: There are easier (and less surreal) ways to fulfill an NBA dream than the Jose Alvarado route.Go undrafted and fight your way onto a roster. Develop a reputation as a defensive menace on the court. Spend four and a half seasons in NOLA. Get traded home to New York mid-season. Help your favorite team from childhood win their first championship in more than half a century. Then parade through the streets of the city where you grew up with a few million people screaming at you.Alvarado sat down with SLAM during his cover shoot for KICKS 29, and the conversation naturally circled back to the improbable route that brought the Brooklyn native here.Asked to choose one word for the Knicks’ championship run, Alvarado answered: “Believe. That’s one thing you got to do is believe the way we did it.”That was especially true in Game Four of the Finals, when New York fell 29 points behind San Antonio and somehow dragged itself all the way back, aided by significant contributions from Alvarado. He said his focus during the comeback was simple: “It was more not really overthinking—like, what can I do to make us win the game regardless if it’s making shots or not.”The championship would have been a massive achievement anywhere. Winning it in New York meant even more for Jose, who grew up in Brooklyn before playing at Georgia Tech and eventually joining the Pelicans.Pondering Jose’s experience, there is always something weird about getting a desperately wanted thing. For years, the dream existed at a distance, beyond the next practice, the next contract, the doubt expressed by others about your size or talent. Then one afternoon, you’re dancing on a float in Manhattan as an NBA champion with your hometown passing by, block by block. “I almost cried on the float because . . . obviously going through the city that I was raised . . . I know a lot of people that’s in the crowd,” Alvarado told SLAM.That’s the part of winning a championship nobody can really prepare for, that transition point when the dream stops being something you’re chasing and becomes something that has happened to you. Sounds surreal. And not to get all Jean-Paul Sartre about it all, but it’s natural to wonder: what’s next?The answer: Your own sneaker and a new contract with the Knicks, naturally. After declining his $4.5 million player option this summer, Alvarado agreed to a new three-year deal with the Knicks worth roughly $14.4 million, with $12 million guaranteed.Furthermore, Jose recently signed with the streetball brand AND1 and showed off his personalized player-exclusive shoes during the SLAM shoot. The partnership makes sense. Few NBA players have built an identity more closely connected to playground basketball’s particular mixture of hustle, swagger, annoyance, and joy. Thus, the SLAM team drove Alvarado back to an outdoor New York court, a familiar environment to the 28-year-old who is currently playing for Puerto Rico in FIFA’s Basketball World Cup qualifiers.In March, I spoke to Jose over Zoom. He was connecting from a hotel room in Utah, grinding out NBA life on the road, still getting acclimated to his new team. What struck me in the conversation was how completely disruptive a mid-season trade is on a player with a young family. “People don’t understand,” Alvarado told me. “You think, ‘They’ve got millions,’ and don’t get me wrong, the financial security is great. But one day you’re comfortable in your forever home, and overnight you have to go to a different city, leaving your wife and kids behind.”He explained that even a month after the trade, he hadn’t yet been able to return home to his family in New Orleans. It became clear how much these players—and their families—must sacrifice for an NBA career.And Jose is not slowing down. Despite the ring, a new contract, and his face on a SLAM cover, Alvarado doesn’t sound particularly interested in staying comfortable.“The only way to stay in the NBA, or to be in a conversation where I want to be, with my goal, is [I] definitely got to have a chip on my shoulder, no matter what,” he told SLAM.That chip is mighty durable. Going undrafted didn’t remove it; making an NBA team didn’t shake it; becoming an established rotation player didn’t loosen it; and neither did coming home, getting paid, or getting to pose for glamour shots with the Larry O’Brien trophy.Asked how he eventually wants people to remember him, Jose went right back to the beginning. “I want them to remember that there was a lot of people that said no to this kid. There was a lot of doubts . . . just remember the doubts and how I overcame all that.”I can think of worse epitaphs for a basketball career. Congrats, Jose.

item.title: As it happened: sprint decides stage 8 of the Vuelta a España on a day where the red jersey changes hands
item.content:encoded: For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. You'll get comprehensive race coverage of La Vuelta a España, subscriber-exclusive analysis from our expert columnists, in-depth features and industry-leading tech insight. Plus, the Cyclingnews app lets you follow the action wherever you go! Hello and welcome to stage 8 of the Vuelta a EspañaAugust 29, 2026 – 7:29 AMFor the first time since stage five, the sprinters have a chance to go for a stage win today - but it won’t be easy. There’s a tough climb crested within the final 30km, which is hard enough to potentially see some sprinters dropped, to see attacks go clear from the peloton. It’s a well-balanced parcours, that promises to be very exciting August 29, 2026 – 7:33 AMThe riders are off from the unofficial start, short of one rider who finished yesterday. Luca Van Boven has abandoned the race after his nasty crash yesterday. August 29, 2026 – 7:40 AMThe four jersey wearers at the start today - Onley, Pogačar, Van Aert and Leknessund. August 29, 2026 – 7:46 AMThe action is set to kick off any moment, but before it does, be sure to catch up with yesterday's stage, the first at this year's race to be won by the breakaway. August 29, 2026 – 7:52 AMThere was a crash in the neutralised zone, which has delayed the official start of the stage. But hopefully we will be racing any moment.August 29, 2026 – 7:59 AMThe peloton are still behind the race car, as the start continues to be delayed as a result of the crash.When things finally do kick off, expect a fierce battle for the break, on a day where their hopes of survival feel realistic. August 29, 2026 – 8:03 AMAnd they're off! Everyone has regrouped and regathered themselves after the crash, and the race has at last began. August 29, 2026 – 8:10 AMSo far it's Burgos Burpellet BH showing most intent. Their rider Sinuhé Fernández has a gap of one minute after attacking from the flag, while his teammate José Luis Faura attempted to join him, before dropping back into the peloton.August 29, 2026 – 8:16 AMThe peloton has already eased up, and allowed Fernández a lead of almost two and a half minutes already. The anticipated battle to get into the break has not materialised; and you wouldn’t expect Fernández to have any chance fending off an entire peloton by himself. August 29, 2026 – 8:22 AMThis was the moment at the start of the day when Fernández attacked, ahead of a disinterested peloton He must surely have imagined he'd have so company when he made the move.August 29, 2026 – 8:29 AMWe have had a first abandon as a result of the pre-flag crash, and it's Kern Pharma's climber Diego Uriarte. That's a shame as he has been lively at this Vuelta, getting into the break on multiple occasions already.Here was a glimpse of the chaotic aftermath following that incident earlier in the day.August 29, 2026 – 8:35 AMFernández has been given a huge lead over the peloton, almost up to 6 minutes. The peloton is taking thins easy, though Visma have taken control of the pace-setting, presumably for their sprinter Matthew Brennan.August 29, 2026 – 8:42 AMUnfortunately, there has been a second abandon as a consequence of the crash at the start of the day. NSN's Floris Van Tricht had been making his Grand Tour debut, but finishes in unlucky fashion. August 29, 2026 – 8:47 AMVisma are leading the peloton, but are a distant 5:30 behind Fernández. It's been a subdued start to the stage.August 29, 2026 – 8:54 AMFor unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. You'll get comprehensive race coverage of La Vuelta a España, subscriber-exclusive analysis from our expert columnists, in-depth features and industry-leading tech insight. Plus, the Cyclingnews app lets you follow the action wherever you go!August 29, 2026 – 8:59 AMA few riders have been held up and are making their way through the convoy back into the peloton. One of those riders is Primož Roglič - he appears unhurt, and it's unclear for now whether he went down. The pace has picked up a bit, but Fernández's lead remains over five minutes. August 29, 2026 – 9:04 AMRoglič did indeed go down, as evidenced by a small rip in his jersey. He does appear to be riding comfortably, though, and is calmly making his way back towards the peloton. August 29, 2026 – 9:07 AMMore bad news to report, as Mattia Gaffuri becomes the third rider of the day to abandon. He was one of the men to go down in the incident a few kilometres ago, and was clearly much worse off than Roglič.August 29, 2026 – 9:16 AM Steven Kruijswijk has been tasked with setting the pace at the front of the peloton for Visma-Lease a Bike, doing all the work by himself. He's keeping the lone leader Fernández at five minutes, as Visma look to set Brennan up for another sprint win.August 29, 2026 – 9:28 AMThere was some speculation yesterday that Pogačar's attack in the closing stages was motivated by anger, and the need to prove a point after being caught by Enric Mas the day before. But the Slovenian himself denied this, when talking to the media yesterday.August 29, 2026 – 9:35 AMCallum Thornley is on bidon duty for Red Bull-Bora Hansgrohe. There's no sign that his leader Primož Roglič is suffering at all following his crash, but we'll only know for sure when he's tested on tomorrow's mountain stage. August 29, 2026 – 9:42 AMFelix Gall, safely in the peloton. He was one of the big winner of yesterday's stage, finishing the best of the rest behind...., and as a result moved up to fourth overall, just 11 seconds away from the podium. He's unlikely to have a chance to gain that time today, but will tomorrow.August 29, 2026 – 9:50 AMStill it's Steven Kruijswijk leading the peloton all by himself, and he's brought the gap to Sinuhé Fernández down to 3:20. The terrain remains flat for a while longer yet, before things get interesting with the category three climb of Puerto de Barx.August 29, 2026 – 9:57 AMFor unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. You'll get comprehensive race coverage of La Vuelta a España, subscriber-exclusive analysis from our expert columnists, in-depth features and industry-leading tech insight. Plus, the Cyclingnews app lets you follow the action wherever you go!August 29, 2026 – 10:03 AMAn interesting development at the front of the peloton, as Steven Kruijswijk pulls off briefly from the front to take a comfort break, and Alpecin-Deceuninck briefly take over from him. Kruijswijk is back on the front again now, but that’s still a hint that Alpecin fancy their chances for the win today with Kaden Groves, despite the Australian’s lack of form and failure to get into the mix on the previous sprint stages at this Vuelta. August 29, 2026 – 10:14 AMThe gap continues to come down, with now just under two minutes separating Fernández and the peloton, still being led by Kruijswijk. The Dutchman does have a posse of Alpecin riders right behind him, ready to try and set Groves up for the win August 29, 2026 – 10:19 AMWhile we assume Kruijswijk is working for his Visma teammate Matthew Brennan, the team also have another potential option for the day in Wout van Aert. The Belgian was in the break yesterday and came close to winning the stage, and as a result is wearing the green jersey, leading the points classification ahead of Tadej Pogačar by two points That’s a slender lead, and one he’ll surely want to defend - but that’ll be hard if he’s working to try and set Brennan up for a win. August 29, 2026 – 10:29 AMWho will sprint for Netcompany Ineos today? Axel Laurance is looking in good form, with a 5th and 8th finish to his name already this week, but also have Ben Turner as an option, who has a bunch sprint stage win at the Vuelta on his palmares from last year. It's a tricky choice for the team, and both riders are capable climbers who will fancy their chances of surviving the climb.August 29, 2026 – 10:38 AMAnother rider to look out for today is Red Bull-Bora Hansgrohe's Jordi Meeus. He’s one of the few riders in the peloton who can rival Brennan for pure speed, and managed to survive the climb on stage five that put paid to so many other sprinters’ hopes. He was second that day, and will be eager to go one better having not won a race for almost three months.August 29, 2026 – 10:45 AM Sinuhé Fernández might not be out in front for much longer at this rate. His lead over the peloton has dropped to only just over a minute, although the chase may slow down if the peloton is reluctant to make the catch to early - the sprinters' teams wont want to leave themselves exposed to attacks on the upcoming Puerto de Barx.August 29, 2026 – 10:52 AMFollowing his fourth-place finish on stage five, Alessandro Romele is also a rider to look out for in the expected sprint today, though he’s made headlines for the wrong reasons most recently. The Italian took responsibility for the crash that saw Luca Van Boven abandon the race prior to today’s stage.August 29, 2026 – 11:01 AMThe riders are approaching the day's intermediate sprint, and as a result the pace in the peloton has picked up. It's Visma-Lease a Bike who have put more men at the front, in search of increasing Van Aert's lead in the points classification, and are set to catch Fernández before the sprint. August 29, 2026 – 11:08 AMVan Aert takes the maximum 20 points at the sprint. Sinuhé Fernández was caught beforehand, and the green jersey was able to take the sprint without anyone competing against him.August 29, 2026 – 11:09 AMThe red jersey is down, and he looks hurt. He's still sat on the floor a minute or so after hitting the deck. His race might be in peril. August 29, 2026 – 11:11 AMPogačar has gone down very heavily, and has shed a lot of blood. He briefly got back up on his feet, but has sat down again, clearly in a lot of pain. His abandonment appears imminent. The peloton has slowed down, but is already several minutes ahead. August 29, 2026 – 11:12 AMThe red jersey has climbed into the medical vehicle, and has left the race. This is a shocking development in the race. August 29, 2026 – 11:15 AMAugust 29, 2026 – 11:17 AMThe peloton looks a little in shock, riding only at a steady pace, with no team taking control despite nearing the start of the climb. UAE riders who waited for Pogačar, some of whom also went down in the same incident, are pacing their way back to the peloton.This is the tenth Grand Tour of Pogačar's, and the first he has ever abandoned. Before today, he'd never even finished lower than third place. August 29, 2026 – 11:20 AMThe race goes on, and the peloton have just crested the day's sole climb, Van Aert claiming the KOM points on offer at the top. No team really took it on, and no attacks came, so it seems like this stage will go down to a sprint, with most if not all of the major sprinters still in contention.August 29, 2026 – 11:24 AMThere's been an attack from the peloton, as Azparren makes an opportunistic move in the aftermath of the climb. He's leading by a few seconds, but the peloton has matters under control. August 29, 2026 – 11:30 AMAzparren still leads the race, but only by about 15 seconds. Visma-Lease a Bike lead the peloton, and have it all strung out as they set things up for the sprint.August 29, 2026 – 11:35 AMMovistar are also present towards the front of the peloton, near Visma-Lease a Bike. They suddenly find themselves in possession of the virtual red jersey, with Enric Mas set to take it on the podium tonight, all being well. August 29, 2026 – 11:41 AM10 seconds is Azparren's slender lead, as he goes under the 10km to go banner.There's been yet another crash, about five riders going down this time, including Carlos Rodríguez and Luke Tuckwell. Roland Thalmann also went down, and has a very nasty looking road rash, but is on his bike and making his way back to the peloton. August 29, 2026 – 11:45 AMThe peloton is bearing down on Azparren as they enter the final, technical 5km. The catch is soon to be made, with Visma still leading. August 29, 2026 – 11:46 AMRed Bull-Bora Hansgrohe have taken control at the front of the peloton, with Alpecin also bringing Groves towards the front, and Brennan still up there for Visma-Lease a Bike.August 29, 2026 – 11:48 AMAzparren was caught 500m ago, and now Netcompany lead the peloton as they enter the final kilometre. August 29, 2026 – 11:49 AMVan Aert is leading out the sprint, but it's for Laporte rather than Brennan, who is further down. August 29, 2026 – 11:50 AMCoquard takes it, the Grand Tour stage he has spent his whole career chasing!August 29, 2026 – 11:53 AMIt was a dramatic finale, with yet another crash in the final few hundred metres taking out several riders. It looked as though Mads Pedersen was going to take the win, but Coquard came from behind and pipped him with a bike-throw. Meeus was third, Turner fourth, and, despite all their work, Brennan was Visma's best-placed rider in tenth. August 29, 2026 – 11:58 AMIt was a very close sprint, with Coquard taking it thanks to an impressive bike-lunge. The Frenchman really wanted that one. August 29, 2026 – 12:03 PMThe story of the day is of course the crash that has seen race leader, and the seemingly invincible, Tadej Pogačar leave the race. Here’s our full report of the incident that has rocked the Vuelta. August 29, 2026 – 12:09 PMOn a brighter note, what a day for Bryan Coquard. This is the thirteenth Grand Tour he has ridden in his career; and, despite having 55 career wins to his name, he’d never before won one at this level. His record of fishing second three times at the Tour de France, and third another two times, has made him notorious as a perennial bridesmaid, so this victory will bring great joy to cycling fans around the world. August 29, 2026 – 12:17 PMRight from the neutralised section, when a crash delayed the start, it was a grim day at the Vuelta, with multiple crashes throughout the stage. Roland Thalmann was one of the worst affected, suffering bad road rashes and a torn jersey when he went down towards the end. A lot of riders have been in the wars. August 29, 2026 – 12:20 PMPogačar's crash has blown this race wide open, with multiple riders now within shooting distance of the red jersey.For now, Enric Mas leads it. Here he is on the podium, sportingly choosing not to adorn the jersey in honour of the stricken Slovenian. August 29, 2026 – 12:31 PMThanks for joining us today, on a stage that has turned this Vuelta on its head. This one had the whole range of emotions, from the devastation of Pogačar's crash, to the ecstasy of Coquard's first Grand Tour win. What had looked like a very straightforward race now looks extremely unpredictable, with multiple riders now in contention for the red jersey. All bets are off, so be sure to join us again tomorrow - which is a monster stage in the mountains, and where the new-look GC race is to start taking shape.

item.title: I asked 100 companies for my data. Some deleted it instead.
item.author: Reece Rodgers, wired.com
item.content:encoded: I filed a request with McDonald’s earlier this month to access all of the personal data the fast food company collected about me, and I received a stunning 515-page report a few days later that detailed my app interactions in granular detail and predicted I would never stop eating there.Under the California Consumer Privacy Act, I have the legal right to request access to information from large companies that collect personal data. So I was curious what others might have on me, and I spent the next week filing more than 100 requests.The CCPA went into effect in 2020, and three of its key provisions are the right to opt out of the selling of personal information, the right to delete that info, and the right to request a copy for yourself.

item.title: Human Powered Health's makeover continues with another big-name signing in Yara Kastelijn
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: 29-year-old Kastelijn has spent her top-level career to date at Fenix-Premier Tech, whom she joined when they were known as Ciclismo Mundial in 2020.Along the way, she's developed into a top rider, excelling in the hills and mountains on the road and winning a European title in cyclo-cross. Alongside top 10s at Liège-Bastogne-Liège and the Vuelta Femenina, she also won a stage of the 2023 Tour de France Femmes with a 19km solo into Rodez.This season, Kastelijn scored the first stage race win of her career, beating Evita Muzic and Uso Ostolaza on the final-day Lagunas de Neila summit finish to win the Vuelta a Burgos. Second place at Itzulia Women is another 2026 highlight."I really liked the confidence they have in me. I spoke once with them, and it really felt like home. It's the trust they have in me to be a good GC contender, and I really think that I can do it in this environment," Kastelijn said as Human Powered Health announced her signing."I'm very grateful for everything Fenix-Premier Tech did for me. I'm very thankful for the brothers Roodhooft and my trainer, but I'm now ready for this next step, and I am really looking forward to it."Human Powered Health have been the most active team in the Women's WorldTour this transfer season, with Kastelijn's signature their seventh for 2027. The US squad has greatly upgraded their sprint lineup with the triple addition of Letizia Paternoster, Amalie Dideriksen, and Sofia van Rooijen.They're joined on the incoming list by punchy pairing Quinty Ton and Marta Lach, while the fourth Dutch rider on the incoming list is neo-pro Fee Knaven. Kastelijn is expected to slot in as a premier GC rider on the team, said general manager Ro De Jonckere, with the Tour de France Femmes her big goal of next season. Her best result to date is 17th place at the 2025 edition."Yara has already shown that she can do that. She has the strength to be a factor in the hardest one-day races, but she also has the consistency and resilience required to fight for a GC over several days," she said."That ability to be competitive across a whole stage race is particularly valuable because it gives us another rider who can take responsibility when the biggest opportunities arise."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Was it a mistake for 99 Colombian guerrillas to lay down their arms?
item.author: Daniela Díaz in Valle del Guamuez and Tiago Rogero in Rio de Janeiro
item.content:encoded: Fighters in legal limbo after accepting ‘total peace’ plan of Petro government just days before hardliner Abelardo De la Espriella took overIn mid-June, 99 guerrilla fighters were flown by helicopter to a small settlement in a rural area of southern Colombia where they lined up and, one by one, handed their weapons to government officials: rifles, pistols, machine guns and grenade launchers.They also stripped off their heavy tactical vests, field packs and camouflage uniforms, which were each piled into a bonfire to mark the beginning of a new life away from an armed conflict that has claimed nearly half a million lives in the last six decades.Continue reading...

Slow start makes me want to stay - Norris extends McLaren deal to 2030
item.content:encoded: In an exclusive BBC Sport interview, Lando Norris explains why he has signed a new contract that will keep him at McLaren until at least the end of 2030.

item.title: Bezzecchi upsets Marquez for Aragon MotoGP pole
item.author: Valentin Khorounzhiy
item.content:encoded: Marco Bezzecchi upset pre-weekend favourite Marc Marquez to claim MotoGP pole position for the Aragon Grand Prix.Bezzecchi was the only rider setting sub-1m45s laps, so saw off Marquez by 0.089s - the latter threatening the benchmark in the final seconds but messing up the entry to Turn 14 and having to settle for second.Alex Marquez will join the pair on the front row for the sprint and for Sunday's main event.Raul Fernandez, points leader Jorge Martin and Pedro Acosta will complete row two. Acosta set his best lap in the elder Marquez's tow, before sliding off on entry into Reverse Corkscrew while trying to improve.VR46 team-mates Fabio Di Giannantonio and Franco Morbidelli ran together on track and were split by just three tenths in the end, but that also meant five positions, Di Giannantonio in seventh and Morbidelli in 12th.Between them were Pecco Bagnaia, Johann Zarco, Diogo Moreira and Fermin Aldeguer. Bagnaia and Moreira had advanced from Q1, despite Moreira crashing late in that session.Jack Miller, whose impending departure from Pramac Yamaha (and MotoGP as a whole) was announced earlier this week, placed 13th as the best of the Yamahas and the best-of-the-rest in Q1 - ahead of good friend and future World Superbike rival Brad Binder (KTM).Joan Mir had a last-second shot at picking off Moreira for the final Q2 spot but came up two tenths short and settled for 15th - though did outqualify team-mate Luca Marini for the 12th time in 13 attempts this season.1 Marco Bezzecchi (Aprilia) 1m44.962s2 Marc Marquez (Ducati) +0.089s3 Alex Marquez (Gresini Ducati) +0.299s4 Raul Fernandez (Trackhouse Aprilia) +0.413s5 Jorge Martin (Aprilia) +0.474s6 Pedro Acosta (KTM) +0.593s7 Fabio Di Giannantonio (VR46 Ducati) +0.653s8 Pecco Bagnaia (Ducati) +0.709s9 Johann Zarco (LCR Honda) +0.821s10 Diogo Moreira (LCR Honda) +0.840s11 Fermin Aldeguer (Gresini Ducati) +0.930s12 Franco Morbidelli (VR46 Ducati) +0.957s13 Jack Miller (Pramac Yamaha) +0.118s to Q214 Brad Binder (KTM) +0.157s to Q215 Joan Mir (Honda) +0.185s to Q216 Enea Bastianini (Tech3 KTM) +0.255s to Q217 Fabio Quartararo (Yamaha) +0.290s to Q218 Luca Marini (Honda) +0.370s to Q219 Alex Rins (Yamaha) +0.481s to Q220 Pol Espargaro (Tech3 KTM) +0.543s to Q221 Toprak Razgatlioglu (Pramac Yamaha) +0.708s to Q222 Lorenzo Savadori (Trackhouse Aprilia) +1.547s to Q2

item.title: Our verdict on Norris's deal + state of the F1 driver market
item.author: The Race Team
item.content:encoded: The long-term Formula 1 driver deals keep coming, as defending champion Lando Norris has extended his stay at McLaren until at least 2030.That's in line with the recent announcement that four-time F1 champion Max Verstappen will remain at Red Bull until the same year, while Charles Leclerc's contract at Ferrari could run even longer than that. Norris's stock right now is arguably the highest it's ever been; as defending champion, he has also won the two most recent races as McLaren's 2026 development begins to bear fruit. So was a berth anywhere else realistic? What does this say about the driver market? And what are the consequences of more and more longer-term deals being announced?Here are our team's thoughts:The F1 driver market is deadIt's unfortunate how static the F1 driver market is at the sharp end.This is not a point about Norris or McLaren specifically - this is a sage deal for both parties - but it feels like whatever incentive structure existed in the past for drivers to sign shorter-term or properly explore alternative options and try to manoeuvre themselves is totally, totally gone.It may have been gone already for a decade or so, but it feels like something you could connect to the explosion in team valuations under Liberty Media. A driver salary cap to go with the cost cap was explored but never introduced and while that's good from a labour point of view, it means truly generational wealth is available to all the top drivers rather than just outliers such as Michael Schumacher and Lewis Hamilton in the past.These deals create security against the natural ebb and flow of a driver's market value. And changing teams is hard, so is a great way of accidentally tanking that market value. It's different in other sports - when you go from, say, Tottenham to Bayern in football, you don't need to learn an all-new ball, you just need to adjust to actually winning games for a change.And, yes, Hamilton-to-Ferrari was an exception but if he were 15 years younger, he'd obviously be on a Mercedes deal to 2035 right now.No possible reason to look elsewhereWhile Verstappen and Red Bull is defining team/driver partnership of the 2020s, Norris and McLaren isn't so far behind. Therefore, it's logical for this alliance to keep a long timeline in place.The choice of 2030 aligns well with F1's rules cycles and also other deals, such as Verstappen's recently announced Red Bull contract. There are similarities there in that Norris has had enormous success with McLaren and clearly feels very comfortable there, but the difference is that, right now, McLaren has less to prove to Norris than Red Bull has to Verstappen.Therefore, there's no possible reason for Norris to look elsewhere, while from McLaren's perspective it is wise to lock down Norris and continues to hold flexibility on Oscar Piastri's seat.That said, Piastri's contract still has plenty of time on it, so there's not necessarily need for urgency in extending that, which gives McLaren the flexibility should it want to make a move for someone else down the line. But don't underestimate how strong a two-driver line-up this is.A big downside to these big contractsFor McLaren and Norris this is the best thing to do: given the opportunity (car) he is winning races and McLaren has the determination under Zak Brown's leadership to get back to its heydays of being a consistent championship-winning team.Also to add to that, in reality, where else is there to go that would give a winning car and a team relationship that Norris currently has?Piastri has had his chance to show what he is worth and he is very good, so I wouldn't be surprised to see him also continue with McLaren. Why not? He fits in well and, again, when he has the opportunity (car) he can win races.However, these long-term contracts are closing the doors to potential up-and-coming drivers and with more or less no testing available to show a driver's talent, how is anyone going to show their worth? Take Leonardo Fornaroli, McLaren reserve and the reigning Formula 2 champion, for example: what happens to him?F1 keeps talking about finding true talent, it even talks about getting a female into F1, but can someone please explain to me how these scenarios can happen? Yes, we have testing of previous cars opportunities, but who really pays any attention to that?Something needs to be done as the stepping stones to F1 through Formula 3 and F2 are just too expensive. It's always been the same and as Alpine has proven with re-signing Franco Colapinto, money is much more important than talent.Norris's extension puts Piastri in an interesting spot.I have zero doubt McLaren doesn't mind which of its drivers is winning races or championships, but only one of them has been doing that recently.So you can imagine how McLaren is starting to become Norris's team. Not that it's favouring him but it's naturally going to start coalescing around the stronger driver, in terms of direction.Therefore you could see why Piastri (and manager Mark Webber) might be considering whether his long-term future should be at McLaren, beyond his likely-end-of-2028 deal.The problem is his stock's taken a knock versus 12 months ago. Since then, he's blown a decent title lead and has looked firmly second-best to Norris this year with too many weekends, by his own admission, spent too far off the pace.So while it's tempting to wonder whether Piastri could be a project leader for someone such as Audi or Aston Martin - and I think he has the raw ability to be - he's got to first get himself out of this current hole or risk being an unattractive second-best to Norris.The market is a very different beast these daysWith what has all the makings of a great Shakespearean play, the House of McLaren, the House of Ferrari and the House of Red Bull are now locked in following Norris's contract extension until 2030.Where once F1's driver market was a source of intrigue and excitement, machinations on this front have now stopped.Instead, loyalty, stability and family are the order of the day. Verstappen and Leclerc have now been joined by Norris in taking themselves off the market for a while; and expect Mercedes to shore up its own situation pretty soon.Stability may be less exciting than the drama of a big silly-season switch but it's the logical outcome in an era of F1 where the cost cap appears (thanks to legacy infrastructure reasons) to have helped edge the top four clear of the pack for now - so prime seats are increasingly rare.The pool of favourable options is narrowed down even more once one team locks in one of their A* drivers, as that makes becoming their team-mate less exciting because it means going up against another big gun with the same equipment.Better to be the big fish in your own still very big pond and make it the best one of there, than face the headaches that come from a topline driver rivalry.Leclerc, Verstappen and Norris all settling down makes perfect sense.Is it exciting for gossip? No. But the family dynasties are now in play to shape F1 until the end of this ruleset, and that in itself is going to throw up plenty of its own drama.McLaren has earned Norris's trustOf all the top teams in recent years, McLaren has proven it is better at developing a car than the rest - so if you're Norris, McLaren is the only option.Sure, Mercedes has started this cycle with a better package, but that was inevitable as soon as it was confirmed McLaren would remain a Mercedes customer for this ruleset.McLaren is fighting Mercedes with one arm tied behind its back given it gets data last-minute from weekend to weekend and doesn't have access to the data Mercedes has had while building this power unit. McLaren has no right being as close as it is. The last two tracks may have flattered it but it's clear McLaren is developing towards Mercedes again and is trending in the right direction.The only real downside is that power unit deficit as a customer, but as the rules cycle wears on that will be less of an issue as the status quo sets in. And in those circumstances, in the last ruleset McLaren became F1's top squad.With Leclerc and Verstappen tied down at the other top teams, and Kimi Antonelli set to lead Mercedes for as long as he wants to be there, there's no better option for Norris. And even if one of those other teams had an opening, McLaren has earned Norris's trust. It wasted a bit of his early career with poor cars but is certainly making up for that now.Going elsewhere is going to get harderOn one level I get this: stability, trust, faith, reward etc.On the other, you could look at it as somewhat shut off and lacking ambition for fresher challenges that can come up. Even, perhaps, dare one say that Norris may have a bit of Stockholm Syndrome in F1.He's only ever known Zak Brown-era McLaren. Of course, it's served him well with a title and 13 grand prix wins so far. But by 2030 he will have raced for the same team for 12 seasons and if he needs or wants a change how much of a shock to the system will that be for him? And would he be able to adapt?You presume that for a driver of Norris's class it would be straightforward. But the longer he stays with a single team the harder it will get as more Antonellis come on to the scene.The bigger question also here I feel is how Norris can stay hungry, motivated and avoid future burnout.Contesting 25 grands prix a year (as will surely soon become the norm) over a decade-long-plus stretch is a big ask for anyone. Mika Hakkinen had to stop after a similar period, and so did Fernando Alonso to an extent with his World Endurance Championship and Indycar 'break' - and in both of those cases that was with much fewer grands prix on the calendar.Perhaps modern drivers are more conditioned for the constant grind and can soak it up better through more understanding of the mental stress these days, which is of course a good thing and one that Norris can keep on top of.

item.title: Norris extends McLaren F1 contract with bumper new deal
item.author: Jack Benyon
item.content:encoded: Reigning Formula 1 world champion Lando Norris has extended his McLaren contract, taking his stay with the team beyond a decade and through the 2030 season.But there is scope for that to run longer - as McLaren's announcement of the deal added there was a "multi-year option to commit beyond" that 2030 date.Norris, who has won the last two F1 races in the upgraded McLaren, became part of McLaren's junior programme in 2017 and earned a race drive for 2019.He has already notched the highest number of starts of any McLaren driver and is on course to extend that record substantially with his new deal.It means Norris joins rivals Charles Leclerc and Max Verstappen in being signed at least through the 2030 season, the planned end of the current engine rules cycle unless an earlier switch to V8s is agreed for 2030."McLaren is my home, and I'm very pleased to be signing a new contract to keep me with the team until at least 2030," said Norris."When I started this journey nine years ago, I was clear about the goals I wanted to achieve: to get McLaren back to the front and to win championships. We've achieved that goal, but we want more, we want to keep on winning, and we know as a team that we're capable of achieving it."Team principal Andrea Stella said Norris had been an "integral" part of McLaren's success, and was a "special human" and "exceptional driver".McLaren Racing CEO Zak Brown added: "His journey with the team is a fantastic example of our commitment to identifying, developing and supporting world-class talent, and his achievements speak for themselves."As part of the deal, Norris will be gifted an MCL39 car from his 2025 title-winning year, a "lasting reminder of his contribution to the team".Norris's deal was the soonest to expire of the lead figures at McLaren, with team-mate Oscar Piastri having committed to the end of 2028 last year, while Brown and Stella agreed new deals within the last two years.

item.title: Norris extends McLaren deal until F1 2030
When does each 2026 F1 driver's contract expire?
item.author: The Race Team
item.content:encoded: Save for the significant arrival of a new Formula 1 team and two returning drivers, there were scarcely any changes to the grid for 2026.But that could all change over the remainder of the season, as more than 50% of the field are due to be out of contract come the end of the year.Here's what you need to know about when each driver's contract ends.Lando Norris - 2030Oscar Piastri - 2028McLaren announced Norris had committed to a new deal through to 2030 - with the option for longer - in late-August, at a point where the defending F1 champion had also won the two most recent grands prix.Piastri extended his contract in March 2025 with a "multi-year" deal that you'd suspect will keep him at McLaren until the end of 2028 at least.George Russell - 2027Kimi Antonelli - 2026F1 2026's two title protagonists were only officially confirmed for this season in October last year.Russell's contract is understood to run into 2027, though the way it was presented could still leave both team and driver free to do something different next year.Max Verstappen - 2030Isack Hadjar - 2026After months (well, years) of speculation about Verstappen's future at the team, Red Bull made the surprise announcement ahead of the 2026 Dutch GP that the four-time F1 champion had agreed a new deal that is due to keep him there until 2030.Hadjar was brought into the Red Bull line-up at the expense of Yuki Tsunoda - that announcement stated only that he would be part of the 2026 line-up - and has compared reasonably well to Verstappen in his first season in the senior team, even if the car's overall competitiveness has been a limiting factor.Charles Leclerc - 2030+Lewis Hamilton - 2027In announcing Charles Leclerc's deal had been renewed, Ferrari released an ambiguous statement ahead of the Monaco Grand Prix that was light on details and stated merely that he would "continue to wear the team's colours for the coming seasons".As Leclerc's existing arrangement (also publicly announced at the time only as being for "several more seasons") was in place until 2029, The Race understands that the new deal is an extension to that and as such will keep him at Ferrari until beyond 2030 - the current longest F1 driver contract.While the length of Lewis Hamilton's contract has never been made official, it was widely accepted to be a two-year-minimum affair and the seven-time champion said at the recent Canadian GP that he was committed at least until the end of 2027.Alex Albon - 2027Carlos Sainz - 2028Williams used the week leading up to the Dutch GP to separately announce that both drivers would be staying on beyond the end of the 2026 season.In the case of Albon, his deal was presented as an "extension" for 2027 - although his existing contract was thought to cover next year already. The Race understands no new racing contract had been agreed and, instead, that the 2027 confirmation relates to exit clauses that existed in the contract.Sainz, meanwhile, agreed a multi-year contract extension that did not specify the length of his contract but will include options over forthcoming years.Liam Lawson - 2026Arvid Lindblad - 2026Lawson regrouped well following his demotion to Racing Bulls just two rounds into the 2025 season, sufficiently so that he was retained for 2026.Lindblad, the only rookie in this year's field, scored points on an eye-catching debut at the Australian GP and added to his tally in the Canadian GP sprint race.They have been presented as Racing Bulls's drivers for 2026 only.Fernando Alonso - 2026Lance Stroll - 2026Two-time champion Alonso and Stroll are currently contracted only until the end of a gruelling first year (that is at least on an upward trajectory) of Aston Martin's works partnership with Honda.Ollie Bearman - 2026Esteban Ocon - 2026Though both Bearman and Ocon are contracted until the end of the current season, Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu recently had to shut down "bulls***" speculation of a rift between Ocon and himself, and the possibility of a mid-season split.Nico Hulkenberg - "multi-year"Gabriel Bortoleto - "multi-year"Audi's having a mixed first season in F1 - with a decent turn of speed being paired with more reliability issues than it would like - and should really have more points on the board than the two Bortoleto scored at the season opener.The 21-year-old is racing alongside Hulkenberg for a second season, following the team's transition from Sauber into the works team.Hulkenberg's deal includes 2025 and 2026, though reports have suggested 2027 is in the mix as well.Pierre Gasly - 2028Franco Colapinto - 2027Alpine executive advisor Flavio Briatore initially held out on committing to Colapinto - keeping his options open in case Verstappen moved to Mercedes and one of Russell or Antonelli became available - but the 23-year-old has since been retained for 2027, which will be his second full campaign in F1.Sergio Perez - 2027Valtteri Bottas - 2027Grand prix veterans Perez and Bottas were both signed on "multi-year" deals that brought them back to the grid with the new Cadillac team.Perez has generally been the more impressive of the two so far in 2026, though speculation that Bottas's place could be at risk - for now or for 2027 - appears to be wide of the mark.

item.title: Luca Van Boven quits Vuelta a España after completing stage 7 with collapsed lung and broken ribs from crash involving Alessandro Romele
item.content:encoded: Lotto-Intermarché have announced via social media that their rider Luca Van Boven has abandoned the Vuelta a España after crashing heavily during stage 7 and managing to complete the day's racing with broken ribs and a collapsed lung.Van Boven fell heavily in kilometre 122 of the mountainous stage, 28km from the finish line, after Alessandro Romele (XDS-Astana) lost his balance after hitting a speed bump in a small town. As a result, the Italian sprinter unintentionally closed out the Belgian, who hit the pavement and crashed.Riding as a support rider in the Vuelta for the Lotto leaders, the 26-year-old hilly Classics specialist managed to remount and completed in 178th place, 33:17 down. He was the last rider to finish on a stage with more than 3,500 metres of vertical climbing.The initial medical diagnosis on the official stage report was that Van Boven had suffered bruises and road rash in his lower back and right buttock "requiring continuous on-course attention for subsequent radiological study."The post-stage check-up revealed the fourth-year pro had suffered two broken ribs and a collapsed lung in the crash, making it impossible for him to continue in the race"Luca will remain in hospital overnight for further observation and will unfortunately not start tomorrow's stage. He will continue to be monitored closely," the team posted on social media. "We wish Luca lots of strength and a speedy recovery."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Mercedes still searching for answers on why it was “rubbish” through high-speed corners in Dutch GP
A lost season, cobbled and track triumphs, and battles with Wiebes – The story behind Lara Gillespie's rapid rise to the top
item.author: cyclingnews@futurenet.com (Dani Ostanek)
item.content:encoded: The fastwomen of the Women's WorldTour peloton are up against it at the moment, with Dutch rider Lorena Wiebes dominating the sprinting landscape and showing few signs of letting up.At race after race, the same question comes up: 'How to beat her?' Fans, riders, and directeurs sportifs alike ponder it, and yet no answers present themselves. After all, she's on a roll of sprinting results unseen in modern racing.Irish racer Lara Gillespie is one of her fellow sprinters currently facing that question. But to get where she is today, Gillespie has overcome far more than a single opponent. If her determined climb to the top of the sport is any indication, she'll find an answer.After all, Gillespie's journey from her first cycling club ride to the Paris Olympic Games spanned less than a decade. While her career included plenty of highs – including a host of Irish titles across multiple disciplines – she also faced more than her share of adversity.Most notably, she suffered years of undiagnosed pain from OHVIRA, a rare gynaecological-renal syndrome, corrected with surgery in early 2022. But then, in the middle of that year, came a torn hamstring, while glandular fever struck in the winter. Taken together, the ailments wiped out a chunk of her 2021 season and most of 2022."When I was sick back in 2020 and 2021, I couldn’t even get out of bed; that’s how mentally draining it was. Sport is my life; it’s what makes me feel good, so when I’m not able to do it, it’s really, really hard on my brain, my nervou. s system, my whole body," Gillespie told back in 2024."There was definitely a period when I really didn’t think I’d ever be racing again, so there’s not one day that goes by when I’m not grateful to be back on the bike. Everyone experiences hard times, though, but once things start going good again, you kind of forget about them."Since then, her progress has been lightning fast. In 2023, she joined the development programme of UAE Team L'IMAD, spending less than a year and a half there before moving up to the top-level squad.She's clearly a rider in a hurry and still on the rise.'She's developed into one of the fastest sprinters in the world'At the time, the win stood as her biggest accomplishment yet, though her Olympic appearances in the omnium, madison, and team pursuit came months later.The following season brought another rapid step-up as her calendar expanded from just six Women's WorldTour race days to 43, including debuts at Paris-Roubaix Femmes and the Tour de France Femmes.Nevertheless, she made an immediate impact in the Classics with three podiums plus a fifth at the Classic Brugge-De Panne and sixth at Gent-Wevelgem.This year, she's stepped it up once again, winning Le Samyn and placing eighth at Paris-Roubaix. Wiebes has proved a tough nut, as yet uncrackable, but Gillespie is more than pleased with her progress."I think just having the consistency – I really had a good winter and also just having the WorldTour girls around me every time," Gillespie told about her 2026 campaign at the recent Tour of Britain Women."We're always showing up with a really strong team in the way we ride. We're protecting each other all day, and as a sprinter, that's all you really want."The Tour of Britain isn't the Tour de France Femmes, but it offered plenty of hills to tackle, with over 7,000 metres of climbing on grippy roads packed into five days.Cherie Pridham, her directeur sportif at UAE, noted that races like this will only help her development and growing versatility."That's why we're here, you know? I think we've shown that Lara is very versatile. She's not just a pure sprinter, but she can also fight on the punchy, small climbs," she told at the end of perhaps the race's toughest day, stage 4's hilly trek through mid Wales."She's done a lot of teamwork here on the Tour of Britain for GC with Karlijn [Swinkels] and with Eleonora [Gasparrini]. And she came into this race having had some illness before, so we had to manage that."She was part of our development squad almost two years before she moved up to the Women's WorldTour team. We moved her up, and she's just progressed. We made a conscious effort to build a team around her for her Classics progress and also, of course, she's developed into one of the fastest sprinters in the world."Finding success across disciplinesAs Pridham pointed out, to reduce Gillespie's talents to a simple descriptor – 'sprinter', for example – is to do her a disservice.Gillespie's journey to the rainbow jersey began almost by accident, even if she enjoyed a sport-filled upbringing in the Irish countryside growing up in Enniskerry, in sight of the Wicklow Mountains.Already a keen swimmer and runner, she fell into the sport after trying triathlon for the first time. Soon after, during her Transition Year – an optional off-curriculum school programme available to teenagers in Ireland – she joined local road club Orwell Wheelers, initially thinking it was a mountain bike club. Just two years later, she won time trial silver at the European Youth Olympic Festival.Road, track, mountain, cyclo-cross – Gillespie seems at ease on any bike and on any surface. For her, switching between disciplines is a privilege and a mental stimulus, rather than an undertaking to fret over. "I love it. I love the switch because, well, for me, I want to get on a different bike every day. Today I want to go on a mountain bike, tomorrow I want to go on a track bike, the next day I'll go on the cross bike, and then eventually I'll go on the road bike," she told Irish sports podcast last December."I also like, for example, when I got injured just before the 2025 Tour, and I thought, 'Maybe I can't do the Tour,' mentally I was like, 'Oh, but it's OK because I have Track Worlds at the end of the season and I will be fit and healthy for that.'"That, mentally, just takes the pressure off because it's not the only thing in my life, and it means that if this doesn't go well, okay, at least I can focus on this."This year, she's switched effortlessly between disciplines. Barely two weeks after Paris-Roubaix, she was racing at the UCI Track World Cup in Hong Kong. After that, she was back on the road for a Giro d'Italia debut and a pair of national road titles ahead of a mid-summer track meet in Pordenone, Italy.Having returned to the road at the Tour de Pologne and the Tour of Britain, she's now primed to get back to the track."Towards the end, I'm focusing more on the track. The Track World Championships are in October. I have a couple more races with the team in September in China, and it'll be nice to go for a few sprints there," she told ."[Switching] worked quite well last year. I get like a month on track before, and then try to speed things up."Looking further ahead, a return to the boards at the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028 figures among her long-term targets, naturally.'She reminds me a lot of André. They're pure leaders'In Gillespie's quest to be the best, she's already racking up wins and major results. Her consistency has been notable, and she can look back on 16 top-five finishes this year, including seven second places. Those results include a pair of second places at the UAE Tour, and two more behind Elisa Balsamo at the Giro.In Britain there was an early positioning misfire – "the girls kept me really safe, but I lost a lot of position in the final kilometre and had to make up a lot of ground in the wind, so I never got to show my power," she said of the Blackpool stage.But there was another second place too, as she punched ahead of Chiara Consonni at the line in Leamington Spa, a positive outcome given that earlier in the race she noted: "I had a very bad bout of illness in the last couple of weeks, and I've been on and off antibiotics, so I'm just kind of taking it day by day."Gillespie's support squad is a major reason for these successes and the progress she's made. That support includes Pridham, the experienced voice in the team car, and a certain André Greipel, also part of the backroom staff.She could scarcely have found a better mentor than the German, who racked up 158 professional wins and stood second only to Mark Cavendish as the defining sprinter of his generation.During the UAE Tour, Greipel praised her rapid development. Speaking to , the German highlighted how quickly riders like the Irishwoman learn and absorb feedback."For sure, the men are longer in the sport than some women. [There are] women in the bunch who picked up cycling maybe three years ago, so every day is a teaching process, and they can learn something new," he said."They are really open to listen and learn to what a sport director, a trainer or even myself has to say. Also, they are really open to get feedback. I think it is really helpful if you have someone who can tell them in certain scenarios what would be a good idea during the race, and I think this would make the difference now to make the right choices and tactics."Personality-wise, Gillespie and Greipel are cut from the same cloth, according to Pridham. That alignment has paid off in their work together, with Gillespie and her lead-out train already delivering a string of results to savour."Of course, we brought in André to help us with the sprint lead-out and the sprint coaching, and that made a huge, significant difference to the team and to Lara. And the results were there. I think we came very close to beating Lorena Wiebes at the UAE Tour," Pridham said, referring to stage 3 in Abu Dhabi Breakwater, where she came achingly close to victory."She reminds me a lot of André. They're pure leaders. She's growing into that leadership role. She understands what energy she needs to give and the right instructions that she expects from her riders."So she's quite specific and clear on that, but that takes some time. But she has a lot of trust now from the girls that support her."'You can't be in the game without believing that you can win'Gillespie is growing on and off the bike, and she's already achieved plenty. Each year that goes by sees another major accomplishment added to a growing list of them.She marked her return from illness in 2022 with two wins – the first in eight years by an Irish woman – at Rás na mBan, followed by a pair of under-23 European track titles in 2023. The next year brought that Olympic debut and a nomination for Irish Female Athlete of the Year before that track world title last year. Le Samyn is her standout this year – so far.With this progress in mind, it's crazy to think that just six years ago, Gillespie didn't know any of this was even possible."I didn't even know you could be a professional cyclist until maybe 2020. From a very young age, I remember saying to myself, 'I'm going to go to the Olympics'. I had a vision of becoming an Olympic champion, but I didn't have cycling in that vision whatsoever," she told earlier this year.So what lies ahead – a Women's WorldTour win? Beating Wiebes? "Obviously, she's the most dominant right now, and you can see she's super consistent every time, able to show up regardless of the circumstances," Gillespie said."But yeah, I think you can't be in the game without believing that you can win. Every time, you have to believe, but it's all about executing it in the end, and you need a team to execute it."Gillespie harbours the ambition to be where Wiebes is right now – the dominant force in the peloton, sweeping sprint after sprint and winning major Classics like In Flanders Fields and Milan-San Remo.As she put it to , "I want to be the best in the world." Her rainbow jersey proves she's already reached that goal in one sense, if not on the road. However, she told the podcast, "to me [they're] different ideas" – it's not about a single victory, but a consistency of success, and repetition of those big wins.For now, reaching that goal will take more work, more progress, more growth. Gillespie has come a long way in a very short period of time, and it's far from the end of her story."We just haven't had the right run now for – like every other team, you know?" Pridham said of the battles against Wiebes."As she is showing here at the Tour of Britain, she can survive the climbs, and then she's almost unbeatable. You need to try to catch her to win. But we're very, very proud of Lara's progress, and she still has a lot more to come."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: Court rules Kalshi sports bets aren't "swaps," just gambling with a different name
item.author: Jon Brodkin
item.content:encoded: Kalshi today lost a major ruling over whether it can evade state gambling laws, as a federal appeals court found that Nevada can stop the prediction market from allowing sports bets. While the Trump administration is trying to help prediction markets avoid state regulation, a panel of three Trump-appointed judges unanimously ruled against Kalshi in today's decision from the US Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit.The Nevada Gaming Control Board today said the 9th Circuit "emphatically reject[ed] the view that the federal Commodity Exchange Act preempts application of Nevada’s gaming laws to sports-event contracts offered by Kalshi, Crypto.com, and Robinhood." Nevada Governor Joe Lombardo, a Republican, said that "prediction markets offering sports-event contracts constitute gambling and must comply with Nevada’s gaming laws and regulatory framework."The judges affirmed a district court order that let Nevada enforce state laws against Kalshi’s sports-related event contracts.

item.title: "RFK Jr. has lied to the Senate": Lawmakers call for criminal probe, ouster
item.author: Beth Mole
item.content:encoded: Senators are renewing calls for anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy to step down or be ousted—and at least one is calling for a criminal investigation—amid the release of documents they say prove Kennedy lied to them during his confirmation hearings last year."This is a pattern, not a slip," Sen. Edward J. Markey (D-Mass.) said in a statement. "RFK Jr. has lied to the Senate, lied to the American people, and jeopardized the health of children to advance his anti-vaccine agenda."Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) said in a social media post Friday that the documents were "Proof we got RFK lying on the record during his confirmation hearing (a crime)." He called for the matter to be referred to the US Department of Justice for a criminal investigation. In a separate statement to The Guardian, Wyden added that "RFK's platform is built on lies and grifts that leave a trail of dead children in their wake. There are consequences for lying to Congress."

item.title: 'A good day to try something' - Felix Gall upbeat after aggressive final ascent at Vuelta a España
item.content:encoded: As at Andorra on stage 4, Decathlon's decision to try to isolate Pogačar worked up to a point, and it even culminated, once again, in an intense drive of around 300 metres by their leader, Felix Gall, to which only Pogačar could respond.However, that was as good as it got, as the Vuelta leader then moved away ahead of the Austrian climber, leaving Gall to continue with a lone pursuit of the Slovenian - but ahead of his GC rivals.Gall crossed the line six seconds behind Pogačar but with a 10-second advantage on Enric Mas (Movistar) and a further 23 on the remainder of his GC rivals. That pushes him up a spot into fourth overall, and with Primož Roglič (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) only 11 seconds ahead, the battle for the podium is growing more intense with each stage that passes.It was a much better performance, too, for Gall after stage 6's difficult day on the gravel-capped climb of Puerto de El Bartolo, where he lost time on Pogačar and Mas. This time round, even if the Slovenian remains out of reach - and he's hardly alone in that - on this occasion, Gall was definitely best of the rest."It's nice to create some gaps, it was a bit of a more of a relaxed day, the most relaxed day of the first part of the race, so that was nice, and I'm definitely happy with the outcome of today," Gall said afterwards."I felt much better today, yesterday was also, in the end, a good day apart from the final, which was pretty bad, but that's how it is in a Grand Tour sometimes."As was only logical, Gall paid tribute to Decathlon for turning in such an impressive all-round performance, one which even if it didn't put Pogačar into difficulties, certainly had the right kind of effect regarding his GC aspirations for the podium."The guys always push me to be more aggressive. Gregor is always motivated, he can always push me to try something. "It was super nice, I suffered quite a bit on Gregor's wheel, that's for sure, but it's a pleasure to race with such a strong team and nice to get some gaps today."The plan to attack on Aramón took shape during the race, he said, with the initial aim to be more conservative, but then it turned out that "it was a good day to try something. We have strong teammates, so you can actually do that."However, whilst only Pogačar able to withstand his assault, Gall recognised there was a limit to his ambitions, and that didn't involve dislodging the Slovenian star from the top spot overall."Tadej was just doing his pace, and I wasn't really focusing on him," he explained. "This is a race for the podium; you take him out of the equation."For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.content:encoded: The Trump administration's blacklisting of Anthropic was illegal, a federal judge ruled in an order vacating government directives against the use of the firm's AI technology.The government illegally retaliated against Anthropic by designating it a supply-chain risk to national security, said yesterday's ruling by Judge Rita Lin in the US District Court for the Northern District of California. The maker of Claude AI technology was barred by the US after it refused to drop restrictions on the use of its products for lethal autonomous warfare and mass surveillance of Americans, the ruling said."The undisputed record shows that the challenged actions constituted unlawful retaliation in violation of the First Amendment," Lin wrote in an order that granted key portions of Anthropic's motion for summary judgment.

item.title: 'I wasn't angry at all' - Vuelta a España leader Tadej Pogačar denies he attacked on Aramón Valdelinares finish because he was upset
item.content:encoded: Stage 7 of the Vuelta a España was business as usual in some ways for Tadej Pogačar as the UAE Team Emirates-XRG leader once again gained time on his GC rivals, but it was a far more muted display than on other occasions.Riding in the group of favourites, Pogačar reacted to a marked acceleration in pace by Decathlon CMA CGM halfway up the final ascent of Aramón Valdelinares, culminating in an attack with their contender Felix Gall.The Slovenian star came through when Gall invited him to collaborate, he told reporters later, and he then accelerated a little more to go clear alone. By the finish, his advantage on Gall was six seconds, with Enric Mas (Movistar), second overall, a further 16 seconds behind and the remainder of the GC rivals at 30 seconds and counting.Not a major gain, then, compared to Pogačar's dominating display at Andorra, where he took nearly three minutes on his chasers, or even the time he gained during his stage 6 breakaway move with Mas, which netted him just over 40 seconds. With the breakaway finally staying away and Uno-X Mobility's Andrea Leknessund winning, there was no stage victory to celebrate either. The gains were so slender, it led to some speculation by Mas at the line that Pogačar had been angry at some point during the race and rather than wanting to gain time, he wanted to prove a point.The Vuelta leader denied that this was the case, explaining that his time gain had come about by a series of circumstances rather than a major plan like in Andorra or Castellò. "It was quite normal, straightforward," Pogačar said."I wasn't angry at all. I would love to ride with a teammate's pace to the top of the climb, but Decathlon decided to race, and they went hard," Pogačar explained."I followed Felix and saw some gaps were growing within the GC guys. Felix flicked his elbow for me to pass, then I contributed, and I opened the gap and then continued to the finish. It was all quite normal, straightforward."Overall, Pogačar's GC margin has stretched to 3:50 on second-placed Mas, with Primož Roglič (Red Bull-Bora-Hansgrohe) now an even more distant 4:50. Although he lost the points jersey to Wout van Aert (Visma-Lease Bike) after the Belgian made it into a breakaway, he reacted a little sharply when asked if the points ranking was 'still a target'."It was never a target so the word 'still' is off the table," he said. "The red jersey is the main goal, and that's all."Talking on Eurosport, Pogačar said that he would have loved to go for his fourth stage win in seven days, but the upcoming climbing challenges, in particular Sunday's lengthy trek through the mountains of southern Valencia to the summit of Aitana, made it better to ease back a little.He explained that it was "better to save the team, and have a bit less crazy day than yesterday [stage 6] because stage 9 will be one of the toughest stages of the Vuelta."Opting to take a more conservative approach once a big enough lead has been established is a textbook strategy for any Grand Tour leader, and Pogačar's advantage of nearly four minutes on Mas is certainly a race-winning one. But it remains an unusual strategy for a rider normally as aggressive as Pogačar to take.On Sunday's ascent of Aitana, we could yet see him revert to type and go for another knockout stage win. Only one thing remains beyond any doubt: he's still the strongest rider in the 2026 Vuelta, and his lead is only getting bigger with each mountain stage that passes.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. 'I didn't have confidence in myself' – Wout van Aert bags green jersey but regrets missed opportunity in Vuelta a España breakaway
item.content:encoded: Wout van Aert said he underestimated himself after a fruitful and nearly sensational but ultimately disappointing day out at the Vuelta a España. The Paris-Roubaix champion made it up the road on a day the breakaway survived to contest the stage on the category-1 summit finish to Aramón Valdelinares, and he made it into a five-man move that fought it out between them on that final climb. Van Aert ticked off his primary target as he collected 20 points at the intermediate sprint with 25km to go but he went on to ride so well on the final climb that it ended up leaving him with a sense of regret. In the end, Van Aert was worked over by two more natural climbers riding with the tactical advantage of wearing the same Uno-X jersey. Andreas Leknessund soloed off to win the stage, while Tobias Haaland Johannessen sat on the chasing Van Aert before skipping clear near the line. "Honestly, I regret maybe a little bit that I didn't have confidence in myself for the last climb," Van Aert said, responding to a suggestion that he'd done a lot of work and spent a lot of energy to drive the breakaway on."During the day I thought it would be nice to take the points at the intermediate and then have as big a margin as possible to do top five on the stage – that was the idea I kept for a while."But then on the final climb, I could see a lot of the others were also tired, so maybe I should have played it a bit smarter, but that's also my nature, I think."When asked if he underestimated himself, he replied: "Yeah."Still, there was consolation for Van Aert in the form of the green jersey. Van Aert was already wearing the green jersey - or rather the green skinsuit - on stage 7, but it was only ‘on loan’ from Pogačar, who was leading the points classification but has the overall leader’s red jersey as his wardrobe priority. Van Aert collected 20 points at the intermediate sprint with 25km remaining, and a further 15 for his third-place finish on the stage. That brought him to a total of 104 points, a slim but clear two points ahead of Pogačar."I hope it will not take as much energy every day as I did on this stage, but in the Vuelta you also need climbing legs to compete in the green jersey classification, so if the legs are there, then let's ride," Van Aert said of his challenge for green.Competition, however, also comes from within Van Aert’s own team, with Matthew Brennan – winner of two stages so far – third in the points classification, albeit a fair bit further back on 60 points. Brennan has been Visma’s chosen man for the bunch sprints and reduced-peloton sprints so far, so has the potential to add to his tally in big chunks if he keeps winning stages. At the start of the stage, Pogačar suggested Visma need to make a decision on who they back as his main rival for green, but that looks almost certainly to be the domain of Van Aert, who has happily worked to set up Brennan in the sprints so far.For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews. item.title: 'I’ll probably need a season where I spend more time on the mountain bike' - Mathieu van der Poel realistic ahead of the UCI Mountain Bike World Championships
item.content:encoded: However, the 31-year-old believes that if he is ever to win the rainbow jersey in mountain biking, he would benefit from racing the discipline more regularly than in recent years.Van der Poel’s best result in the Cross-Country Olympic race (XCO) Worlds came as far back as 2018 when he was third at Lenzerheide, with his subsequent attempts being blighted by poor luck and bad start grid positions. As if to prove his point, a second place at last weekend’s World Cup in Les Gets was not only his best result in the discipline since 2021, but his first race of the 2026 mountain bike season. A decent result in the short track race allowed him to start from the second row, something he admitted was a benefit. However, having raced so little in recent years, he will have no such luck on Sunday."Starting from the fifth row obviously reduces my chances," Van der Poel told a press call by the Alpecin-Premier Tech campervan in Val di Sole on Friday. "In Les Gets I saw again how big the difference is when you start closer to the front, you’re immediately part of the race. If I really want to give myself the best possible chance of becoming world champion one day, I’ll probably need a season where I spend more time on the mountain bike so I can earn a place on one of those first two rows. For Sunday, though, the situation is what it is. I’ll have to make the best of it and maybe have a little bit of luck as well.""I came out of the Tour in much better shape this year, and winning on the Champs-Élysées obviously gave me a lot of confidence and motivation. Last year I wasn’t really at my normal level. This time the switch to the mountain bike has been much smoother. I also spent a lot of time on the MTB during my altitude camp in Livigno, and I think I needed that."Though he’ll ride in the orange jersey of the Netherlands this weekend, he has been supported this week by his trade team, Alpecin-Premier Tech, who have brought in Matteo Berta as technical coach to give both Van der Poel and their hope for the women’s race, Puck Pieterse, the best chance of success. The Italian will check the course and give riders advice on the best lines. However, he will not be able to compensate for the poor start position, though Van der Poel has at least learnt after getting over-excited last year, when he finished a lowly 29th. "Last year I actually had a good start, but I was probably a little too eager to move up immediately. If you go too deep early on, you pay for it straight away, and often that’s exactly when the guys at the front accelerate again. But at the same time you don’t want to lose contact with the race. Finding that balance will be important."Wherever he finishes Sunday’s race, Van der Poel won’t let the result tarnish his stellar career. Not only does he have eight elite cyclocross rainbow jerseys to his name, there are a host of honours on the road, including eight Monument victories and Grand Tour stage wins."It’s definitely an important goal for me, but I think it would be too simplistic to say I need an MTB world title for my career to be successful," he explained. "I wouldn’t look back on my career disappointed if I never won it. But of course I really want to add it to my palmarès. If it doesn’t happen this year, hopefully there will be another opportunity."I’d definitely like to have a year where I can put a bit more focus on mountain biking. But that’s something that has to be discussed with the team because there are other commitments too. But yes, I’d like to give it a proper try.”For unbeatable coverage across road, gravel and tech, subscribe to Cyclingnews.
