item.title: Friday Posted & Toasted Notes: International Knicks, KD & Dray & T-Mac talk too much
item.author: Antonio Losada
item.content:encoded: I let everybody down not publishing notes in a week, thinking there was nothing happening around the League but still saving clippings into a document that ended up growing monstrous. Won’t happen again, for my own health.Jalen Brunson’s wrist recovery remains the biggest health variable hanging over the Knicks. Dexter Henry of the New York Post stressed the difference between Brunson being medically cleared and actually looking like Brunson again, while Bryan Fonseca argued that New York’s repeat hopes effectively disappear if its Finals MVP cannot return to his pre-injury level. All we know is that Brunson is still not participating in basketball activities and has described the rehab process as “frustrating.”James L. Edwards III of The Athletic has heard estimates ranging from roughly $54-$62 million over three years for Hart’s next deal, although Edwards believes something closer to $70-$80 million might represent fairer value.Hart spoke to our own Michael Zeno and opened up about how much New York has come to feel like home after years of bouncing around the league. Hart also revealed he has no plans to undergo another procedure on the troublesome ring finger of his shooting hand despite playing through the injury last season. “But now, I’m in New York. I feel like I have a home here, and I’m extremely happy.”“No, I’ll let it go. At the end of my career, when I’m done hooping, I’ll probably have to get a joint replacement in it, but for now it’s fine.”Hart offered a nice explanation for what keeps him grounded through an NBA season, mentioned his wife, Mikal Bridges and Brunson as people who help him navigate the grind and, in perhaps Hart’s best reflection on the championship he just won, he said roughly 90 percent of fans who approach him mention either their father or their son when discussing the title. Worth read in full!Jose Alvarado kept his dream year going, now internationally. The Brooklyn-born Knicks guard is representing Puerto Rico at the FIBA World Cup, and he already scored a team-high 19 points for Puerto Rico in an 89-75 World Cup qualifying loss to Argentina. The Knicks guard shot 7-of-15 from the field and added six rebounds and four assists. Former Knick Pablo Prigioni coached Argentina.Pacome Dadiet, who does not represent France, also made his senior international debut, helping Ivory Coast beat Mali 83-77. Dadiet scored nine points on 4-of-12 shooting and struggled from deep at 1-of-8, but grabbed a game-high nine rebounds, including five on the offensive glass.The Knicks’ third-center search took another hit with Nick Richards going to the Miami Heat. With Ariel Hukporti already gone to Philadelphia and Mitchell Robinson in Boston, New York still has not filled the final, third-string center spot behind Karl-Anthony Towns and Andre Drummond. The increasingly likely outcome? A training-camp competition between veterans on non-guaranteed deals to determine he earns the gig.The Knicks, meanwhile, still have all three two-way roster spots open with training camp approaching. Rookie Tyler Nickel remains unsigned and could fill one of them if he begins his professional career rather than returning to college.Leon Rose received major praise from CBS Sports’ Sam Quinn for building one of the strangest championship rosters in league history, as the Knicks just became only the second NBA champion ever to win without drafting a single member of its starting five, joining the 2020 Lakers.The Athletic’s latest NBA power rankings put the Knicks at No. 1 overall entering training camp.“It’s easy to put the Knicks at No. 1 after their dominant postseason run. Ten of their top 12 players return, though NBA Finals MVP Jalen Brunson has to recover from wrist surgery on his shooting hand. Drummond replaces Robinson, but the team still doesn’t have a replacement for Hukporti. We know the Knicks want to replace Hukporti, because they signed center Moussa Cissé to an offer sheet that the Dallas Mavericks matched.“The regular season will be interesting for the defending champs. There hasn’t been a dominant regular-season Knicks team in the 21st century, as the Knicks haven’t won at least 55 games since 1996-97. Will that matter? How many regular-season losses would it take before we start to believe the Knicks might not be a repeat threat come April? Those are the real questions.” — Law Murray(Not) shockingly, ESPN’s summer forecast is much less convinced the Knicks will repeat. Its panel picked New York to win the Eastern Conference with 68 points, comfortably ahead of Philadelphia at 51… but ranked the Knicks a distant third in NBA championship voting behind Oklahoma City and San Antonio. The Thunder received 84 points, the Spurs 74 and New York only 11.DeMar DeRozan is headed to Denver on a one-year, $3.9 million deal after being waived by Sacramento. Meanwhile, Klay Thompson officially joined Miami after clearing waivers following a buyout with Dallas.Jonathan Kuminga finally found a home, agreeing with Minnesota on a two-year contract that includes a player option.Kevin Durant called the Knicks’ championship run “the best championship as a viewer that I’ve ever seen.”“I was on the fence on if they were going to win. And then they got down every game, and I’m just like, ‘I don’t know.’ And then they started coming back. I didn’t become a believer, to be honest, until the last game. I was just like, the Spurs would be up 15 points every game, 29 points, and then they’d just come back and steal a game. That’s probably why that was the best championship as a viewer that I’ve ever seen.“Not just because of the Knicks brand winning, but just the fashion they won those games in, it was insane. It really showed you the power dynamic in the NBA: a veteran team that was put together through trades vs. a team that drafted everybody that a lot of people would have loved to see win. For the Knicks to do it that way, I felt they made a statement.”Durant also weighed in on Jalen Brunson’s decision to leave roughly $100 million on the table, acknowledging he understands why Brunson made the sacrifice and credited the move for helping New York build a championship roster. That said, KD admitted he probably would have been talked out of doing the same.“I understand his thought process and why he actually executed that. I can’t put myself in that position and just say, ‘Yeah, I would have done it or not.’ For him to make that decision and come out the way it did, kudos to him. But hopefully he gets that back on the back end.“I would have gotten talked out of it. I probably would have been like, ‘All right, I’m cool with it.’ I’d have sat down and talked to all my people like I usually do, Rich, all my friends. Like, ‘What? Are you serious? Why do you need to take that risk when this dude’s a billionaire?’ Nobody would do that.”Draymond Green likes Klay Thompson’s move to Miami but wonders how the famously independent Thompson will mesh with “Heat Culture.”Green also pushed back against treating the signing as though Miami is getting 2018 Klay, comparing the move more appropriately to Ray Allen joining the Heat late in his career.“I don’t like how everybody’s trying to act like, ‘Oh man, it’s Klay Thompson’ like Klay to the Heat, like this is Klay of 2018. The reason I don’t like it is because I feel like everybody’s trying to set Klay up for failure. And so, I’m going to say it right here, right now. Let’s stop acting like 2017 Klay is going to Miami.“Don’t try to set my brother up like you about to get the 2017 Klay, so the moment you don’t, y’all can bash him. That’s bullsh*t. He’s going into Year 16 of his career. We obviously know the injuries that he’s faced.”Tracy McGrady offered another contribution to the endless rings-versus-individual-awards debate, arguing that a regular-season MVP carries more weight than winning a championship. Sheesh…Ice Cube remains convinced BIG3 players should represent the United States in Olympic 3-on-3 basketball, calling USA Basketball “crazy” for not using what he believes are the best 3-on-3 players in the country. And he’s damn right.“They’re crazy not to use our athletes as the U.S. Olympic team in 3-on-3. The last two Olympics have been a disaster for USA when it comes to what USA Basketball has been putting together to represent the US. I hope they have a ‘come-to-Jesus moment’ and realize that we have the best 3-on-3 players in the world. It’s not even close. They should use our athletes to represent the U.S., especially on U.S. soil. Will they do that or not? Egos may win and prevail, and the U.S. will suffer because of that.”Blake Griffin is moving into late-night television, starting on Oct. 20.Metta Sandiford-Artest attempted to buy a one-percent stake in the Lakers for $100 million but was swiftly turned down.

item.title: What should the Knicks do with a Karl-Anthony Towns extension?
item.author: Michael Zeno
item.content:encoded: As we go deeper into the dog days of the offseason, the Knicks are a team with relatively few questions. After all, they just won the title (still feels great to say that) and returned almost all of their production from that title run, but there are still things to discuss as we patiently wait for more basketball on our screens.High up on that list of things pertains to a potential contract extension for a player whose postseason buy-in was unlike anything we’ve seen before on both ends, who had a real case to win Finals MVP before the league mandate to both extend the series and prop up Wemby forced him into repeated foul trouble to end the series.That’s, of course, Karl-Anthony Towns. No player, not even Jalen Brunson or OG Anunoby, has experienced a better PR boost from this title than Towns. The median NBA fan would call Towns an overpaid, zesty (whatever that means), defensive liability to undermine just how dominant an offensive player he is, but his defensive buy-in and versatility as an offensive engine for a dominant playoff run changed hearts and minds. He’s now unanimously considered a top 15 player in the game.But how should said player be paid? Handsomely, surely, but it’s more complicated than that.It’s 2026, and although player empowerment is by far the social norm, there have been considerable efforts to curtail it, particularly with the current CBA and the introduction of the second apron.It’s meant to give players a proposition. You can either make what you want or have a sustainable winner. If you get the max contract, you’ll be taking money away from your supporting cast, which will decrease your odds of winning a championship. If you take less money, you’d be getting paid less than some guys who clearly don’t deserve to be in your same tax bracket.Brunson is a perfect example. He could’ve waited a year and signed a five-year, $269 million mega-extension in 2025, but elected to take four years and $156 million a year early for a myriad of reasons. If he wanted to make the most money, he likely wouldn’t have gotten a co-star in KAT, given the team’s aversion to the second apron. Role players like Jose Alvarado wouldn’t be here. Big moves would be made year after year to fit a few specific salaries, preventing the team from geling properly.But while his extension has brought him the ultimate glory and likely earned him a massive future extension, it didn’t come without risk. Beyond the fact that there’s no guarantee he would’ve been given another big extension if he regressed in the ensuing four years, he was now making less than guys like Desmond Bane, LaMelo Ball, Michael Porter Jr., Darius Garland, Domantas Sabonis, Ja Morant, Zach LaVine, Paul George, and more. He’s the 47th highest-paid player in 2026-27, despite being a top-five player in the game. These guys can’t lace his boots.Towns can do the same thing that his co-star did: take less money, but should he? Unlike Brunson, who was entering his age-28 season when he signed it, KAT is going to be 31 in November. The extension would start when he’s 32 and likely take him through age 36, when, barring LeBron-esque longevity, he’ll be diminished. This will be his last big paycheck.The max he is eligible for this offseason is a huge sum of four years and $272 million. That’s $68 million a year. His current 2027-28 salary is a player option worth $61 million, so based on the contract escalators, he wouldn’t make too much more, but it would put him on the books for north of $70 million into his mid-30s. While the salary cap will continue to rise and make it less of an issue, that’s a lot of money for a player exiting his prime.It’s also inhibitive of roster construction, particularly if James Dolan continues to drag his feet over even one season of the second apron. The Knicks currently have $226 million of salary on the books for 2027-28 with 10 players rostered, sitting just $7 million under the projected second apron. Any raise for Towns against his player option would be prohibitive and make it impossible to stay under the second apron without trades, particularly if the team has any desire to keep a guy like Deuce McBride. The Knicks already won their championship, so the team should be in a state of enjoying the riches that they’ve earned, but it’s not 2018 anymore, when Joe Lacob was just able to spend infinite money on maintaining his superteam with no roster restrictions. Dolan has the money, which is what makes the decision even more bizarre, particularly when the repeater tax does not apply until next season. If there was any year to go into that second apron, it was this year, so I have my doubts he’ll do it next year.The Knicks should extend KAT. He, like Brunson and Anunoby and maybe more, should go down as a Knicks legend and either retire here or be defined by their tenures here. If he merely plays out his contract, Towns will spend just three (or four) years as a Knick, a tenure that is dwarfed by his near-decade in Minnesota. The guy who’s the first star center to lift the Larry O’Brien in the orange and blue since Willis Reed should be remembered as a Knick, plain and simple.That’s going to have to come with some sacrifice, though, and that sucks. We’re at an unprecedented point where a team is going to have to ask an All-NBA talent to take less money winning a championship, and ask isn’t even a strong enough word. If he doesn’t take less, this core will likely begin to be disassembled next offseason.So what’s the sweet spot? How much would both properly pay the Big Bodega for his contributions while also allowing this team and this core to get as many bites of the apple at a second championship as possible?I thought about this for a good bit, and ultimately came out to a four-year pact worth about $230 million, shaving $42 million off the top of Towns’ max for an average annual value of $57.5 million. It might be a tough ask for a guy as valuable as KAT to take eight figures less per year, but let me show my work.This would give Towns a Year 1 salary of approximately $50 million, which is $11 million less than his 2027-28 player option. While certainly a tough pill for him to swallow, it would make him anywhere from the 12th to 17th highest-paid player in basketball, depending on the exact dollar amount ($50.3m would put him 12th, for example). That’s fair money, even if the guys in his range aren’t worth it (Jamal Murray, Evan Mobley, Paul George).The bigger emphasis here, though, is roster building. By saving $11 million, the Knicks would suddenly be $18 million beneath the second apron with five open roster spots in 2027-28, giving them more than enough money to stay beneath the threshold, albeit still with losing McBride. There’s at least a path to retaining McBride with some creative financing (and maybe a cheaper Hart extension) by declining Pacome Dadiet’s team option, which would put the team over $23 million beneath the apron.As the extension progresses, Towns would make $54 million in 2028-29, $58.3 million in 2029-30, and $63 million in 2030-31, which would likely be a player option. Deducing financials from this point would depend on other moves, particularly with Shamet and Alvarado’s team-friendly, partially guaranteed extensions, but also whether McBride or Hart get a new contract.I’d be surprised if he went into this season without an extension, mostly just because I expect nothing in-season and it’d be shocking to see him deal with those rumors all season with a player option looming. We’ve seen it happen with a bunch of other players, but KAT doesn’t strike me as that kind of guy.Training camp will be fun.

The Moroccan may not have expected one of those to be a centre-back by trade. Marc Guéhi will be eager to make a triumphant return to Crystal Palace and may well have the opportunity to do so from central midfield, where he played last weekend in the victory over Bournemouth, scoring the equaliser. The centre-back was a surprise selection in the blocker role next to Elliot Anderson, but equipped himself admirably and was not limited to the dirty work, often being found in more advanced positions in open play and happy to have the ball at his feet. His long-term future is unlikely to be outside defence but further proof of Guéhi’s adaptability will be a positive for Maresca, as a long season awaits. item.content:encoded: Bruno Fernandes is the only surviving attacker from Ole Gunnar Solskjær’s attempt to bridge gap to rivals in 2021Five years is a long time in football. Manchester United’s summer of 2021 is now remembered as the turning point in Ole Gunnar Solskjær’s reign; the sentimental decision to sign Cristiano Ronaldo the headline act as United set off on the wrong course after a few years of building steadily.But back then, even before the signing of Ronaldo, there was optimism aplenty around Old Trafford. United swatted aside Leeds 5-1 on the opening day to fuel talk of a first genuine title charge since Alex Ferguson’s retirement. They had, after all, just signed the most coveted young English player on the market in Jadon Sancho and looked to pair the £73m man with Bruno Fernandes and Paul Pogba, their creative fulcrum, and an exciting set of forwards.Continue reading...

item.title: His name is Enes Kanter
item.author: Matthew Miranda
item.content:encoded: Not a lot broke right for David Fizdale’s 2019 Knicks, but if a broke clock is right twice a day that’s 730 times a year, so even Fiz had his moments. One came a few months into another lost season, after he got over the shock of Kevin Durant and Zion Williamson not walking through that door, looked around the locker room and decided the Knicks’ future centered on its two young centers, Mitchell Robinson and Luke Kornet. That pair went on to play supporting roles as backup bigs for NBA champions. The center they displaced did not.Enes Kanter’s postseason history is short and direct, like a shiv. He was Oklahoma City’s only real reserve big man in 2016, what with Kevin Durant, Serge Ibaka and Steven Adams each playing 30-40 minutes per playoff game. Three years later, Kanter was the starting center for a Portland side that made the Western finals before being swept by Golden State. The next season he played bit minutes for Boston the first two rounds before barely seeing the floor in the ECF vs. Miami. Spoiler: Kanter existing right as the NBA downshifted to pace-and-space and 3s was like the dinosaurs existing the same time as the asteroid. Tough break.Fizdale likely figured Kanter — older, more worldly and presumably more mature than Kornet or Mitch, three and six years his juniors — would handle the news with grace. Brace yourself: Fizdale was wrong.“For me to get to the next level, just be a good teammate, support my teammate out there and clap for him and cheer for him,’’ Kanter said at the time. “I’ll go out and do my job and help my team win. If we’re winning, it’s good. But if we’re losing it’s a problem. If this adjustment is going to get us a win, cool. But if not, there’s a problem.”There’s a problem all right. Not that I’m surprised Kanter could both state it and miss it, simultaneously.He changed his name years ago, because like the bottle-blonde Leavitts and low-T-hating Hegseths of the world, Kanter has no sense of shame. He’s open publicly about changes he’s made to his identity to better reflect the way he wishes to be seen by others. But as one who literally hugs the flag fails to recognize what such a slovenly act says about them, Kanter isn’t merely lacking in self-awareness. Self-awareness is entirely beside the point. Because “Enes Freedom” really isn’t about freedom. Which is sad.For years, Kanter has been an outspoken critic of Turkish dictator Recep Erdoğan. The personal may be political, but it’s often the other way around, too. Born in Switzerland, Kanter gained Turkish citizenry through his parents. He’s endured Erdoğan’s forces imprisoning and oppressing his loved ones in Turkey and escaped a Turkish kidnapping attempt in Indonesia, so you can see how even a man bigger than Charles Oakley could be scared. He’s only human; he wasn’t looking to become a political target. You can understand why he sought American citizenship, understand him saying, “I feel like this is my home now.”The D.C. kleptocracy abhors Europe in general and birthright citizenship in particular, so you might not expect them to view Kanter fondly, nor he them. Yet hate makes for strange bedfellows, so wealthy, anonymous powers-that-be fly their willing human cargo to Chicago with primo seats for a Sky game, claiming he’s there to “support women.” That manifested as Kanter going harder and louder after the Sky’s Natalie Cloud than he ever did Royce White. White recently joined Kanter in “supporting women” by facetiously stating their intent to enter the WNBA draft, after which we learned White’s ex-wife and the mother of his son was granted a 50-year order of protection after years of White’s abuse and intimidation. It was the same story with Damyean Dotson, Kanter’s former Knick teammate who faced rape charges while at the University of Oregon. The district attorney’s office dropped the case, though not without stating “there is no doubt the incidents occurred [ . . . ] the conflicting statements and actions by the victim make this case unprovable as a criminal case.” The victim won a settlement from the school after a case that saw Dotson’s defense peddle in the pathetic, including the claim that “because the University [sic] disciplines male students for sexual misconduct but never female students, it is biased against men.” Hospitals treat the sick but never the healthy, therefore they’re biased. And who among us doesn’t remember where they were the first time they heard Kanter’s impassioned support for women after Michael Beasley was accused of stripping, choking and raping a woman? Or wait — was that after Kyle O’Quinn allegedly punched a woman? Or Kristaps Porziņģis was accused of rape? Kanter’s former teammate Ime Udoka cheated on his wife with a woman in the Celtics organization, who unless she’s the owner’s wife is by default less powerful within the Celtics than Udoka was as the head coach. Oh, to have been a fly on the wall when Kanter let Udoka have it after being personally and professionally in the red. Plenty of opportunities to support women by punching up. The 49ers owner was arrested this week for soliciting prostitution from an undercover cop. One of the football Giants’ owners is more than a little linked with Jeffrey Epstein’s child rape racket. James Dolan forces facial recognition technology on millions of unwitting people. Kanter thinks he’s edgy for bugging Cloud at her job. “Never, ever hide,” Kanter told Fox News in a 2023 interview. “Hiding is not an option. I know it can be a bit dangerous sometimes, but . . . we live in a free country.” Not everybody, Enes. Yesterday in Connecticut, ICE waited for school kids to get on the morning bus, then kidnapped their parents. The cruelty was the point: when the kids get home after school, they can’t find their parents and have no idea what’s happened to them, nor where to search without subjecting themselves to the same cruel system. ICE shoots and kills women in the face. They rape and kill women in their concentration camps. Contrast that with the article photo: literally, angry man yells at Cloud. That night, Kanter’s head hit the pillow with him proudly centered as both hero and victim. The kind of man a woman would rather avoid than a bear. I won’t call him Enes Freedom anymore. Freedom means sharing the rights and responsibilities you demand for yourself with those you live with and around. Escaping oppression, only to pile on some other oppressed people, is not freedom. That’s impunity. After a string of DNPs near the end of his days in New York, Kanter kissed the Garden floor after finally returning to action. “Obviously, on the court and off the court I’ve been having a very rough time the last three weeks with Turkey issues and basketball issues,” he said. “The support that they are showing just meant a lot to me.”

item.title: The Bruiser Refusing the Final Buzzer: Charles Oakley, MSG, and The Last Enforcer
item.author: John Gove
item.content:encoded: The recent dismissal of Charles Oakley’s long-running lawsuit against Madison Square Garden marks a brutal collision between the unwritten code of loyalty and the court’s objective reality. For a third time, Judge Richard J. Sullivan of the Southern District of New York dismissed Oakley’s remaining assault and battery claims. The nine-year battle stemming from the infamous ejection in February 2017 consistently ends the same way. However, for anyone who has read , the legal defeats barely explain the feud’s full scope.Oakley’s memoir serves as an oral history of moral correctness, providing the context for why a retired player refuses to let an almost decade-old legal dispute rest, even as mounting losses and legal fees pile up. Reading the book alongside Judge Sullivan’s latest ruling highlights an interesting contrast. It pins the reality of the American judicial system against the stubborn, emotional pride of a basketball enforcer.To understand this endless litigation, we have to look back at the era of basketball Oakley helped define and the specific role he carved out. Throughout his memoir, Oakley discusses his time under Pat Riley and Jeff Van Gundy. During the 90s, he established himself as the alpha bodyguard, specifically for Patrick Ewing. He describes willingly sacrificing his body to shield his teammates from harm on the court and scrutiny of New York’s media. He constructed the blue-collar intimidator identity that defined 90s Eastern Conference basketball. The irony of his current situation is painful. The sacrificial dynamic Oakley details in his book contrasts with his current standing with the Knicks organization. The man who bled to defend his team is now treated as a hostile trespasser by the franchise he protected. He draws a direct line between how the franchise treats its legends and its corporate culture. Oakley argues that the organization as a whole does not respect the players who built the foundation. Unsurprisingly, Oak pulls no punches when discussing James Dolan. Throughout the book, he portrays him as a privileged figure with thin skin who demands compliance. Oakley strongly claims the Knicks owner abuses his power, holding grudges against anyone who dares to criticize him or the team. For Oakley, the ejection from MSG was never about legal statutes. Instead, it was about standing up to a bully who used arena security to settle a personal vendetta. What makes the book’s portrayal so compelling is how MSG’s actual corporate behavior mirrors Oakley’s narrative. After the recent ruling, MSG didn’t simply issue a standard public statement. Instead, they went on the offensive, declaring their intention to pursue legal action against Oakley’s attorney, Douglas Wigdor, and his firm, accusing them of “frivolous litigation” and “blatant abuse of the judicial system.” This combative retaliation illustrates what Oakley continuously revisits in his memoir.While Oakley succeeds in painting himself as a marginalized hero battling the corporate monster, courts do not operate by locker-room codes. They stick to evidence, which repeatedly dismantles Charles Oakley’s claims. Judge Sullivan provided a definitive ruling, noting that ample evidence proved the Knicks legend was never pushed to the ground. It stated that Oakley had a reasonable opportunity to leave The Garden peacefully but resorted to physical violence instead. Sullivan also concluded that no rational jury would find that security intentionally created fear or unlawful contact. For the former power forward, the legal reality of this whole circumstance has been quite costly. Beyond having his claims dismissed three separate times, the litigation has carried a steep financial burden. In 2025, a judge ordered Oakley to pay nearly $642,000 in attorney fees and costs related to MSG’s efforts to recover deleted text messages after the incident. Unfortunately for Oak, the evidence and the judicial system have unquestionably sided with Dolan and the Knicks organization. Despite the defeats, Enforcer’s primary theme explains what takes place next. The same stubbornness and refusal to back down that made Charles Oakley a beloved legend is what keeps him appealing the lawsuit. Whether it’s on the basketball court or in the courtroom, he does not know how to back down from a fight. Just one day after the most recent dismissal, Oakley used Instagram to display a photo from his playing days, adding “#ItsNotOver” and “#JuryTrial.” To complement the Instagram post, his legal team has already indicated its intention to appeal to the Second Circuit Court again. Though unlikely, they hope to get a jury trial this time around. This whole ordeal marks the tragedy of an enforcer who fails to hear the final buzzer. While the court issued a definitive ruling, the friction between Oakley’s narrative and MSG’s aggressive postering ensures this messy dispute isn’t over. Concluding whether Charles Oakley’s legacy will be defined by his on-court enforcement or this endless legal battle remains a complicated discussion, potentially creating more divisiveness before it’s through.

item.title: McLaren rejects Mercedes claim it cannot afford aggressive upgrades in F1 2026
Josh Hart talks Scouting America ambassadorship, championship run
item.author: Michael Zeno
item.content:encoded: The champs have been busy this offseason, continuing their media tours with new sponsorships, talk shows, and overall just enjoying the best few months anyone could ask for as kings of their respective worlds.The extra media attention has given us some pretty cool opportunities at P&T. Kento talked to Karl-Anthony Towns last month, Russ got a chance to talk to the ever-mysterious OG Anunoby, and I got the opportunity to talk to everyone’s favorite glue guy, Josh Hart, as part of his recent ambassadorship announcement with , formerly known as “Boy Scouts of America”.Hart was in the Scouts program for much of his childhood, joining it to follow in the footsteps of his older brother, Moses, and one of his close friends. He gradually rose through the ranks before putting it off at age 13 as life and basketball started to pick up for him. At 16, he returned to the program at the wish of his father, who wanted him to keep his years-old promise to see things through. Josh eventually earned the rank of Eagle Scout, the highest honor, a week before his 18th birthday.When asked why he decided now to be an ambassador for the program that shaped much of his upbringing, Hart cited what the program meant for him growing up.“It’s always been an uphill climb in my career, but I’ve always had life lessons that I’ve gotten from Scouting, and I think now is a good time to partner with them and try to influence other kids, parents, adults, and tell them, you know, you can do both.”“You can do sports, you can do arts, you can do engineering, or whatever walk of life you want to do as a kid, but you can also do Scouting,” he added. “You don’t have to pick between one or the other.”I followed up by asking him about that sort of balance that he mentioned of being able to do both Scouting and pursue things like basketball, as he did growing up. For him, it was about time management and sacrifice.“The big thing is sacrifice,” Hart said. “There’s going to be times you might not be able to hang out with friends, or there might be times when you can’t go to a camping trip or a basketball camp or a football camp. There’s going to be sacrifices, but as long as you’re good with managing the time and saying, ‘I got to do X for this merit badge; I got to put the work in on the court this week. Let me lock in for this.’ You’ll put yourself in the best position to be successful.”Scouting wasn’t for me, personally, growing up. I tried it once because one of my close friends was super into it, but it just didn’t stick for me. A lot of people I know learned valuable lessons there, so it was nice to pick the brain of someone who went through the system and has applied what he’s learned to everyday life and, particularly, his role as a “glue guy” in the NBA. “You have to have that teamwork mentality,” Hart said about applying his lessons in Scouting to his basketball career. “It’s not always about you, and sometimes that’s hard to realize, but Scouting helps you understand that more and more.”“You can’t be out on a trail, 15-20 miles from civilization, when someone gets hurt and think about yourself, he added. ” You’ve got to make sure you’re not focused on yourself, but on how you can help this person, how you can help the group, and navigate where you are and the dangers. I think that [Scouting] definitely helped with the foundation of being a servant.“The purpose of this interview was to, of course, shed light on Josh’s ambassadorship, but we’d be remiss not to talk ball. I first asked him a question about both Scouting and basketball, giving him a chance to make a basketball merit badge, which he said would require being able to “dribble, shoot, have lateral quickness, leadership”, while adding that the latter aspect would be earned through certain game situations. I can think of a guy who’d get this badge quite easily.We got some physical media attached to the interview opportunity, which came with the following image of Hart doing the Boy Scout sign, which entails raising three fingers on your right hand. See if you can find what piqued my interest here:The ring finger on his shooting hand was a topic of discussion in Knicks circles all season long, particularly when he had his low points from the perimeter. He underwent a procedure on the finger after the 2024-25 season, but aggravated it during training camp, electing to play through it with a splint all of the following season. With the finger still appearing to be busted, I asked if he had any plans to repair it, whether now or in the future:“No, I’ll let it go,” Hart said. “At the end of my career, when I’m done hooping, I’ll probably have to get a joint replacement in it, but for now it’s fine.”He agreed with my subsequent comment about not messing with what’s working, and I can see why. Hart notably shot a career-high 41.3 percent from downtown on reasonable volume, attempting 3.7 per game. Game 2 against Cleveland was a perfect example of how he didn’t let the injury impact his efficiency:I stayed away from asking about Hart’s contract situation, in which he’s currently eligible for an extension with a team option currently on the books for 2027-28, but I asked about what it’s been like to have stability in New York, particularly after winning a title and seemingly entrenching the core of this team even further.“When you’re young in the league, you’re trying to prove yourself and have a long career in the league, and that gets harder and harder the more you’re moving around,” he remarked before adding that he was always traded for a star prior to coming to NY. “It’s tough to try to solidify yourself when you’re going from team to team. Before I came to New York, I had six different coaches in my six years in the league, so it was tough.”“But now, I’m in New York. I feel like I have a home here, and I’m extremely happy.”Before getting to the good stuff about the championship, I also touched on the slog of an NBA season and how a guy like him, renowned for his tremendous hustle, sticks with it over the course of the season.“I think it’s family, obviously my wife is a huge part of that, I’m with her almost every day, so she always keeps me grounded,” he said, touching on a few things that keep him in it. “Having close friends on the team—Mikal, JB— me and JB sit on the plane, so we talk about a lot of game or family stuff, so there’s that, but also my faith.”“Friends, family, faith, those are the three ‘F’s’ that ground me and help me through tough times, whether that’s tough times on the court or off the court.”His Twitter feed is always entertaining, but what stood out this week was the rehashing of that moment in Game 4, where the Knicks were on the verge of taking their first lead after the 29-point comeback on a steal and a Hart breakaway, but he missed the layup before committing a foul on the other end. After the whistle blew, he sat frustrated on the ground, only for his teammates to help him up and keep him focused on the end goal.“They just told me to get up and move on,” Hart said about that moment. “Jose, KAT, JB, pick me up. You can see Landry yelling and motioning for me to get up, and I think that just shows the togetherness we had, where it’s like, ‘Okay, there was a mistake, but now let’s regroup, let’s figure out how we’re going to overcome that mistake and persevere in the moment.’”“I think that just shows the tight-knit culture and team that we had, and I think that’s a big reason why we won.”Lastly, I wanted to ask him about what it’s been like to essentially achieve basketball nirvana. It was said for decades that when big stars were linked to the Knicks, “Just imagine what winning a title there will do for their legacy.” How they’ll never have to pay for a meal again in the greatest city in the world. To be elevated beyond the pantheon of champions to being forever beloved in the city that never sleeps.He used that opportunity to talk about what’s it felt to feel that kind of love by directing it back at the fans and seeing what it means to them.“The thing that’s super cool for me is that about 90 percent of the people that have talked to me about it, they always mentioned either their dad or their son, and I think that’s the coolest thing.”“You never want to have a 53-year-long championship drought, but that’s generations. There are people who’s dad’s watched 1973 who were waiting for another one and raised their kids to be Knicks fans, and now they watch those games together. It’s so cool, because it really seemed like it just united families; it gave families that thing throughout all of New York, so it was super cool to hear that.”That part really hit home with me, even as someone who’s too young to have witnessed the Patrick Ewing era, let alone the ancient (in basketball terms) championships in the 1970s. The second the buzzer sounded in Game 5, I immediately hugged my 39-year-old brother, who’s the reason I became a Knicks fan. He was alive for the 90s; he was alive to see all the pain and failure from the 2000s and early 2010s while I was way too young to understand the game like I do today. It’s really a powerful moment to have decades of heartbreak spill out, and it’s nice to know that the people who provided us with this happiness that some never thought would come appreciate the love the same way we appreciate them for ending a decades-long nightmare.

item.title: Hamilton claims Dutch GP radio outbursts weren't "the best version of me"
On This Date in Knicks History: Julius Randle re-commits to New York
item.author: Russell Richardson
item.content:encoded: Ahhh, the 2020–21 season. I remember it well. After years as a punchline, the Knicks unexpectedly became competitive under first-year, veteran coach Tom Thibodeau and breakout star Julius Randle. They finished with a winning record, earned the fourth seed in the Eastern Conference, and returned to the postseason.Randle’s stellar season (24.1 points, 10.2 rebounds, six assists, All-Star, second-team All-NBA, Most Improved Player) helped the team go from the butt of jokes to something more competent. He was high-usage, physical, available, and visibly invested in the work ethic Thibs demanded. Randle defined the season on April 21, 2021 when—after scoring 40 points and grabbing 11 boards to beat the Hawks in overtime—he famously told the MSG crowd, “We here.”We loved it, this weird, slippery feeling he brought back to us called . The Knicks lost to the Hawks in the first round, but we were undeterred. For the first time in a long time, the hope felt real.Randle was taken seventh in the 2014 draft by the Lakers. Take a look at how young and unrefined he was back in 2019, at his first media day as a Knickerbocker. He would come a long way in a short time under the bright lights of NYC.On August 25, 2021, Randle signed a four-year extension worth a reported $117 million with incentives and a player option in the final year. It was the most the Knicks could offer under CBA rules, but a sight less than Randle might have earned by reaching unrestricted free agency in 2022. Had he maintained something close to his All-NBA production, projections put his next deal near five years and $200 million. (I’d love to know how he explained that to Mrs. Randle.)Randle justified leaving tens of millions on the table by saying he believed the decision would give the Knicks greater flexibility to build a contender. After earlier career stops with the Lakers and Pelicans, where he had not always been happy, Jules wanted to lock into a situation he believed in. The big fella received security, continuity, and a chance to help shape the franchise. And the fanbase received an encouraging sign that sophomore team president Leon Rose was committed to building around what the Knicks already had rather than waiting for a free-agent savior.The immediate results were a tad worrying, however. Randle regressed in 2021–22, and the Knicks missed the playoffs. The frustration peaked on January 6, 2022, against Boston at Madison Square Garden. After the Knicks fell behind by 25 and heard boos from the crowd, Randle responded to a fourth-quarter bucket with a thumbs-down gesture. Asked afterward what it meant, he replied, “Shut the f*** up.” He later apologized on Instagram, and the NBA fined him $25,000 for the language.There are many reasons that season went off the rails, including the gamble on Kemba Walker’s knees and the mixed results from Evan Fournier. Randle’s prominence on the team, his mood swings, and his drop in production made him the most obvious target for fans who, less than a year earlier, had such high hopes. There’s that word again, the slippery bastard.Nevertheless, the organization did not regress into perpetual reconstruction. Thibodeau’s culture of toughness and accountability took root around Randle and holdovers such as RJ Barrett and Mitchell Robinson. The Knicks had begun to resemble a credible basketball operation again, and that mattered in 2022, when they cleared cap space and signed Jalen Brunson to a four-year, $104 million deal.Brunson quickly became the primary creator and eventual face of the franchise (and captain!). Randle adapted to playing alongside him, producing additional All-Star and All-NBA seasons. Success followed.The Knicks became regular playoff participants while improving the roster through savvy front-office moves. Josh Hart, OG Anunoby, and eventually Mikal Bridges joined the group. Then, in October 2024, Randle’s part of the story ended. New York sent him, Donte DiVincenzo, Keita Bates-Diop, and a first-round pick to Minnesota in the three-team trade for Karl-Anthony Towns.The front office publicly thanked Randle for helping establish the foundation and culture, and the trade showed how far the franchise had advanced. New York could exchange one accomplished All-NBA player for another whose skill set better suited the roster around Brunson. Towns brought size, shooting, and secondary creation to a starting five reinforced by Anunoby, Bridges, and Hart.That group eventually reached the mountaintop Randle never could as a Knick. Thibodeau was replaced by Mike Brown, who coached the 2025–26 squad to 53 wins, an NBA Cup championship, and the franchise’s first NBA title in five decades. Brunson became Finals MVP, while Towns delivered consistently on the biggest stage.Five years after the extension, the anniversary is bittersweet. Randle never won the big prize in New York, but our appreciation for his contribution has grown in retrospect. He joined a dysfunctional franchise, restored respectability and expectations, embodied its culture of hard work, and ultimately became a valuable enough asset to help acquire the third-best center in the league (according to . . . any guesses whom they put ahead of KAT?).On the timeline from the crappy years to the championship, Randle’s 2021 extension stands as a pivotal moment. The line extends from there through Brunson’s arrival, the Towns trade, and the hanging of the banner (coming soon!). Randle is back in New York these days, about to start a season with the Brooklyn Nets. If you see him around the city, give him a nod and show some respect. The championship we are celebrating now might not have happened without him.

item.content:encoded: Manchester United’s under-powered attack, Brentford’s £39m bargain and Dewsbury-Hall delivers for EvertonArsenal’s treatment of Gabriel Martinelli has been questioned by Ian Wright after the Brazil forward was left out of their squad for Friday’s opening game against Coventry. Martinelli turned down a move to Galatasaray last week after Arsenal had agreed a fee with the Turkish club and the former striker Wright revealed on Sky Sports after the Coventry game that no one at the club has spoken to the 25-year-old to discuss his future. “I know they might want him out, and a lot of people might say: ‘Yeah, it’s time for him to move him on.’ But there’s ways of doing that and it should suit him as well, how he wants to leave,” said Wright. “He’s done enough with this squad to be treated with a little bit more respect than he’s being treated with at the moment.” Continue reading...

item.title: Hull punished United defence in victory but Carrick’s attack is bigger area of concern | Andrew Beasley
item.author: Andrew Beasley
item.content:encoded: Manchester United again struggled against a back five as the promoted hosts exploited a set-piece weaknessHull scored nine league goals from set plays last season, the joint-fewest in the Championship. Yet two in 21 minutes earned them a victory over Manchester United on Saturday.It was a disastrous start to the campaign for the visitors. While Michael Carrick said before the game it would not be easy, he would not have expected victory being so straightforward for Hull. It was a match United simply had to win given the gulf in resources and expectation. Opta rated their chance of victory at 68.9% before kick-off.Continue reading...

item.author: Will Unwin at the MKM Stadium
item.content:encoded: Bruno Fernandes: ‘We gave too much of the ball to them’Sergej Jakirovic happy Hull proved critics wrongMichael Carrick says he will not overreact, but has called for improvement after Manchester United started the season with a 2-0 defeat at Hull. United lost their opening game for the fourth time in the past seven years as Semi Ajayi and Nobel Mendy took advantage of poor defending from set-pieces.The United head coach presented a professional exterior despite United’s performance not reaching the desired standard as they were deservedly beaten by Hull, who finished sixth in the Championship last season.Continue reading...
